view of the minister's statement on July 27 giving the cost of salaries in the Lethbridge income tax office as $15,620 for 1951 and $17,060 for 1952, has the minister in reading the Holberton letter, a copy of which I put into his hands on August 7, noted that Mr. Holberton positively states that the staff in the Lethbridge office during 1951 and 1952 consisted of only one man and a stenographer? Will the minister tell the house how his informant arrived at the impressive salary costs which the minister gave the house on July 27 in relation to the upkeep of the Lethbridge income tax office, namely $15,620 and $17,060?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did receive a letter from the gentleman mentioned and also a copy of that letter from the hon. member for Lethbridge. I see no reason why the matter should promote any controversy at all. I prefer to take the statements of my officials rather than those of an ex-employee of some five or six years ago who has made some contradiction with reference to the accuracy of the reported costs of that particular office. The matter of costs is not at issue; the matter at issue is whether or not the course we have taken of closing the office at Lethbridge is in the best interests not only of the department from an economic point of view but of the taxpayers of southern Alberta, whom we feel will get much better service by dealing with the Calgary office rather than with a suboffice at Lethbridge at which there are but three employees who were not in position to give the type of service we want to give.

No one can express facts any better than the minister has in his recent statement, but that is exactly what we are concerned about. I am asking whether the minister's statement which he gave to the house on July 27 was accurate, and that is also an equally important matter.

To the best of my knowledge the statement is accurate to a nickel. I prefer to take the statement of my officials rather than that of someone who is more or less disgruntled and who was an employee five years ago.

May I ask the minister if he is certain he can rely on the men who prepared the statement given to him?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of the news report over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation this morning that the United Kingdom is reducing her NATO forces in Europe due to the Suez canal crisis by perhaps as much as a division, can the Prime Minister tell the house what effect this will have on Canada's military commitments to NATO?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED REDUCTION IN UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext: The news report over the radio may be accurate, but we have not yet received any official information from the United Kingdom that they do intend to reduce their forces in Europe. We prefer to wait until we get official information before we attempt to assess what effect it may have on the forces of the North Atlantic alliance.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED REDUCTION IN UNITED KINGDOM FORCES
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Does the Prime Minister not consider that this proposed reduction in NATO's forces is a serious threat to NATO's present military effectiveness?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some three or four weeks ago I spoke at some length about the Canadian trade position, and I do not intend at this time to repeat what I said on that occasion.
Very briefly, our trade is thriving. Exports are at remarkably high levels. Imports continue to pour in to meet the demands generated by our rapid development and prosperity which cannot be satisfied within Canada. As I said before, the resulting deficit on current account is a sign not of weakness but of strength, since it results primarily from developments which strengthen the economic fabric of the country and which will in the future increase exports and reduce imports.
On this occasion I should like to discuss not the figures of trade but the efforts which Canada has made and has participated in

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to maintain our markets abroad and to provide new opportunities for greater trade.
First, a word about the Canadian foreign trade service. During the past year a new office was opened in Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia, bringing to 54 the number of our trade offices located at strategic centres abroad, which compares with a total of 31 only ten years ago. Our files show that in 1955 the 112 trade commissioners who manned these posts played a direct part in bringing to Canada more than $100 million worth of new business. Periodic conferences of trade commissioners are held, such as the recent one held in Ottawa of our officers stationed in Latin America, at which representatives of Canadian industry were present and participated in a valuable exchange of views.
The foreign trade service carries out a continuous review of world markets to determine where our trade interests would benefit through having a resident trade commissioner. This year consideration is being given to the opening of new trade offices in Hamburg, Colombo, Los Angeles and Teheran. To meet the service's growing personnel needs we are seeking to recruit men of the highest caliber, men who are interested in serving Canada in what, to my mind, is one of the most interesting and rewarding careers of government service.
As I indicated a year ago when the decision was made to bring the Canadian international trade fair to an end, greater emphasis is being placed on participation in overseas trade fairs. We are doing everything possible to bring Canadian goods to the attention of the buyer in his own country.
In the course of the current year the Department of Trade and Commerce has prepared major exhibits for ten international trade fairs abroad. The fairs at Utrecht, Osaka, Milan, Brussels and Hanover have already taken place. Later this year we shall be exhibiting at the fairs in Lausanne, Manchester, London, Paris and Bogota. Smaller exhibits were arranged at a nutrition fair in Havana and a food show in Los Angeles, and we shall assist our footwear manufacturers at an industry show in Chicago in October.
In addition to participation at these international fairs and industry shows, we have continued to operate our Canadian showroom in Rockefeller Centre in New York. This "sales laboratory on Fifth avenue" as it has been termed, is enabling some of our manufacturers to test and enter the valuable New York market with their products.
I turn now to Canada's part in trade negotiations, in other words to the efforts being
made to improve the opportunities for trade upon which Canadian prosperity so largely depends. Canada is the fourth largest trading nation and her share of world trade has increased. Our present economic well-being and our continued expansion depends on high levels of trade.
It is for these reasons that Canada has continued to play a leading part in the constructive work of international co-operation under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. As a result of the four rounds of world tariff negotiations held under GATT, tariff levels have been significantly reduced over a very wide area of world trade. We have enjoyed a degree of world tariff security and stability never known before. Canada has taken part in each of the tariff conferences held under GATT, and we have obtained tariff concessions of value to our exporters in every region of Canada and affecting all our major exports in almost every important market.
The United States is by far the largest market for Canadian exports. I am happy to say that our exports to the United States increased by $142 million in the first six months of 1956 in comparison with the first six months of 1955. At present over one-half of our exports to the United States enter that country free of duty. This includes many of our major exports. Of the dutiable goods, over two-thirds now enter at United States rates of duty equivalent to about 10 per cent ad valorem or less. Many of our products enter the United States at tariff levels which had been reduced prior to this year to one-half or less of the levels prevailing before GATT, and to less than one-quarter of the rates in effect in the 1930's.
Here are some examples of Canadian exports on which the United States tariff has been significantly reduced over the years: the United States tariff on apples which was 25 cents a bushel in the 1930's has been reduced to 124 cents a bushel; the United States tariff on birch plywood which was 50 per cent in the 1930's has been progressively reduced to 15 per cent; the duty on a wide range of electrical goods has been reduced from 35 per cent in 1930 to less than 15 per cent; the duty on aluminum was 4 cents a pound in 1930 and will be reduced to 1J cents a pound in the near future; on a wide range of iron and steel manufactures the United States tariff has been cut from 45 per cent before GATT to 19 per cent in the most recent negotiations; on synthetic rubber the duty before GATT was 20 per cent and will shortly be reduced to 84 per cent; the duty on a large variety of chemicals has been reduced in GATT negotiations from 25 per cent to 104 per cent.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
In our relations with the United States we are, of course, most vitally concerned not only with the tariff levels affecting our goods but even more with the direction of United States tariff and trade policies generally. Without wishing in any way to minimize the threats created by United States restrictive action, it is of interest to note that only in two cases has the United States actually withdrawn concessions negotiated with Canada under GATT. Since 1948, of the 57 investigations completed by the United States tariff commission to determine whether imports were causing injury to United States producers, only seven resulted in action by the United States President to increase the tariff, and of these only one case affected Canadian trade. With reference to United States import restrictions upon certain agricultural products, there have been no new developments to report in the past year. We are extremely gratified that the President has recently given approval to the customs simplification act which has been under consideration for a long time. While this act does not go as far as we had originally hoped, it promises to be a real step ahead in the solution of some of our customs valuation difficulties in the United States.
The government has likewise continued at all times to promote the expansion of trade with the United Kingdom in both directions. In so far as the tariff is concerned, Canadian goods enter the United Kingdom either free of duty or at low preferential rates. Similarly, we provide preferential tariff treatment for most United Kingdom exports to Canada. Over the past few years United Kingdom import restrictions have also been considerably relaxed, and most basic foodstuffs and industrial materials, including about 80 per cent of our current exports to the United Kingdom, are now free of all import controls.
One of the most significant features of our trade with the United Kingdom was the sharp rise of Canadian exports to that country. Our exports rose by $116 million above the levels of 1954 to reach a record level of $769 million last year. We are fully aware that the United Kingdom market will be opened up to our goods in direct measure to the success achieved by the United Kingdom in sales to Canada and other countries. In this connection I am happy to note that in the first six months of this year United Kingdom exports to Canada have increased by 30 per cent to record levels and that this appears to be a continuing trend.
Our exports to our commonwealth partners other than the United Kingdom increased in 1955 by $42 million. This increase, which

is being maintained this year, was made possible by extensive relaxations in import restrictions which have taken place in commonwealth countries in recent years. Last month the Australian government announced a tightening up of import restrictions to protect its balance of payments. I am pleased to be able to inform the house that this intensification is apparently not intended to apply to products imported from Canada. We are hopeful, therefore, that we will fully maintain our markets in Australia.
In South Africa further relaxations of import restrictions, particularly on manufactured goods, were introduced to take effect this year. For the last two and a half years these controls have been non-discriminatory. In New Zealand about 150 products or groups of products may now be imported without restriction from Canada. Among these are such products as agricultural machinery, tobacco, textiles, paper products, metal products and a considerable variety of manufactured goods. In the new federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland 500 additional items were removed from import restrictions early this year. These products may now be imported freely from Canada. Hon. members will recall that last month I announced in the house that further products had been removed from import restriction in the British West Indies.
Our sales to European markets have constantly risen in proportion with our growing total export trade, and Europe has retained her traditional position as our third largest trading area, taking about 9 per cent of our exports, the same proportion as pre-war. Last year our exports to Europe rose by $40 million over 1954 to a total of $390 million. In the first five months of this year Canadian exports to Europe increased again by $54 million.
It has been most gratifying to see the significant progress that has been made in the United Kingdom, in other commonwealth countries and in Europe in the dismantling of import restrictions originally imposed for balance of payments reasons. The United Kingdom and other countries that had found it necessary to impose dollar restrictions themselves recognize that their export industries must become fully competitive in world markets. Any other course would breed high costs and inefficiency, and would multiply rather than resolve their basic economic problems.
I now wish to refer briefly to the government's trade agreement program in recent years. Canada now maintains most favoured nation trade relations with almost every country in the world, either through separate trade

treaties or through our participation in GATT. We have paid particular attention to establishing a sound basis for the development of trade with the countries of Latin America. We now have most favoured nations relations with every country in that area.
The trend of our exports to Latin American countries has, however, been disappointing in some respects. The statistical totals are well below the peak level which was achieved in 1952. There were exceptional circumstances, however, such as the high level of wheat sales and the aftermath of the Korean war which accounted for that peak, and it is not too difficult to see why our exports have fallen since then. From a longer point of view, our exports to Latin America are running at a rate which is ten times the level pre-war, say of 1938.
In 1954 Canada concluded a trade agreement with Japan, a country which had become our third largest market. As a result of this agreement Japan removed all discriminatory restrictions on the importation of wheat, barley, flax seed, wood pulp and certain other Canadian products. Our trade with Japan has continued at high levels and is directly contributing to the prosperity of many Canadian industries.
The trade agreements negotiated with Spain and Portugal in 1954 have placed our relations with those countries on a more assured basis and have created, for the first time since the war, continuing opportunities to sell Canadian salt fish in those traditional areas.
On February 29 of this year I announced the conclusion of a trade agreement between Canada and the Soviet union designed to provide a new and important market for Canadian wheat, and which may also create new opportunities for the export of other Canadian products.
To summarize, Mr. Chairman, we are pursuing an active and successful export promotion policy designed to strengthen the Canadian economy and to create favourable conditions for continued growth in the future. We wish to live in a world where Canada has fair and equal access to world markets, where the countries who need our goods can buy from us freely and we in turn can buy from whatever markets are in the best position to supply our import requirements. This, we believe, is the only kind of a trading world that makes sense in the long run for any country dependent on trade, and this is the only kind of trading world in which Canada can fully develop her resources and her industries on a sound competitive basis. Canada's interests can best be served through continued policies of multilateral trade.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, the Department of Trade and Commerce this year asks approval of estimates totalling $24,226,785, which is an increase of $4,859,715 over last year's approved estimates of $19,367,000. As compared with this last figure of approved estimates for the fiscal year 1955-56 the actual expenditures of this department in the fiscal year ended last March 31 were $17,653,459, indicating that the house voted 9 per cent more than the department found it necessary to spend. The increase in this year's estimates over last year's actual expenditure is therefore $6,573,326, or 37 per cent more than the department found it necessary to expend last year.
There are two items in particular in this year's estimates which have been enlarged; they are item No. 423, for the Brussels exhibition, and item No. 429 for the census.
It is usual on this first item to have a general policy debate, and because trade and commerce covers such a wide range of governmental activity and policy usually the debate has ranged widely. This year I think without loss of any profitable discussion the debate can perhaps be somewhat abridged by reason of some recent debates which have been held in this house. I refer in particular to four debates.
The first was the debate on April 18 on the resolution to ratify the trade agreement with Russia. The second was on July 9 and 10 on our Conservative amendment to the supply motion, which amendment set forth our national development policy. That debate embraced our views on trade quite extensively. The third debate was that of August 1, during the review of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs when, as reported at page 6811 of Hansard, we had the opportunity to renew the plea of this party that the government call a commonwealth conference on trade and economic questions. The fourth debate was on August 6 on the resolution to approve the international wheat agreement, during which the whole subject of wheat marketing was extensively debated.
The importance of trade to the world and to Canada has been emphasized by all that has happened since a year ago, when the house debated the estimates of this same department. We are aware that Russia has turned from the cold war to an economic struggle for world mastery. Mr. Khrushchev is reported as having stated to some Americans visiting Russia last autumn:
We value trade least for economic reasons, and most for political purposes.
While Canada has always valued trade for economic purposes, we cannot close our eyes

Supply-Trade and Commerce to the importance that trade holds in a political sense in the kind of world in which we live. We are therefore glad that in 1955 a new record was established in the value of world trade, and that Canada retained fourth place among the trading nations of the world in terms of value, ranking after only the United States, the United Kingdom and the Federal Republic of Germany. On a per capita basis in 1955 Canada ranked second only to New Zealand among the trading countries of the world.
I have a few remarks to make on the subject of total trade. The annual report of the department indicates on page 15 that Canada's total commodity exports in 1955 rose from $3,947 million in 1954 to $4,351 million, an increase of 10-2 per cent. The increase in imports, however, is much more striking, these having risen from $4,093 million in 1954 to $4,712 million in 1955, an increase of 15-1 per cent. In 1955 for the third successive year Canada incurred what is called nowadays a deficit balance on commodity trade. The excess of Canadian purchases over Canadian sales last year was $360 million.
The figures for the first six months of 1956 are perhaps even more striking. Due to the increase in our exports of wheat our total exports rose from $2,063 million in the first six months of 1955 to $2,304 million in the same period of 1956, an increase of 14 per cent. Again our imports have risen in a much more significant degree, from the 1955 total for the first six months of $2,209 million to $2,831 million for the first six months of 1956, an increase of approximately 30 per cent. With this substantial increase in imports has come a remarkable increase in our total trade deficit. During these six months Canada purchased abroad $537,500,000 more than she sold abroad. This is a record total commodity trade deficit.
I have a word to say about the direction of Canada's trade. We have drawn attention repeatedly in the past to the concentration of Canada's trade in one channel. This has been described as placing Canada's trading eggs in one basket, namely the United States. We have drawn attention to the peril of increasing this concentration in one channel, as it makes Canada's external trade position very vulnerable to changes in the trading policies of our friendly neighbour to the south. On page 16 of the annual report of the department for 1955 hon. members can see the figures on trade with certain countries.
