speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Give it to the provinces.
And to the public.

Is there a penalty attached if the truck-owner or driver does not comply with this request for information?
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would think not, probably. I do not think the individual truck drivers would fill out these forms. I think they will be filled out by the trucking companies. If a large trucking company refuses to comply with a request from the dominion bureau of statistics the owner may hear from them. I imagine he would because there is the Statistics Act in existence in this country which provides certain penalties.

That is exactly what I am coming to. The minister says there is the act and if the form is sent out and the man does not comply by filling it out he will hear about it pretty soon. I can confirm this and I know what I am talking about because I have been a victim of this sort of thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: One should always comply with the law.

Yes. A form came to me as a processor and packer. Having had a crop failure that year I did not fill it out. Pretty soon I received a letter, and then another, and finally a registered letter. I informed the writer to come to my office in the parliament buildings to discuss the matter and I have not heard about it since.

Mr. Chairman, I simply wish to clarify one point. In relation to these reports requested from the truckers I think the minister ought to make it clear that this is a particular survey and it is not intended that this should be a continuing form of return required to be made by those operating trucks.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, that is the case.

I want to ask a few brief questions regarding the availability of some figures I have not been able to obtain. The first set of figures concerns our wheat shipments to Poland. In this case it may just be necessary for the minister to say why the figures are not available. I do not care whether or not I receive the figures now but I would like to know why they are not available. I am interested in the figure for the total amount of wheat in bushels rather than the total amount of wheat expressed in dollars. I would also like to know the places where the wheat was bought from the wheat board; that is, whether the quantities were shipped through Prince Rupert or Vancouver, and so forth. I would also like to know the cost of the wheat to the Manitoba Northern Sales, the amount of export credit insurance payable by the shipper, the amount of interest paid or payable to the federal government for these moneys that have been advanced, and
7310	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce then I also want to know the dates of the shipments, and the names of the ships.
If the minister does not have this answer readily available perhaps he will tell me why the information is not available, and if I might expect it at some future date.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This is a case
which is sub judice. My hon. friend is trying to help out some of his lawyer friends. Such facts as are available are published by the dominion bureau of statistics. My hon. friend is well aware of that. This is a private row and he had better let the boys do the best they can and I will do the same.

That is all right. I just wanted to know why the information is not available.
I want to ask again this year if it is still not possible to obtain monthly figures of the exports of Canadian goods through Canadian ports and United States ports? Those have never been made available on a monthly basis in the same way that the imports are made available and I would like to know why it is not possible without too much extra effort to obtain monthly figures for exports similar to those which we obtain for imports.
I might say we are vitally concerned with these figures and in this way we would have a comparison by the month. Without these figures we will be unable to ascertain what progress is being made to eliminate the sad injustice which is in existence in Canadian ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I presume the reason is that the United States figures come from authorities in that country.
I understand it is a matter of delay in receiving the United States figures and I do not know of any other reason. Of course, at the year-end my hon. friend has no trouble in obtaining them because all those reports are published by the bureau of statistics. It seems to be a matter of delay in getting the information to the United States authorities which prevents the monthly statements coming out.

That may be true. The department compiles records of imports coming into Canada through Canadian and United States ports and I presume that in one case the figures would be United States and in the other they would be our own, or would they both be United States figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have complete figures with regard to imports, this would be Canadian information.
When those are available, why cannot they be obtained for exports?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Our customs
authorities are not interested in exports. The customs department gets no percentage out of exports. The customs are interested in imports but not in exports.

I realize that, but I suggest that it would not be much trouble. Surely there is some kind of check on goods going out of this country. If you can compile them on a yearly basis it should not be too much trouble to compile them on a monthly basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have no one here really to advise me on that problem but I shall look into it. If it is possible to improve the situation I shall be glad to do it.

Item agreed to.
429. Census, including a contribution as detailed in the estimates, the expenditure for which not to exceed the amount shown unless otherwise approved by treasury board, $4,710,429.

Mr. Chairman, I think the committee would be interested to have a report from the minister with reference to the census, particularly as there has been a large increase in the appropriation this year for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The census has been completed except for the compilation of the figures, and I understand it went off very smoothly and successfully. We hope to have the figures all complete by early next year, but some will be complete before the end of this year. The census was carried on from coast to coast and we were able to effect some economies as my hon. friend will note if he compares the expenditures. We were able to save about $200,000 of last year's appropriation. For instance, the statistics had always been taken down by pens supplied by the government at a cost of $3.59 each, and this year we did it with pencils at a cost of 29 cents each. Also we were able to use less expensive stationery and varitype printing instead of the usual type. There has been a great deal of progress in cutting down the cost of the census work which of course is a gain for the future.
May I ask if it is intended to turn out as many volumes containing extensive analyses as were turned out recently in connection with the decennial census?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This is a skeleton census and the information obtained is skeleton in character.
How many volumes will there be?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: One.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The census is taken on punch cards and the registration is by age groups. I suppose the highest age group on the card is 90 to 100, and whether it would be wise to add another age group to cover those 100 to 110 years of age would have to be considered. I saw where someone died the other day who was 110 years of age. I am getting on myself but I think I can get along with the present card.
Then I take it that what I have asserted is in fact true. Is there any record of people in Canada who have reached the ripe age of 100 years?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sure the dicennial census will show that. This is a skeleton census which does not go into detail.
I should like to ask about the number of questions asked agricultural producers as compared with those asked other people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The five-year census was originally an agricultural census which was mandatory in the prairie provinces. We extended that census to all the provinces. The answer to my hon. friend's question is that the agricultural census is a complete census whereas the census of everything else is a skeleton census.

It seems to me that when you ask farmers 75 questions and receive such a small part of the national income you are leading them to believe you are going to do something about it. I know very well that the government has no intention of doing anything, but it just seemed to me to be out of proportion to ask these people 75 questions when the ordinary householder is asked only seven.
Mr. Pallet!: Am I correct in understanding that the census figures will be ready for distribution before December 31, 1956?
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Certain figures are essential to certain provinces and we have to get them out before the end of the year. I know in Manitoba they have a problem and they are anxious to get some figures. The complete census information will not be out until some time next spring.
Will the census as it applies to the prairie provinces be used in connection with the redistribution next year in the western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a statutory provision; the constitution provides that in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta there must be an agricultural census taken every five years. The census was taken to meet the constitutional requirement as far as those three provinces were concerned, but it is less detailed in the rest of Canada.
Is it the intention that it will be used for the purposes of redistribution in the prairie provinces next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We give the statistics to the provinces as we are required by law to do and what they do with them is up to them.

Item agreed to.
Board of grain commissioners (Canada Grain Act) -
430. Administration, $149,780.

I believe the minister asked that we discuss any items dealing with grain under this item. I want to protest the move that has been made to refuse to license any further off-site storage. The practice that has been followed during the past year of licensing, for the storage of grain, buildings away from the elevator site, provided that they came up to certain standards, is one of the best policies that has yet been devised for storing and handling surplus grain.
Many communities have constructed large buildings of the Quonsett type that could be used at a future date as rinks in their respective communities, and this action has had a great many advantages. It has provided a building that will have a great value to the community over the years, whether as a building for the storage of grain or as a building to provide recreational facilities when we enter a period of no congestion.
Moreover, the provision of additional facilities by this means for the storage of grain has allowed farmers to market their grain and to obtain the initial payment when their grain has been marketed. We in this group for many years have advocated the payment of farm storage and the payment of cash advances, and the government has refused

Supply-Trade and Commerce both. But when the government did two things, allowed off-site storage in the form of rinks to be licensed for the storing of grain and provided that the federal treasury would pay the storage costs for wheat in excess of 178 million bushels, it went a substantial way to providing both storage payments for the community and advance payments for the farmer. This has been a method by which communities themselves are able to obtain part of the payments made for storage.
I can see no good reason at all why rinks will no longer be licensed for the storage of grain. There have been two arguments against the policy. One is that they say that the buildings have to come up to standard. Of course, no matter where a building is located, it can be built to any standard that the builders may desire. Some of these buildings in the form of rinks, I am convinced, are the very best storage that has yet been provided for large quantities of grain, and I am sure that the grain in these buildings will come out in many instances in better condition than grain in the so-called annexes built alongside the railway site.
The second argument is that the grain is not readily available. Of course, that argument will not stand up, because these storage facilities are within a very short distance of the elevator that has leased them, and it is just a matter of putting the grain in the truck and taking perhaps two minutes to drive the truck from the storage building into the elevator and dump the grain. So the grain is just as readily available as though it were in the so-called permanent annex.
There is no difficulty in putting the grain into the storage facilities. I was at a marketing point in western Canada a few weeks ago -Drinkwater, Saskatchewan-and I noted that they had built there a modest-sized rink in which they were storing 80,000 bushels of grain. According to the farmers who built the rink and according to the elevator agent, the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners had informed them that it was one of the best buildings that had yet been constructed for the purpose of storing grain. It cost the elevator company nothing to put the grain in, because the farmers drove into the elevator, had their loads weighed and dumped, and had the empty truck weighed. Then the spout was opened and the grain loaded back into the trucks. The farmers drove across the street and themselves unloaded the grain into the very large rink building that they themselves had built.
I hope that the government will reconsider this policy. There is only one possible reason

I can think of for discontinuance at this time, the only one that I should think has any logic to it at all, and that is that it may have been decided to discontinue further licensing of such buildings until the size of the new crop is known. If that is the case, I have no objection. I shall have no objection if the policy is reversed, should we harvest the very large crop that is now in evidence in western Canada.
So I should like to ask the minister whether or not the government will reconsider its policy in this connection within the next month or two when we find out the size of the crop and, if so, whether or not grain in such buildings will be entitled to the regular storage payments.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The government adopted the policy of off-site storage on the recommendation of the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners. In view of the congestion on the prairies, it seemed the right thing to do. The government reconsidered the matter, on the recommendation of the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners that the time had come to issue no new licences for off-site storage. The reasonableness of the position has more or less been confirmed by the fact that we had 35 million bushels less wheat in storage at the end of the last crop year than we had at the end of the previous crop year; and also in view of the fact that there was very much more empty storage on the prairies this year than a year ago, there does not seem to be any reason to encourage new construction to house wheat when there seems to be plenty of space available to do the job. If the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners change their minds and suggest that we need more offsite storage, I daresay that the government will consider it, but at the moment we have no intention of altering the decision which was announced some time ago.

With regard to the extra storage space that is available, I think the minister knows that the storage that is available is only at certain points and that there are hundreds and hundreds of marketing points in western Canada where there is little storage available and where the provision of such additional facilities would be valuable. I shall be quite content to end this discussion, as far as I am concerned, if the minister will say that he will take another look at the situation in October, after harvest, to see whether or not there may be some real need for reversing the policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will say that 1 shall do so if I am asked to do so by the wheat board or the board of grain commissioners.

There is one other question in connection with this. I know of two or three rinks that are being used for storage purposes. Are the towns that operate or own these rinks receiving anything in respect of storage? The other day I was reading of one in my former constituency of Lake Centre where there was a very large storage in the rink, and it was said that the return that was being received for storage payments would be sufficient in a matter of two or three years, if continued, to pay for the actual cost of the rink. Is that storage being paid officially or is it a local matter whereby payment is being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I expect some day to get trophies from both the curling associations and the skating rink associations of the prairies. I believe more rinks have been built to store grain in the past three years than have been built in the prairies ever since the first settler arrived. The storage is paid under an arrangement with one of the line elevator companies, which is responsible to the wheat board and has authority to move that grain into offsite storage, which is the rink, and pay the owner of the rink a fee out of his receipt for storage which is supposed to be onsite storage. It is a legalized arrangement, but the offsite storage arrangement is made between the line elevator company and the owners of the offsite storage.
That rather answers the question that my hon. friend raised, that sometimes the objection to the licensing of rinks is that the rinks are not up to standard.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

The fact that by an indirect means there is achieved that which he suggests might be done directly and which I support would indicate that there should be a reconsideration of this problem in the event that again this fall as the result of a large crop tremendous amounts of wheat will have to be stored on the farms. If this arrangement can be operated in certain areas by this indirect means, I see no reason why it should not be considered as a direct means of storage. It would mean that during the period from May until the end of the crop year on the 31st of July a very considerable amount of wheat could be stored in that manner and made available whenever the necessary transport could be secured at the several marketing places.

The minister has said that he is probably entitled to trophies from the curling and skating rink associations of western Canada for the fact that there have been so many rinks built in the last three
7313
Supply-Trade and Commerce years. Perhaps that is a good suggestion but I think there should be a rider to it that the minister will continue the policy so that there will not be any discrimination as between communities.
The minister said one thing that I do not think he intended to say, namely, that these arrangements are made between line elevator companies and community associations. I think the minister knows that the wheat pool organizations as well as the line elevator companies, all elevator companies, have been prepared to consider such arrangements. In some communities in my constituency the line elevators have leased the premises and at other points the pool elevators have done so. I think that generally speaking the arrangement is approximately the same. The elevator company gets 10J cents per bushel per year and the local rink association gets 6 cents of the 10J.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I should amend the term "line elevator" to "line of elevators". I apologize to that extent.

I should like to ask the question now that I wanted to ask on the first item with regard to storage in eastern Ontario and eastern Canada. I refer particularly to southern Ontario. Because of the cold and late spring this year the farmers found that they had to feed their stock for a longer period of time than usual. The winter stored grain in the elevators in southern Ontario apparently had been depleted and the farmers had to pay the entire rail freight on their grain from the west. That put the price up almost to a prohibitive figure.
I am wondering whether some steps should be taken to move more grain into southern Ontario during the period when navigation is open so that the same situation will not prevail next spring. It could prevail because on account of the late, cold spring not as much acreage of grain was sown in southern Ontario as in other years. There is every indication that next spring there will be another shortage of feed and more feed will be required.
A question was asked the other day by the hon. member for Mackenzie in the same connection arising out of a telegram sent to the minister with regard to the scarcity of feed grain even at the present time in southern Ontario and the trouble some of the merchants are having in obtaining feed grain, probably as a result of the shortage of box cars and other things. They are having trouble continually in getting sufficient feed grain from the elevators. Can the minister give any indication as to what the department can do with respect to moving more feed grain into eastern storage in the fall?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The department has nothing to do with feed grain in Ontario.
I have tried to make that clear. We have no authority to do anything. We have gone a long way to make it possible for dealers or whoever wishes coarse grains in Ontario to buy them. We have arranged an agency basis so that the buyer can take the grain, make a deposit on it and adjust the price as of any date he wishes. That is quite a concession. But the grain will always be available at Fort William. If arrangements can be made to have the grain available at the bay ports we will do so but the grain there moves into export and it is very hard, especially in the season of open navigation, to make it available to buyers. Certainly users in Ontario have been forewarned as to their requirements and if they do not take care of them some time between now and the close of navigation I hope they will not blame me for their failure to do so. We just have nothing to do with the distribution of grain in Ontario.

There is one other feature of the storage problem that in my opinion requires attention and that is the matter of terminal storage. Canada's capacity to produce grain is going up every year and the figures for the long term average have to be revised every year; 1956 appears to be another year when we are going to have a big crop.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If my hon. friend reads the bible he knows about the seven fat years and the seven lean years, so let us not get the averages too far out of line.
No, but if we are going to have fat years and prepare for the lean years we will have to have somewhere to store the grain.
As far as the farmers are concerned they are all lean.

At any rate, the experience of the farmer in the past few years has been that he has found himself in very difficult circumstances through being unable to deliver his grain. The minister knows the difficulty the farmers had last year with regard to cash advances and farm storage, and the loss of grain on the prairies has been a most regrettable thing. When you find wheat piled up in large piles in the fields and exposed to the weather you know that losses are almost inevitable.
We have a problem with respect to terminal storage for grain. Surely the best place to put the grain is in the terminals where it is available for export. Canada's terminal storage has not increased with Canada's ability to produce. Because of the fact of sales

being lower than they were three years ago and the continuation of large crops the storage problem is one of increasing difficulty.
Then there is the matter of box cars. When the railway companies haul grain in their box cars to the terminals they find all too often that there is no space in which to dump the grain and the latest move, which is causing a great deal of concern among western growers, is that the railway companies are now applying to the board of transport commissioners for permission to charge demurrage on cars that are left for any more than 48 hours at terminal points. This means an additional and rather heavy expense which will fall directly on the backs of the producers who are already facing difficult times with increasing costs and decreasing returns.
I suggest to the minister, the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners that it is time that Canada took a look at the terminal storage problem and made provision for the storage of our surplus grain. As a national problem surely the weight of it should not be borne entirely by the farmer. It is surely not good business to leave grain stored in box cars and have demurrage charged that will have to be paid by the farmer. I suggest to the minister that a continuation of the present condition of lack of space at terminal elevators to unload box cars is going to lead to the producers having to pay heavy demurrage charges, and they are going to feel very badly about it and resentful that action has not been taken to take care of this surplus commodity. As to the "seven fat years", we are enjoying that period as far as production is concerned, but they certainly have not brought a great deal of increased well-being to the producer. His problems today are increasing. His costs are increasing. With a declining income, this is a serious problem. I hope that the board of grain commissioners will advocate the construction of more elevator space. Already the government is in the elevator storage business. I believe they rent elevator storage space at the present time. I believe the leases for them are due to expire this year. I hope this suggestion will be looked upon with some favour. I refer to the suggestion that the government consider the building of more storage space in order to do away with the vexing problem which is increasing year by year.

There is a question I should like to ask the minister about the personnel of the board of grain commissioners. I believe there soon will be a vacancy on the board if there is not technically a vacancy now. When the minister is considering appointing a person to fill that vacancy, I wonder

whether he will not discuss with the farm organizations-I refer to both the farmers union and the grain organizations-the question of a person that would be satisfactory to both. I know it is the minister's prerogative to appoint to the board anyone he cares to appoint. But I think it would be better and would lead to easier administration if the minister would discuss with the main farm organizations the question of the person to be appointed. I do not really feel that there would be any difficulty in coming to an agreement and recommending a given person. I do not think such a move would lead to any controversy.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The vacancy has not occurred as yet. When it occurs, we shall be glad to keep my hon. friend's views in mind. We usually get the views of the interested grain co-operatives. That has been the case on every occasion, I believe. We get names from each of them and we pick out the man we think is best qualified to do the job. We shall doubtless do that again. The only appointment I have heard was announced in the agriculture committee. My hon. friend appointed a new chairman for the board. That is causing me some embarrassment. However, I will not embarrass him now by suggesting a man for the board.

When I was appointing a new member of the board, I did not realize that it would cause any embarrassment. As to the information that I had when I was making my so-called appointment, I consider that I obtained it on the highest authority and it was not told to me in confidence. Mr. Chairman, these items on atomic energy do not require a great deal
Supply-Atomic Energy of discussion in view of the fact that a special committee of the house has been dealing during the present session with the activities of the government in the fields of research and of atomic energy. I had asked for the setting up of such a committee on several occasions; last session, again this session and also, I think, in 1954. As hon. members know, this committee was set up during the present session. I think it would have been wiser to have the committee deal exclusively either with the national research council and other problems of research or with atomic energy. As the minister will recall, we had some disagreement about that point at the time the motion setting up the committee was under debate. I pointed out then that last year he himself had suggested that there should be separate committees. In the actual working out of matters, that suggestion has proved to be right. This committee has not been able to cover either field adequately and, as a matter of fact, has not yet made a report. There were some hearings during which we heard from officers of the research council. Then there was one trip to the national research council premises. On the atomic energy side we heard from Mr. Bennett an extremely interesting report, and the committee had a trip to Chalk River. But in my opinion the work of that committee was not as effective as it. could have been if we had been dealing only with one subject. I suggest that in future years it would be wise to give any such committee only one of these two extremely important fields to cover.
In the atomic energy field we were all again greatly impressed by what we saw at Chalk River. This was my third trip to Chalk River. I have always believed that the spirit there was a model for any activity in Canada. I have never encountered a higher morale than is to be found there. Certainly magnificent leadership has been given by the men who were responsible for setting up that project and for directing it in the intervening years. It would be a good thing if a great many more Canadians could go there and see just what is being done.
Today I should like the minister to tell us what he expects to be the expense for this atomic energy program, say, for the next five years. The government estimates ahead just what these expenditures will be. When the minister replies, I would ask him to give us those figures. The costs seem to have a way of going up higher than the estimates. For example, we had the case of the new reactor known as the NRU reactor which originally was to cost $30 million- I think that is the correct figure-and which

Supply-Atomic Energy we now find will cost something over $50 million. I think Mr. Bennett told us it would be $52 million or $53 million. I suppose it is difficult to estimate accurately just what the-e costs will be but they seem to get higher as the years go by.
Then, there are three different points in connection with this whole program on which I should like to have an expression from the minister. The first is this. We are now moving into the field of producing power by means of atomic energy. We are about to build a small power reactor in conjunction with Ontario hydro and Canadian General Electric. There will be more of this work done as time goes on. We realize that plans are being laid for the expansion of work of that kind. I am still concerned as to whether the government is determined to spread out these reactors in such a way that they will be of benefit primarily to those parts of the country which are short of other types of power.
This first reactor is to be part of the Ontario hydro electric system. While I realize that Ontario is faced with a possible shortage of power I hope the emphasis is not going to be placed upon providing power by atomic energy for the larger centres of Canada. It seems to me there is not enough drive in the direction of getting this type of power into areas like Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and other parts of Canada where there is not as much other power potential. The tendency seems to be to follow the principle, "he that hath, to him shall be given". This could mean so much in the development of the parts of Canada which are handicapped if the government deliberately adopts a policy that will help them first.
The next point on which I would ask the minister to comment has to do with the production of heavy water. He and I had a little disagreement about that earlier in the session over the question of whether the atomic energy plant at Chalk river used any heavy water produced at Trail. I am not going to go into that further today. The evidence we got in committee made it quite clear that at least some of Canada's heavy water did come from Trail. What I am worried about is this. The plant at Trail was owned by the United States atomic energy commission. This year that production ceased and Canada is no longer producing any heavy water. We are now buying our heavy water from the United States atomic energy plant at Savannah, Georgia, which is the only plant on the North American continent producing this commodity.


The Canadian atomic energy program depends entirely on heavy water. We have gone into that field as distinguished from the use of graphite. Canadian research on atomic power plants is centred on the use of heavy water both as a moderator to control atomic reaction and to keep the reactor cool. We pioneered this field and Canada is the leading nation in the use of heavy water for the production of atomic energy. All the reactors at Chalk River use heavy water and the new power reactor will do the same. The reactor we supply to India will be of the same type. We hope eventually to get into the business of exporting power reactors, all of which will be heavy water reactors. Unless there is some change in government policy the only heavy water available will come from Savannah, Georgia.
I think Canada could be taking steps to get into this business again herself. We have had this experience at Trail and there must be many scientists and engineers who are capable of operating a plant of that kind. It does seem strange that we are just dropping out of that picture. The demands for heavy water in Canada will be extensive. We were told by Mr. Bennett that the NRU reactor would require 66 tons, I think it was, of heavy water. In an economic forecast of the role of nuclear power in Canada made by Dr. Davis of the economics branch of the minister's department and Dr. W. B. Lewis, I find at page 15 some very interesting statements with regard to heavy water. They say this:
The situation with regard to heavy water is something else again. Here, the necessary tonnages may he many times that of the nation's present production capacity.
I realize the production at Trail was comparatively small.
What could, in time, become a sizeable segment of Canada's chemical industry may, therefore, have to be created in order to cater for this large and rapidly expanding demand for this unique material.
Phased in five-year intervals, the cumulative material needs of a recycled natural uranium system might be expected to run somewhat as in table V.

Production of natural uranium for domestic consumption, apparently, would have to run into tens of millions of dollars a year. The third and final point on which I would ask a report is with respect to uranium. I would ask the minister to bring us up to date on that situation. From press reports it appears that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited will be contracting for $1,250 million worth of uranium. That is to say, it has entered into or will be entering into contracts that will aggregate that value when this uranium has all been delivered. That figure is taken from a press dispatch of July 23, 1956. It is, of course, a very large sum and Mr. Bennett was quoted as saying in June that uranium would likely be Canada's top metal in value in future years and he prophesied an approximate production of $300 million per year.
I gained the impression from Mr. Bennett's evidence that once these contracts had been filled there was likely to be quite a drop in the demand for uranium and I think it was based partially on the fact that there would not be such large requirements on the part of the United States for defence purposes. If that is so, it seems to me the effect might well be to discourage prospecting for uranium and its production.
This atomic energy field is opening up so rapidly that I think its importance will be a great deal more vast than any of us realize at the present time and by 1962 the demand for uranium may be a great deal higher than we even dream of now.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It may be a great deal lower, as well.
It may be a great deal lower; that is right. The minister is not often a pessimist.

speechtext: The hon. member was speculating on one side of the question and I was simply speculating on the other, just to show the two sides. I am not taking a position.
I am just wondering about this whole situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am glad he was not positive because we have nothing in the form of a guarantee.
I am not saying that he is right or wrong and I have a great deal of respect for Mr. Bennett and his judgment. I have watched his career with interest for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

I would like the minister to clear up that situation and also to tell us just what will happen to the mining companies that have not been able to get in on these contracts and will not be able to sell the uranium they produce. Is there any provision made for companies of that type? I do not see how this business can be kept going ahead, and yet remain in the hands of a comparatively few companies which have contracts, unless there is some other plan in mind. Perhaps the minister could deal with these points when he replies.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will try to cover the ground that has been outlined by my hon. friend. I believe he wanted a forecast of the cash requirements for Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. To March 31, 1961 it adds up to $115 million. Do you want it year by year?
Yes, please.

For 1957-58 it is $30 million; for 1958-59 it is $20 million; for 1959-60 it is $13 million; for 1960-61 it is $15 million; or a total of $115 million. Supply-Atomic Energy
That is assuming there would be larger revenues than at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, it is the estimated cash drain on the treasury of Canada. For example, these atomic piles do certain commercial work for which they get paid and they sell certain plutonium for which they get paid. We expect the cost to the government of Canada to be as I have outlined it.
Concerning the question about the distribution of generating equipment, it is not the purpose of the government or Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to change the constitutional position of the federal government as regards generating power in various parts of Canada. We have taken responsibility for experimental work at Atomic Energy and we regard it as the duty of the government to keep Canada in the front ranks of progress as far as the development of power from atomic energy is concerned. It was never our intention that the government of Canada would build plants in various parts of the dominion.
The plant now under construction is being built in Ontario because it was possible to make arrangements there which we could not make elsewhere in Canada. The province of Nova Scotia was anxious to have the plant located in that province and the private power company offered certain arrangements there.
It being a small system the difficulty was that we had to give a guarantee; first, as to when the power could be put on the line; second, what the power would cost; and third, I think we had to give a guarantee that the plant would be operating for a certain number of years. We were unable at that stage to give those guarantees. We do not know too much about power generated from atomic energy nor does anybody else.
Ontario said they would pay for the cost of the installation other than the atomic pile part; they would operate the pile and pay for the power and use the power. They required no guarantee as to the future of the development.
This power from the original plant is not going to be cheap power. The plant is too small to be an economical unit and, as I say, it is an experimental plant. The purpose is to test out the process and to gain a great deal of information that would be required for a commercial plant. The reason it is being built in Ontario is that we were able to make much better financial arrangements in that province than we could by building elsewhere.
The work of the power development is under the direction of a group made up of representatives of practically every power 
authority in Canada, whether public or private, and the decisions are taken with the advice of that group. The purpose is to make information available in every part of Canada. We stand ready to give advice on design and scientific work that may help any project, but it is not our intention to build such projects, and push them out into various parts of Canada. We simply act as consultants for whoever wants to go into the business of building atomic power plants.
The second question had to do with heavy water. There is nothing mysterious about heavy water; it is not even classified. There are two or three processes for making it which are well known. Anyone can build a heavy water plant if he wishes to do so. We have a favourable arrangement for the purchase of heavy water. We have always bought it from the United States atomic energy commission. The United States atomic energy commission owned the plant at Trail and we may have received some of that water from Trail, but we never bought it direct. When the atomic energy commission decided that it no longer had use for the Trail plant the commission offered the equipment to us. We tried to make an arrangement with Trail for a price for the product competitive with what we were paying, but were not able to do so. Had we made an arrangement with Trail we would have been paying 25 per cent more for our heavy water than we are paying now under our present arrangement. The price we are paying now is $28 per pound.
In any case the Trail people were not keen to make an arrangement with us, at least they showed no real desire to do so. I had lunch with them once or twice and discussed the matter. However, we decided we would purchase our heavy water in the cheapest market. When you are dealing with a commodity worth $28 a pound, and you need a lot of it, a little difference in the price per pound can go a long way toward $1 million.
In any event I see no particular reason for Canada producing heavy water. If we were not buying it in the United States we might be able to buy it somewhere else. They make it in Norway and in other parts of the world: I do not know whether or not they are about to produce it in New Zealand.
I understand the New Zealand plant has been closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps, because the costs were too high.
Is the minister sure it is being made in Norway?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. The New Zealand project was dropped when they

found they could buy heavy water at $28 a pound. I do not mind going into any business if we must, as a government, but I did not see any reason why this government should go into the heavy water business.
Is it not rather risky to have only one plant on the continent producing heavy water?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Perhaps it is, but the demand for heavy water does not spring up overnight. Even if the plant were damaged it would not take very long to put it back into condition. There is nothing mysterious about heavy water, it is just a commodity the same as anything else.
As to uranium, we have made arrangements with the atomic energy commission of the United States which seem to be quite satisfactory to the mining industry of this country. We have certain contracts with the mining industry which to a large extent have been underwritten by the atomic energy commission of the United States. Those contracts extend to 1962 and provide for the complete write-off of capital expenditures at the mines in the period up to 1962.
The hon. member asks what happens to the mines at the end of 1962. They would have their mine plants all paid for and probably some profit in their pockets. They would be in a position to strike out on their own and we hope they will be able to do so at that time. Through arrangements being completed with the United Kingdom we probably will be able to extend the demand beyond that date to some extent. Certain arrangements have been made with mines which have been late getting into the business which may provide some extension of the present contract. This is a fluctuating situation and involves a terrific amount of money. I would rather not discuss the details at this time. I understand that a good deal of this information was given in the committee and appears in the committee records. I think it would be better if my hon. friend would check that information without asking me to extend myself further.
I do not think any evidence was given as to what would happen after 1962.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend and I need not worry very much. I am simply saying that all the capital cost of the mining plants will be written off by then.
Just those that have contracts?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Everybody has a contract who is in a position to get into production before the deadline. Perhaps there will be youngsters coming along and
Supply-Atomic Energy they may have to do the best they can. But as I say, the underwritten commitments to the mines total well over $1 billion. I think Canada has done pretty well toward getting her uranium mining industry established.

Mr. Chairman, I concur entirely with what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said with regard to the operations at Chalk River. I have had the opportunity to visit there a number of times and have always been impressed with the energy and interest which is being shown there. I was quite interested in the remarks of the minister in connection with the plant near Chalk River for the production of power. I understand that the objective is to provide thermonuclear power plants in different parts of Canada. On page 26 of the evidence given by Mr. Bennett, president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, he gave the following as one of the objectives:
To contribute to the development of economic nuclear power in order that nuclear power may be available for use in Canada in those regions where conventional methods of developing power are no longer economic.
That would seem to indicate that the intention would be to develop power by this means in parts of Canada where power could not be produced economically as hydroelectric power or from coal. Certainly they have more power in Ontario than is available in other parts of Canada; they have more than they have in Saskatchewan, more than they have in the maritime provinces and more than they have in the north country. I had rather hoped that that was the idea, to establish reactors in different parts of Canada like the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend overlooked the words "to contribute".

If this power is to be developed in Ontario it certainly will not contribute to the development of power in other parts of Canada. I will admit that the experimental work being done in Ontario is a contribution to the development of power in other parts of Canada provided reactors are established there, but it will not be if they are not established in other parts of Canada. As a matter of fact, we all know that Canada, in order to assist in developing power in India, for instance, where it is difficult to develop either hydroelectric power or thermal power, is contributing to a reactor in India for this very purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. I should like to correct that statement immediately. It is not a reactor for thermal power; it is a reactor similar to the NRY reactor at Chalk River.

Supply-National Research Council It is designed purely for experimental purposes and is quite a different kind of reactor from the one my hon. friend is talking about.

What we are doing is initiating perhaps one of the first steps for the development of nuclear power in India. As I said a moment ago, I was a little disappointed to hear the minister make the statement that it was not intended to produce or construct reactors in other parts of Canada. He mentioned the fact that it was not cheap power at the present time. We all know that, but we were told when we were at Chalk River that there were great possibilities of its becoming cheap power.
I might ask the minister or the government why they should expend all these millions of dollars for the purpose of investigating the development of nuclear power in Canada if we did not expect at some time to utilize it. I do not think the use of nuclear power is very far away, even here in Canada. I should like to quote from an article I read in an English newspaper not so long ago. It states:
At Calder Hall in Cumberland, it was announced by the atomic energy authority, the first uranium furnace of the nuclear power station had started working.
The actual time was 7:15 p.m., and the actual date May 22.
The pile was charged with slugs of uranium. The control rods were drawn out. A needle began to move on a dial. A red sign lit up-"pile operating". Calder Hall was getting ready for business.
Next the heat transfer system has to be tested. Soon after, the turbines will begin to hum.
Again, the following appeared in the Montreal Star in July. The heading is "Great Atomic Power Plant is Year Ahead of Schedule". It states:
Dounreay plant, the world's most advanced "breeder" station, will produce large amounts of power for the electricity grid.
Because of simplified engineering processes it is now almost certain to be ready by the early part of 1958.
That shows that England-and I might add the United States and other parts of the world-is fast going ahead with the development of atomic power for electrical purposes. I am not going to labour that point any further except to say that I was disappointed with the statement of the minister. Some of the other questions that I intended to ask have already been asked by he hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and so I shall take no more of the committee's time.

National research council-
282. Salaries and other expenses, $15,470,139.

As I mentioned before, when I thought we were dealing with this item instead of the atomic energy item, the committee did go into the work of the national
[Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) .1
research council to some degree but did not make a thorough investigation. We were very much impressed to hear again what is being done by these scientists and engineers. They are making a great contribution to the national life and, I think, deserve the support of the people from coast to coast.
I am not going to go into any details in connection with these votes, other than to bring up one question; that has to do with the numbers of scientists and engineers now available in Canada and who will be available in the years that lie ahead. This question, of course, has been brought to the fore by reports of the great strides made in Russia in the training of engineers and scientists. I do not know whether or not those reports are exaggerated, but in any event they have caused a good deal of concern in the United States and also in Canada. I notice that the very first paragraph of the annual report of the president of the national research council deals with scientific manpower. It reads as follows:
When the National Research Council was founded in 1916, its first move was to survey Canada's resources of scientific manpower. This survey revealed some serious deficiencies. The council immediately undertook two remedial steps:	a
system of scholarships in the natural sciences and of grants-in-aid of university research, and a system of associate committees on a nation-wide basis. Both programs were so successful that they still form an important part of the council's activities.
I am wondering whether the minister thinks the program now being carried out by the national research council is adequate to meet the present-day needs for scientific manpower? This question will also be of interest to the Minister of Labour, but I should like to have the minister's comment on that point. The officers of the research council gave me the impression that they thought the reports from Russia were exaggerated and that Canada's position in this field is not too bad, but I should like to have some assurance from the minister. An ordinary civilian or member of parliament is not in a position to know.
Evidently Russia, the nation with which the free nations are competing, is making some sort of a drive to produce very large numbers of engineers and scientists. Of course, it is difficult for us with our different system of living to do that. We cannot say to this young man that he must be an engineer and to that young man that he must be a scientist. We do not believe in that sort of thing. We have to use persuasive methods. However, I should like to know from the minister whether or not he is. satisfied with the present situation and, if he is not, whether there are any steps

he can suggest that should be taken in order that Canada may train larger numbers of scientists and engineers than she is at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Well, the question is a very difficult one. In a vote where you could use X amount of money, as much as you like, you ask if the $3 J million that we spend at the present time on grants and scholarships is enough. I think that the research council has contributed greatly to bringing up the standard of educational facilities in this country in order to produce as many engineers as we have produced. I believe there are about 50,000 to 55,000 engineers and scientists in the country today and we expect that number to double by about 1965. The present output of the universities will produce about that many by 1965.
I presume as the engineering population of our universities steps up the size of the grant should probably expand. I doubt if the shortage of engineers and scientists in Canada is as acute as it is in some other countries. We are short, certainly. Every engineer and every scientist is certain to have his services in great demand, but I would not say that we could stand a 50 per cent increase in the number of scientists and engineers right away and feel we would not have a surplus. That is only my own estimate after talking with people who seem to have a good deal of information on the subject.
But I think that the national research council is studying the situation carefully year by year. The grants are being stepped up, and I think it is the consensus of university people that a good deal of judgment has been used in working out the system that we have today.
