Mr. Chairman, there are one or two rather controversial matters on which I wish to direct questions to the Prime Minister under the first item in connection with the privy council. As I remember the situation in the past, this item allows the house to ask the Prime Minister certain 67509-465J
Supply-Privy Council questions which he alone can answer. I start with one arising out of his answer today on the orders of the day to a question asked by the Acting Leader of the Opposition with regard to certain opinions expressed yesterday by Canadian ex-officers of high rank, namely General Simonds and General Macklin. In answer to the question asked today the Prime Minister used these rather unusual words. He was referring to the statements which they had made, one by General Macklin to the effect that our link with the United States imperils our defence and the other by General Simonds that of the 20,000 members of the armed forces recruited for Korea, some 7,000 deserted, information which had never been given before in this house. The Prime Minister said this:
I think-
Referring to these statements.
-they were intended to be alarming by those who made them, but I do not think they have created the alarm in the public mind that was intended.
I found it difficult to understand that answer today from the Prime Minister who usually gives a reasonably comprehensive answer to any question asked. One naturally asks oneself the question as to why the Prime Minister should have left so sinister an inference with regard to the words used by these officers who not so long ago held a very high rank in the Canadian armed forces and who must then have been regarded by the Prime Minister and the government as worthy of the utmost respect and of the responsibility which was theirs. I simply ask the Prime Minister to elucidate what he meant this morning in that regard. Whatever they may have said at the moment, it is difficult to understand how officers who held responsibilities which all of us regard as of the first magnitude, representing as they do our survival, should have it ascribed to them that they intended to alarm or to create alarm in the public mind.	One
naturally asks oneself a simple question and it is this. If they enjoyed the confidence of the government in the positions they held, what has happened recently which made it necessary for the Prime Minister to leave the inference which was clear and patent from his words, namely that what they were saying was not worthy of credibility, that it had an unworthy purpose in mind, and that it was designed to create alarm but had not been successful. If the Prime Minister did not mean that, that is a different matter. But those are the words, and they are strikingly significant words having regard to the

Supply-Privy Council fact that those two officers enjoyed so high a position of authority under this government for so long.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not before me the exact words of the question that was put to me by the hon. gentleman who was Acting Leader of the Opposition, but he had spoken of the alarm caused by such statements; and in using the words he used or a paraphrase of them, I said that I thought they had intended to alarm the public. There was nothing sinister in that statement. I think they have both for some time been trying to create in the public mind the impression that I found in some of the excerpts I read of the statements, namely that, because we had not resorted to compulsory military service in this country since the last war, we were not taking proper measures for the right kind of defence for this country. I do not think they were saying anything they did not believe it proper for them to say. I think they were saying it for the purpose of trying to induce the public to take perhaps a more serious view of what each of us should be doing to ward off the dangers they foresee.
I have not seen the text of their statements. I have seen the excerpts that were published in the newspapers. I thought I sensed some sort of contradiction in the statement attributed to General Macklin when he said that we were still preparing for the war before the last war, whilst in another part he was saying that there was altogether too much emphasis being put upon the preparations being made to prevent war in which nuclear weapons would be used. There were certainly no nuclear weapons that were threatening or that were looked upon as having to be warded off in the war before the last war.
Not only in this country but in many other countries I think there is some rivalry between the different branches of the armed forces as to which service can be the most important and the most effective. We have heard divergent views expressed in this house. It is not so very long ago that the military critic for the official opposition was reproaching the government for not attributing a larger portion of its appropriations to the strengthening of the air force. There are opinions that I think are honestly held by all these officers in high positions as to what would be the best way to provide for the effective defence of the country.
Of course they would not be worthy of our confidence if they did not recommend everything they felt would be useful as measures of defence. But everything cannot be done. Since these two distinguished officers who
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
formerly served with the army have retired, they have been speaking on many occasions of their dissatisfaction with the manner in which the defence forces of the country are being organized and provided for. I think they feel that they should alarm the public about that matter. There was nothing more sinister than that intended in my answer to the question in which I endeavoured to use the language that the question contained.

Mr. Chairman, there is something that I feel must absolutely be said while we are discussing this particular point. I want to take just a minute, but I am quite upset about it. I was going to raise this matter on the orders of the day or as a question of privilege tomorrow but the opportunity to deal with it has arisen right now. In tonight's Citizen there is a heading which reads as follows:
Thousands Were Recruited from Jails for Korean
Fight, General Discloses
Then the report states this:
The Toronto Star quoted him-
That is General Macklin.
-as saying that because of inadequate army forces "10,000 criminals and useless men" were taken from prisons "after they had committed every crime starting with murder and working up."
If the general said that, I as a veteran of the service myself feel that I must say this. I say that is the grossest insult to the armed forces who served in the Korean war. I think some 20,000 to 25,000 were recruited. That means that the general is saying that nearly 50 per cent of those boys who served in Korea were criminals. If that is the type of irresponsible statement upon which we have to answer questions put up by opposition members in this house, I think we are certainly wasting the time of this chamber.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I was somewhat apprehensive when the hon. member for Prince Albert raised this question as I felt that it was not a proper one to raise under a privy council item. I am confirmed in that opinion by what has just transpired. It seems to me that this is a matter which could more appropriately and more relevantly be discussed under the estimates of the Department of National Defence. Under this item dealing with the privy council office I am afraid it could not be answered.
I may say that I did not interrupt the hon. member for Prince Albert or the Prime Minister because I understood the hon. member was asking the Prime Minister to explain an answer which he had given earlier today. I do not think we should embark on a further

discussion of this question, which is really one of national defence, under the privy council office.

Surely the responsibility of the Prime Minister enters into a discussion of the estimates of the privy council. In this instance, as I understand it, the hon. member for Prince Albert was simply asking the Prime Minister, in view of his general responsibility, for some clarification of his statement earlier today with regard to a very important matter. In the course of the Prime Minister's remarks I think he did an injustice to General Macklin through a misunderstanding of the report. I, like the Prime Minister, have not seen the text of General Macklin's statement. As I read the newspaper article and the earlier articles by General Macklin appearing in other journals I thought that General Macklin's criticism did not contain a misconception, as the Prime Minister suggested.
I understood the Prime Minister to say that General Macklin on the one hand was saying we were preparing for the war before the last war and, at the same time, General Macklin was commenting upon the development and use of thermonuclear weapons, which is obviously making preparation for the next war. What I gathered from the article was that General Macklin was speaking about the army not being prepared for the war before the last war, and instanced from that that, in the 10 years that have elapsed since the conclusion of the second world war, the army has not been brought up to modern standards with regard to mobility and with regard to air transport.
I see nothing there to indicate that there is any discrepancy in General Macklin's statement. Thermonuclear war has to be prepared for, and at the same time the army has to be prepared for action under thermonuclear conditions. But if thermonuclear weapons are not used the army must be prepared to use conventional weapons according to modern practice, and without mobility it is an army of pre-1939 vintage. I judge that is what General Macklin was aiming at.

There is one question I should like to place before the Prime Minister and that has to do with the fact that he still has one minister handling the portfolios of veterans affairs and post office. This condition has continued since November 8, 1955; in other words, for over nine months. I should like to register a protest against the failure of the Prime Minister to have a minister for each of those portfolios.
In the first place, the Department of Veterans Affairs has to do very directly with
Supply-Privy Council between 250,000 and 300,000 veterans and their dependents in Canada. It is impossible to get an exact figure because there is some duplication. In other words, a man may be getting benefits under Veterans Land Act and may also be getting a pension. But there are at least a quarter of a million Canadians very directly concerned with what is done by the Department of Veterans Affairs. In addition to that, according to the figures given in the estimates book, there are nearly 14,000 employees in that department. It is a very important department having to do with a lot of questions which affect people very directly. I cannot urge too strongly upon the Prime Minister that there should at all times be a minister whose sole responsibility it will be to look after that particular department.
Then, the same is true of the post office department. There are about 25,000 employees in that department. There again problems arise affecting people very directly. I can see no reason why one minister should have been called upon to perform these double duties for nine months. I am not criticizing the minister at all. I think it was unfair to him, as it would have been to any other minister, to expect him to fulfil all the obligations entailed in directing these two departments. I hope that the Prime Minister will take steps right away to see that there is a minister in charge of each of these departments. It has been a strange situation that throughout the whole session one minister would be asked to continue in charge of these two departments. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that this situation should be ended without any further delay. May I have an explanation from the Prime Minister as to why that situation has been allowed to continue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It has been and still is a temporary situation.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, I have never received more answers to my letters during my 21 years than I have from the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I thank him for it.

Just for a moment I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that he give consideration to the addition of another member to his cabinet, a minister in charge of responsibility in the field of provincial affairs and provincial relations. I am not going to explore this subject at great length, but the reason for the suggestion is that the federal government's relations with the provinces have expanded greatly during the past few years. They are being carried on by various members within the cabinet, all of whom have some small area

Supply-Privy Council of responsibility in this field. It seems to me that the co-ordination of these efforts and the establishment of a focal point to which the provinces could go when they wish to talk to the federal government would be of great advantage to both these levels of government.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that the situation is one parallel to the field of foreign affairs where, for quite a few years, the Prime Minister carried both his own portfolio and that of Secretary of State for External Affairs. In the last few years it was seen fit to divest the Prime Minister of this responsibility. While when he had the burden he acquitted himself quite well in that field, I do think that the opportunity to have somebody who specialized in that field and was free to travel when necessary and to acquaint himself more intimately with these problems has been of advantage in this particular field.
Now, the cases are not exactly parallel but they are very close to being parallel. I point out one further fact in case some one should suggest the establishment of this position would be an invasion of provincial rights. I fail to see that it would be any more of an invasion of provincial rights to have someone charged with the federal government's liaison with the provincial authorities than it is an invasion of the rights of other countries to have a secretary of state for external affairs.
Knowing the Prime Minister's wide background and his personal acquaintance with this subject I will not labour that point any further but while I am on my feet I would like to ask the Prime Minister one question and it is this. How extensive is the newspaper clipping service which is operated in the office of the privy council? It is my understanding that it occupies about two people on a full-time basis; and before I present my other question I wonder if the Prime Minister would care to give us at least some idea of the extent of this operation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am told, Mr. Chairman, that there are seven people in the clipping office.
That is more extensive than I had anticipated.
You are really getting clipped, eh?
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Prime Minister would inform us what use is made of this material and to what extent it is available for reference purposes by hon. members of the house?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think there has ever been any application from hon. members of the

house but if there were they would be very sympathetically considered. I see perhaps less than 5 per cent of the clippings that are filed. Almost daily four or five clippings are brought to my attention. I just put my initials on the sheet after I have perused it and send it back and then when there is any requirement for consultation I ask for the clippings of editorial comments on a specific subject and the clippings are gathered together and brought back to me. If at any time the hon. gentleman wants clippings that he would find it more convenient to obtain from us than elsewhere, if he will just let us know I hope we will be able to accommodate him.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if we could hear from the Prime Minister now a somewhat more detailed report of the conference which he attended in London last month? We were interested and pleased, and to some extent concerned, to know that the Prime Minister had conversations with the prime minister of India, as I understand it, outside the scope of the full conference itself. While the conference itself has been dealt with to a very limited extent in the communique tabled in the house we would, I know, appreciate it if the Prime Minister could enlighten us on the scope of the conversations with the prime minister of India and what conclusions, if any, or what mutual agreements were arrived at on that occasion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there were no mutual agreements arrived at on that occasion and these conversations, as the hon. gentleman would appreciate, are of a confidential character that I would not like to discuss publicly.

Well, surely the Prime Minister can tell us the area which they covered. I am not asking him for a verbatim report; but what were the subjects of mutual concern which caused the Prime Minister of India and the Prime Minister of Canada to get together? Surely, the Prime Minister could take the committee into his confidence to that extent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There were no problems of mutual concern to our respective countries that caused us to get together. I accepted an invitation from the prime minister of India to lunch with him and was accompanied on that occasion by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We discussed some of the matters that had already been discussed in the plenary conference but we made no agreements and we endeavoured to be as frank as possible with each other in respect of our views concerning the international problems that we were discussing in the general conference.

If there were no areas of mutual agreement were there some of mutual disagreement? If so, what efforts were made in this sphere of international or commonwealth relations to explore such questions as the situation in the Middle East and Cyprus and to determine what were the views of the respective countries and what could be done in the way of reconciling them, these matters which are of such vital concern, not only to this country in particular but to the commonwealth in general?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not care to disclose the nature of these confidential conversations which the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I had with Mr. Nehru and Mrs. Pandit on that occasion.

Mr. Chairman, I intended to ask a question somewhat along the same line. I have before me the text of a commonwealth conference communique and as the Prime Minister has said the most recent one has been tabled in the house. Very little is disclosed in these communiques as to what importance these conferences now hold for this country and for the commonwealth. I am not going to inquire of the Prime Minister what was said at the conferences. I might say that the communiques really do not tell us anything.
Hear, hear.
Certainly they do not indicate either areas of agreement or disagreement. What I would like to ask the Prime Minister is this. What purpose is now being-
Achieved.

Achieved; yes, that is a very good word which was supplied to me by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and it is true that he is a corporation counsel.
What purpose is now being achieved by these conferences and what may we expect to achieve through them in the future if this same course of conduct is followed? It seems to me, sir, that it is vitally important to us to know what we can expect from this type of meeting in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think that we can expect to have the good relations with the other members of the commonwealth that we have enjoyed during the whole period in which I have been attending those meetings. I can assure the hon. gentleman that I felt it was of real value to have personal contact and conversations with the two prime ministers I had not
Supply-Privy Council met before, the prime minister of South Africa and the prime minister of Ceylon; and also to have conversations in his capacity as prime minister with Mr. Mohammed Ali, whom I had met before in another capacity but who is now the prime minister of Pakistan.
We realized that from different parts of the world we saw the world's problems from different angles and it was, I think, of real value to have the opportunity of this personal appraisal of the viewpoint and difficulties of each of the other prime ministers. The communique is a responsibility of all of us and nothing goes into it that is not acceptable to every one of those who are there. That is perhaps why there is so little of much importance that is disclosed because some of the things that several would wish to have included in the communique would not be acceptable to others. We did put out this time, as on other occasions, a communique to which no one of those present would have any objection.

Does the Prime Minister feel that within the terms of reference-I think I can properly use that expression-under which these conferences are held they perform a useful function for Canada as a member of the commonwealth in connection with defence and in connection with our trading position within the commonwealth, and does he feel that these conferences have assisted the commonwealth as a group in connection with its possible common defence throughout the world and its trading position throughout the world? If those questions cannot be answered in the affirmative it seems to me that we are beginning to waste our time with conferences such as this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have
never felt that time was wasted. While there are no specific agreements reached I have always felt that the time was well spent and did serve to keep us as close as possible together. On this occasion there were no specific arrangements made about defence but there was a lot of information exchanged about the position in which each country found itself in relation to defence and its contribution to the maintenance of peace and stability in the world.

Surely the Prime Minister must admit that no one here can deceive himself or be deceived as to the obvious nature of the fact that in such a situation as has developed in connection with the Suez other nations of the commonwealth, notably Australia and New Zealand, have made statements in support of the position taken by the

Supply-Privy Council United Kingdom in that dispute which are at marked variance with the very cautious reluctance of this government to commit itself one way or another in connection with that situation. I should like to know what is the purpose of these conferences and what goes on there. For instance, is any consultative machinery set up which would result in a common stand, or if there be not a common stand, which would result in a clear statement of a divergent stand on such a matter as the Suez incident?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Suez incident had not arisen at the time of that conference.

I am aware of that; I am as able to calculate dates as is the right hon. gentleman. What I am pointing out is that after the Suez incident arose other countries of the commonwealth appeared to have been able to take a definite position in support of the position taken by the United Kingdom. Is there better consultation between those countries and the United Kingdom? Are they better informed than we? Were these matters discussed? Were the things which led to a different approach discussed at the conference or did the conference concern itself with generalities and not with specific problems or specific approaches to the world situation? We are not to be content with vague generalities forever. This commonwealth means something or it does not. If we carry on with the policy of drift as we appear to be doing then it will not be very long before the commonwealth means nothing and will in the future be in danger of disintegration, and the attitude of the government of Canada will have contributed more than anything to that disintegration if it does take place.

Was any record, either ver-oatim or in gist form, kept of the proceedings of the conference? I appreciate it would be confidential in view of what the Prime Minister has said. I recall for instance some previous conferences, particularly the famous conference of 1921. At that time I think a verbatim record was kept of the discussions which led eventually to the denunciation of the British-Japanese alliance. Is such a record kept of these conferences, and in particular was such a record kept of this conference for posterity?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was no verbatim record kept but Sir Norman Brook kept a record and was busy writing practically all the time the discussions were going on.

No one has the information the Prime Minister has on this question and I am asking as a matter of information what is the background which dictates to other members of the commonwealth the acceptance of a family of nations joined together, either as self-governing nations or as republics? What is the philosophy that brings a republic into the commonwealth? Is there any joint responsibility for defence in so far as a republic is concerned? What is this new concept which is so difficult for us to understand, who knew the commonwealth as it used to be, made up of nations joined together, equal in status but not in function? What has the change been that brings in bodies that have no relationship or responsibility to the other members of the commonwealth? What is that basis? If the Prime Minister could enlighten us it would be most helpful because that is one of the most difficult anachronisms for those of us who have never heard it explained. Certainly political scientists cannot explain it and the only one who possibly could explain it is one who had taken part in the achievement of that new concept.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I took no part in the achievement of that new concept. It emerged before I commenced attending these conferences. It may be very difficult to explain but it is a relationship that exists and which we all feel is productive of beneficial results for those who are members of the commonwealth.
Could the Prime Minister give us the number of orders in council passed last year as well as the number of treasury orders passed during that period of time?

That information was supplied quite recently. I assume what the hon. member refers to are the orders submitted to the Governor General for his signature, and when he refers to treasury orders he means the minutes of treasury board which come to the cabinet for approval several at a time with the order of approval then being submitted to His Excellency for approval. I am informed that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration gave the number to the committee during the discussion of the Indian Act. It was on that occasion put on Hansard, but I can secure the exact number. The orders in council are numbered consecutively.
If they were given, I did not notice them.
I would have to ascertain the number of minutes of the treasury board.

There is just a brief question I should like to ask the Prime Minister. Some time ago, as I recall it, it was reported in one or two of the Ottawa newspapers that the Prime Minister was going to divest himself of the direct responsibility for the federal district commission. I should like to ask the Prime Minister at this time whether he is considering divesting himself of this direct responsibility and passing it on to some other minister of the cabinet such as the Minister of Public Works?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That matter has been under consideration, and no decision has been reached.

In view of the fact that the committee has been sitting for some time, and the federal district commission has handed in a report, and these estimates were obviously prepared some time in advance, does the Prime Minister intend to modify the estimates in view of the report of the commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, the estimates do not require to be modified at this time.

Item agreed to.
333. To authorize payment of the ninth instalment to a special account in the consolidated revenue fund, known as the national capital fund, established under vote 809, Appropriation Act No. 4, 1947-48, $2,500,000.

Would the Prime Minister give a general picture as to what is being contemplated for next year in connection with developments of the federal district commission in Ottawa. What are the general plans, and what will be the amount of expenditure expected?

For this fiscal year, there is no change being suggested in the estimates, which were prepared some time ago. For the next fiscal year, we shall have to consider whether or not we shall adopt the recommendation of the committee that, instead of there being statutory grants for administration, there be a budget for the administration of the commission submitted to parliament each year.
The hon. gentleman knows that there has been a statutory grant of $300,000 and then supplementary votes. The committee has recommended that there be a yearly capital grant as there has been in the past but that for the current administration of the commission it should have to prepare and submit to parliament for approval a budget for all its current expenditures. The amount that will be recommended in the next budget will
Supply-Privy Council depend upon the consideration, and the decision after that consideration, that is given to these recommendations of the committee.
As for the capital expenditure, that will depend to some extent upon the availability of supplies and manpower. There are some of these things that are not so urgent that they should not have to give way to some other private or public enterprises that might put a strain on the supplies of material and manpower.
The hon. gentleman has no doubt read the report and has probably read some, if not all, of the thousand pages of printed evidence that was given before that committee. I have read the report and I have read some portions of the evidence, but it will take some considerable time to come to a conclusion as to the projects that are most urgent.
There is one, of course, that is always under consideration and always proceeding, and that has to do with the reorganization of the railway situation in the heart of the city. That proceeds as rapidly as the negotiation with the railways brings about results.
Another that will be undertaken at a very early date is the Queensway, which wil] occupy the roadbed of the cross-town railway and about which a proposal has been submitted to the city of Ottawa and accepted after negotiations between the government of the province of Ontario, the federal government and the city authorities. That is regarded as one of the urgent projects to be got under way.
There are some of lesser magnitude, such as the work going on for the approaches to the interprovincial bridge. Consideration will have to be given to the replacement of that bridge in due course.
Another matter which was one that occupied the attention of the committee was the pollution of the Ottawa river, about which the Ontario government has set up a commission. Of course, that is a provincial and municipal project but it will probably be carried out in a manner that will be fitted into the general capital plan. It may very well be that, to fit it into the general capital plan, it will be desirable for the commission to make some contribution to the over-all cost of the project.
Another recommendation which will receive very careful consideration is that the act be revised, that it be called the national capital act, and that the commission itself be called the national capital commission. That is a recommendation which appeals to me personally at first blush; but it will be given serious consideration.

Supply-Transport
There is a recommendation that there should be more active efforts made to coordinate the plans of the commission, of the provincial authorities and of the municipal authorities, not only of Ottawa and Hull but of the surrounding district. There certainly is room for co-operative and conformable action by the three levels of government. I hope that it will be possible to have that co-operation.
Within the last couple of hours, I received two letters from Her Worship the Mayor, one accepting the proposal for the exchange of properties which would make Green island available for the construction of a city hall and which will assure to the future capital that the old city hall site will not be built upon. The other has to do with the tentative agreement reached at the meetings between our Minister of Public Works, the Ontario minister of highways, and the city authorities, about the manner in which the project of the Queensway can be proceeded with and the cost distributed between the three interested organizations. So there seems already to have been an improvement, not perhaps in the desire for collaboration and co-operation, but in achieving collaboration and co-operation.

Mr. Chairman, the description that the Prime Minister has given of the Ottawa to be is one that I know will meet with the support of Canadians everywhere, a capital plan making this, the capital of Canada, a city in keeping with the aspirations of the Canadian people. All of us, regardless of what part of Canada we come from, are joined in agreement that what is being done is in accordance with Canada's potential greatness and will bring joy to generations yet to come.

Can the Prime Minister tell us whether the planning committee intends to maintain the cobblestone drive from the west gate up the hill for the next hundred years or whether something can be done to cover them up?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sure those cobblestones will not last for a hundred years.
Item agreed to.

Marine services-
440.	Marine services administration, including agencies, $670,240.

Mr. Chairman, before this item is dealt with may I bring to the minister's attention the fact that on Saturday last, as reported at page 7040 of Hansard and as also found at page 2 of the English translations

for that day, the hon. member for Chicoutimi asked the minister this question:
In conclusion, I would ask the minister whether it would be possible lor him to table in this house a copy of the contract between the Canadian national authorities and the U.S. controlled Hilton company, concerning the operation of the new hotel which is going up in Montreal.
The minister apparently overlooked that question.
I did not overlook it at all. I ignored it.
The hon. member asked me to bring that up and ask the minister whether there would be any objection to tabling the contract.

The question was brought up last year and I dealt with the matter then. I explained to the house that it was not the custom of the railway company to table contracts that it had made and that that has been the invariable practice. The whole subject was discussed in the standing committee on railways and shipping owned by the government, as the hon. gentleman knows.
With respect to item 440, would the minister explain to the committee just what part his department plays in this search and rescue service?

Mr. Chairman, on re-reading in yesterday's Hansard what I said last night I think perhaps I may have given a wrong impression in some of the comments that I made after the hon. gentleman's first question. The impression that I wished to give was that the responsibility for the co-ordination of search and rescue activities was the primary responsibility of the Department of National Defence. The responsibility for providing the vessels that would take part in search and rescue operations would, I think, fall on the Department of Transport primarily-
For which?

For the provision of vessels in connection with the search and rescue operations, because I think the department unquestionably has more of those vessels than any of the other departments of government. But I should like to correct any misapprehension that my remarks may have caused last night that the whole responsibility rested on the Department of National Defence. Their responsibility is that of coordination of the activities but it is not a sole and exclusive responsibility.
Suppose there is a wreck on the west coast. Who has the authority to order out the ships belonging to the Department of Transport?

I am informed, as I think my remarks indicated, that the responsibility rests on the air force, the Department of National Defence, for communicating with the various agencies concerned and apprising them of the circumstances and determining whether or not they are in a position to be able to afford assistance.

Does the air force have the authority to order a vessel belonging to the Department of Transport to go to the scene of the wreck or must that go from the air force to the Department of Transport and then from the Department of Transport to the master of the vessel in question?

My information is that the request would be conveyed directly to the master of the vessel and not to the department itself. The hon. gentleman has used the word "order". I think perhaps if he changed it to say "request" that would be more appropriate language to use. I do not think it is the intention or the practice that the search and rescue organization should order other departments, even including the navy, but I am sure the hon. gentleman will realize that we are really merely bandying words if we talk about an order or a request whenever the vessels are available.

I take it that when the minister suggests that government vessels commence a search or rescue operation on the initiative of the search and rescue co-ordination centre he is referring to the general departmental vessels of his department and also other departments such as the Department of Fisheries. However, I believe that that situation-and I should like to know whether my understanding is correct-would not apply to the boats at the lifeboat stations on the west coast of Vancouver island. Is it not true that those lifeboat stations have the authority to undertake a search or rescue operation on their own initiative without reference necessarily to the search and rescue co-ordination centre?

My information is that there are only a few of the stations to which the hon. gentleman refers, two, I believe, and that they may act on their own authority or they may act on the request of the search and rescue organization.
As the minister well knows, there are many people who think that two are not enough. However, I will not pursue that question further.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Transport Marine service steamers-
441.	Administration, operation and maintenance, $7,393,793.

There is quite a large increase in this vote, Mr. Chairman. It is over $325,000. In the details at page 545 we find that there is an increase in "professional and special services" of over $90,000, and in "repairs and upkeep of equipment" of $120,000 and in "charter of vessels for northern transportation", of $75,000. Will the minister explain those increases.

Mr. Chairman, the main reason for the increase is a transfer to this particular subitem of an expenditure which was provided for otherwise in previous budgets. I am referring particularly to the stevedoring costs in connection with northern transportation which are set out for the first time as "professional and special services". They account for an addition to this item of some $90,000.
What about the other increases?

I am informed that the item with regard to northern transportation is attributable to an increase in that particular activity and in the volume of material and freight that is carried northward on the supply mission during the summer.

What policy is followed by the government in chartering these vessels for trips to the north? Perhaps the minister could tell us how many ships were chartered this year. I presume that charters have already been arranged for the current year?
Yes; they have.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is item 441 carried?
No, Mr. Chairman; it is not.

Would the minister like to take this opportunity to reply to my few remarks on icebreaking? The three new icebreakers are listed under this item. It would be a good opportunity to have my reply. As an hon. gentleman has just said, would the minister like to break the ice at this point?

If the hon. gentleman is saying it for himself, I shall not give an affirmative answer to that question. Mr. Chairman, what I should like to say on the subject of icebreaking is simply this. As hon. members know, we had the misfortune to lose the Lady Grey not in the winter just past but in the winter before last. That loss has naturally thrust a considerable burden on the remaining icebreakers. We have endeavoured to meet the situation first of all by providing for the construction of an additional icebreaker to replace the Lady Grey. It is at present under construction at Levis, Quebec. We hope it will be available for service in the coming winter.
We have recently called for tenders for the building of a further icebreaker of what I might describe as intermediate size. I hope it will be possible before too long to award the contract for the construction of that vessel. As my deputy minister points out, that vessel would be assigned principally to service in Newfoundland and in the gulf of St. Lawrence.
We also have in mind the construction of a larger icebreaker of the same general class as the D'Iberville. I hope it will be possible to call for tenders for the construction of that vessel some time later this year.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has any specific questions with regard to icebreaking. I may tell him that we are in receipt of a large number of requests to which it is quite impossible for us to accede, having regard to the dimensions of the icebreaker fleet at the present time. When these new icebreakers are in service we hope to be able to do more than we are doing at the present time.
[Mr. Marler.)
Another most important factor in connection with icebreakers, of course, is the use to which they are put during the summer months for carrying out the northern supply mission to the many points in the north which can be served only by ships accompanied by an icebreaker or by icebreakers themselves.
The minister has more or less explained away the reasons why we must have three new icebreakers in the estimates this year or plans for three new icebreakers.
No; plans for two.
Yes, but there are three icebreakers.

Yes; the item includes expenditures on three. As I say, one we hope will be in service shortly; the second has been the subject of a tender call already; and the third we hope will be the subject of calls later this year.

I realize that it is probably difficult to make a definite statement about this icebreaking matter generally; but frankly, I may say it is increasing now to a stage where they have the St. Lawrence open for a period that extends at least a full month into the close of the season and they have an early opening of about that same period. As I have said before on many occasions- and I am not going into the history of it-we are worried about the plans for the future in the St. Lawrence. The other night I mentioned the new icebreakers that are available. The old excuse of flooding in the St. Lawrence does not mean anything to me now, because the flooding has always been there. If one icebreaker could look after that condition formerly, surely it has not increased to the extent that more icebreakers would be necessary. A great many of these vessels are icebreakers and other types of ships; in other words, they combine two duties. I say that it is a back-door method to continue icebreaking early in the St. Lawrence. We had trouble last February, I believe, with respect to the early opening of the St. Lawrence. Vessels were damaged and pilots made statements that the season was being pushed to an extent that was alarming. Frankly, we are worried about it in Saint John and I think they must be in Halifax, as it affects the future of our ports.
Two or three times I have asked questions regarding the additional costs or for an estimate of the cost of these icebreaking operations. It should be possible to estimate the length of time that these vessels are on duty. It should be possible to give the payroll and other additional expenses. I think

that we are entitled to a statement regarding the future plans. Here we are subsidizing the icebreaking and increasing the length of the season in the St. Lawrence, while at the same time we are spending money on the harbours at Saint John and Halifax. These two expenditures are definitely in conflict. We only have the winter business and the season has been decreased now to an extent where our longshoremen, as I said the other night, cannot even get 24 weeks of work in order to qualify for unemployment insurance. I should like the minister to say if the department has examined this icebreaking matter. Helicopters are used, I understand, to survey the weak spots in the ice and see where it is possible to break a channel. The modern vessels have reinforced plates and each year the season for our ports grows shorter. We are worried about our future, and I feel it is going to be an increasing worry and burden. The department must tell us just what is going on, and what their plans are about icebreaking.

I would hope I could disabuse the mind of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, Mr. Chairman, as to the icebreaking activity in that portion of the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. It is not a matter of subterfuge. We have endeavoured to ameliorate the conditions of flooding below Montreal. The activity of the icebreakers has materially cut down that flooding in the last few years, and our purpose in carrying out icebreaking is not to make possible the use of the port of Montreal at an earlier date than common sense dictates. The prime purpose of carrying out the operation is to relieve conditions that would otherwise result in flooding.
The hon. gentleman seems to be concerned about the possibility of icebreakers being used in the St. Lawrence to the disadvantage of the port of Saint John. I think that is the substance of the comments he has just made. The difficulty, Mr. Chairman, is that we are not faced with a request for additional icebreaking only in the upper St. Lawrence. We are faced with a request for icebreaking from places on the Gulf of St. Lawrence and down in the province of New Brunswick. They have asked us to do something to make their ports available during the winter months. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman wants me to say we propose, because of the representations that he has made, to turn a deaf ear to the representations of other ports in New Brunswick, and refuse to provide icebreakers for them so that the port of Saint John will enjoy an exclusive advantage over the others. I do not think that is in his mind.
Supply-Transport
I fully understand that he wishes to promote the interests of Saint John and that I think is quite natural. Unfortunately, or perhaps fortunately, it is not possible for us to administer an icebreaking program designed to favour one port in particular. We have to meet this flooding condition that arises below Montreal. I believe we will have to expand our activities in the Gulf of St. Lawrence where there are important developments which will need facilities open to a much greater extent than at present. I think the same applies to ports in New Brunswick which, in my perhaps uninformed opinion, have made out a pretty good case for interest on our part in facilitating a greater use during the winter months of what seemed to me quite natural and suitable facilities.
The hon. gentleman, either on Saturday or today, has spoken about the comments of a pilot who attributed a collision which took place in the lower St. Lawrence to the fact that navigation was opening too early. The collision occurred in the lower St. Lawrence at a point, as I remember, somewhat above Quebec. I should like to tell the hon. gentleman that a most thorough inquiry was made into the circumstances of that particular incident and the pilot was not regarded as being excused by the conditions to which he referred. In fact, as I understand the circumstances, the pilot referred to was suspended as a consequence of that particular accident.

I will leave this item now, but I do want to say for the record that the money of the taxpayers of Canada is being used to provide icebreakers which in turn are opening the port of Montreal and other ports on the St. Lawrence early to the detriment of the business of eastern Canadian ports. I realize that there are some other explanations for the use of icebreakers. As I say, it may be a back door method, but in the very near future I can see that we will not have any business in eastern Canadian ports and that with modern methods the expenses of the department will be greatly increased because the St. Lawrence will be open all winter long.

I do not want to provoke a discussion, but I would hesitate to peer into the future as far as the hon. gentleman and predict the time when the St. Lawrence is going to be open all year round for navigation between Quebec and Montreal. He has more confidence in the economic possibilities of that than I have. While I fully appreciate that he may wish to take a particular attitude with regard to the port of Saint John it is

quite impossible for me, as Minister of Transport, to accept the position that I am going to discourage operations in the St. Lawrence regarding flood conditions that we are attempting to correct, and say that this is done so that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert will have a port that will be more useful under the circumstances.
I am surprised that he should talk about that just at the time when the port has had a record-breaking year in the transportation of grain. I find it strange in the face of conditions which are record breaking that the hon. gentleman should have so little optimism as to the future of his own port.

The point I am trying to make, and the minister hedges around it, is that the money of the Canadian taxpayers is being used to provide icebreakers, which in turn are allowing the St. Lawrence to open earlier and private vessels are thus enabled to move up to the St. Lawrence ports above Quebec and Montreal, and in that way we are losing out in the competitive battle. Mr. Chairman, in the particulars of this item on page 549 I find that there was a vote of $355,000 odd for lighthouse keepers' assistants. That is an increase of about $60,000 over last year. Mr. Chairman, my note with regard to the lightkeepers' assistants which represents an item of $355,621, or an increase of $57,131, is explained by the fact that in 1951 the department assumed the sole responsibility for the payment of assistants to light-keepers, classes 1 to 5. A further amendment in 1952 revised the rates as follows. Where one assistant only is employed payment may not exceed $1,800 per annum. Where two assistants are authorized payment may not exceed $1,800 per annum for the first assistant and $1,620 per annum for the second assistant, except at Prince Rupert and Victoria where the rate has been set at $2,100 per annum for both assistants.

With regard to the other question, Mr. Chairman, I think in a general way that we endeavour when there are vacancies in lights or positions in the more settled and attractive points to provide opportunities for advancement to those who are at the remote stations so that there is some prospect for people in remote stations to move back to conditions that are probably more agreeable and certainly more attractive than being in some remote place where conditions are perhaps somewhat lonely and desolate. I think that covers the situation in a general way and if the hon. gentleman has any further questions I will certainly try to answer them.

What I was wondering is this. These assistant lighthouse keepers apparently are not considered as civil servants because earlier in the item there are shown quite large numbers of lightkeepers of different classes. There are no lightkeepers' assistants in that list and they are shown in the supplementary list. I take it from this that they are not engaged as regular employees of the department; at least, they cannot become permanent civil servants. Is that correct? If so, why is there not some permanence to this position of assistant lighthouse keeper?
The minister has pointed out that a lighthouse keeper who is serving at a remote point would be given the opportunity to take a position at a less remote and more agreeable centre and I think that is a very wise policy. Does the same policy apply to the assistant lighthouse keepers? That is, do they get any advantage at all or are they merely hired as temporary employees?
I have heard that they are hired by the lighthouse keeper; in other words, that the man keeping a light hires his own assistant. I did run across one case in which that appeared to have been done. Mr. Chairman, I might say that it is somewhat like choosing a wife. One chooses a wife with compatibility as one of the qualifications. The same thing applies to the selection of lighthouse keepers' assistants.
Well, compatibility is a factor.

My hon. friend would realize, of course, how undesirable it would be if the assistant of the lighthouse keeper was incompatible with the keeper himself and, as my deputy minister has just pointed out, these men have to board together. I am sure the hon. member will realize that whatever

merits there might be in making this a civil service appointment the difficulty posed by incompatibility is not one that can be covered by the usual tests.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the committee that last year a small departmental committee considered the whole question of dredging on the St. Lawrence and that the principal purpose of this item is to provide for improvements to the ship channel which are required in order to reduce the hazards to ocean going shipping which plies the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. The work which it is proposed to carry out consists of the further widening of curves and critical sections of the dredged channel between Quebec and Montreal as recommended in a detailed and very complete report which this committee of officials prepared and completed earlier this year.
In addition to the rather broad description I have just given, the work contemplates the completion of dredging in certain areas under the 1952 contract which could not be accomplished in 1955. That is a relatively small item. In addition there is the cost of expropriating Boat island which is six miles below Sorel just above lake St. Peter in order to straighten the channel to a minimum 800 feet and improve the run of ice which jams here. Then there is quite a long list of proposed dredging projects which are to be carried out under contract in 1956 as recommended by the committee. Unless the hon. gentleman would like to have the details, perhaps I might not burden the committee with them.
I should like to say that the experience of the department has been that it is good business to call for a four-year contract to carry out a long term program rather than to do it piecemeal from year to year. The contract was awarded after tenders had been called for publicly and the successful tenderer was the lowest tenderer. The practice is, I think, good, sound common sense. I think that is the way in which we can best spend our money in carrying out the dredging.
