I have not in my book here the exact figure, but the total amount of the contract slightly exceeds $13 million. I think it is $13,250,000 or thereabouts.
That is for the four-year program?
For the four-year program. The expected expenditures this year amount to a little over $3J million.

Item agreed to.
Railway and steamship services-
451.	Repairs and expenses in connection with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars under the jurisdiction of the department, $56,240.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to compliment the minister on the way in which he has answered our questions. That is one of the reasons why we like to assist him as much as possible. I should like to get some information from him. It is in connection with the rumoured curtailment of service up in Bruce. I might read this copy of a letter which has been sent to our postal clerks on the railways between Kincardine, Palmerston and Southampton. It reads as follows:
Plans of the Canadian National Railways call for removal from service of a number of passenger trains effective 30th September, 1956. This will necessitate considerable changes in the railway mail service in this district.
Plans have not yet been finalized but it now appears practically certain the railway mail clerk positions at Southampton, Kincardine and Goderich headquarters will be abolished.
You are, of course, vitally interested and I am therefore, passing this information along to you at this time.
It is anticipated that no postal car will operate in the Palmerston and Southampton branch, (also Kincardine and Goderich lines), and the only postal car operations between London and Palmerston will be in Trs. 168 and 169-29.
That letter is signed by J. A. Flaherty, district director, London. I may say that the hon. member for Huron, who is not able to be here tonight, is also very much interested in this prospective change. I am happy to see that the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has recently come into the house. I think probably he will be interested as well, because it affects part of his district. I should like to say that on August 3 the minister answered a question of mine. My question, as reported at 6923 of Hansard, was as follows:
I have one more question, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask the minister if he thinks it is wise to curtail train service into Bruce county at

Supp ly-Transport
this stage when it is expected by all economists in Canada that the population of this country is going to increase very greatly.
The minister answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I could not answer the question in general terms in which it was put. I think every case must be considered on its own merits.
At the present time I should be very glad if the minister could give us an idea as to what merits we have up there in Bruce in not wanting this train service cut off. As I think it has been suggested previously in this house, we are increasing in population and in industrial production up there. I should therefore like to know the minister's views on what we may expect up in that part of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I am not in any better position to reply to his question than I was the other day when the hon. gentleman first brought the matter up in the house. I may say that I communicated his observations to the Canadian National Railways but I have not yet received a reply to the inquiry which I addressed to them. In the second place, I am not in a position to express any opinion with regard to the service to which he has referred. I will say this, however: I think that all railway companies would hesitate to give up services that are profitable. I have merely inferred from the questions that have been put that if a reduction in service is being contemplated or is being put into effect, it is because the service as at present rendered is not proving to be profitable.
I would share the hon. gentleman's regret if it is found to be necessary to curtail service over the lines to which he has referred. I should like, first of all, to point out that this is a decision of the management of the railway, not of the Department of Transport; and I think it is guided by the factors of public interest, its responsibilities to the community it serves and also the general consideration of what its effect is on the accounts of the railway company.
Did the minister say that it is a decision of the transport commission?

No. I said that the decision to reduce such service, if such a decision has been taken, was that of the management of Canadian National Railways. I do not want to appear to be too apologetic for the fact that I do not know every detail of the Canadian National Railways administration, but I should like the hon. member to understand that the reason for my unfamiliarity with the matter is that it is a C.N.R. decision and not one by the Department of Transport.

I realize that the minister is doing a good job and a big job, and we would not expect him to know all these things. But after the questions that were asked the other day, I would think he might have familiarized himself with what has happened. If I may be allowed to tell the minister what has happened, I shall do so. The C.N.R. has notified the postal department that these trains are going to be cut off. I think it would be wise for the minister to familiarize himself with the situation and look into it, because he is at the helm.

Mr. Chairman, this item is one that deals with the private railway cars owned by the government. I think it would be interesting to have a little bit of information from the minister at this point. How many cars are there actually in operation at the present time, including the governor general's, those used by the board of transport commissioners and those used by the cabinet ministers? Concurrently with that answer, could the minister give us any comparative mileage travelled by those cars, for instance, this year, the year under examination, in comparison with that in previous years so that we may see what use is being made of them?

Mr. Chairman, I must say at once that we do not keep a record of the mileage of the cars. So far as I am concerned myself, in the last 12 months I think altogether I have travelled between 50,000 and 60,000 miles. I do not want to suggest that I have travelled all of that mileage by rail. If I had done so, I would be on the railroad 365 days of the year. However, I have travelled very extensively by rail. All I can say is that I think these cars serve a very useful purpose. I think perhaps hon. members may imagine that when one gets into a railroad car, the first thing one does is to sit down, relax and enjoy the greatest of luxury therein wherever one happens to be going. Unfortunately, it has not been my experience to be able to use for those purposes the official car which is at my disposal. So far as I am concerned, I have found that it was merely a sort of extension of my office. It had the great advantage of privacy. I could read confidential documents and lay out plans. I could accomplish a lot of uninterrupted reading that I can assure hon. gentlemen opposite is very difficult to accomplish in one's office.
At all events, if I could reply more directly to the hon. gentleman's question, this vote includes five cars, two of which are at the disposal of His Excellency; one for the Prime Minister; one for the Minister of Transport

and one for general use. There has been no change in the situation while I have been minister. I think that the number has remained the same for some considerable time. I should like to add one further word of explanation in connection with the cars and that is that the railway companies move these cars without any charge whatever to the government so that it is not a matter of paying a substantial sum each time a cabinet minister uses an official car to go from one point to another.

Just to deal very briefly with the minister's observation, I must say that I sympathize with him in so far as the value of being at ease and being able to work while travelling on a railway is concerned. Some of us poor, ordinary commoners who do not have the benefit of private railway cars, find we can operate quite successfully in a bedroom or compartment.
Oh, oh, bragging.
That is not an admission I would care to make.

I am
afraid, Mr. Chairman, that is the level to which the government will sink in order to find something to misinterpret in one's remarks. I find I was not operating at a very high level.
It shows the directions of the hon. gentleman's thoughts, anyway.

I do
not know of what value it is to have a private dining room or how much assistance that is in the minister's reading. I do not know how much the chef assists him in his work or the car steward. I would point out to him that there are many businessmen across this country who do manage to do business quite successfully in the usual type of accommodation which is provided by the railways.
The heads of railways who are in the transport business have private cars.
think the president of the Canadian National and the president of the Canadian Pacific do have their own private railway car.
And each vice-president.

Certainly, I would be quite happy to see the Prime Minister have a car on occasion but I am not aware that each director of the C.P.R. has a car.
Supply-Transport
Each vice-president and every divisional superintendent across the country has cars.

I am
not arguing with that. If we extend that argument indefinitely, we are going to find the government arguing that a deputy minister should have a private railway car. The point I am making-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The point you are making is pure jealousy.
He wants a bigger field of operation.

The
point I am making is this. In the past several years the trend in business has been away from the rails to the air. In line with that trend, and I cannot argue against it, the government has seen fit to provide itself with air transport under the direction of the Department of Transport. I might at some point have occasion to examine whether all those planes now operated by the department are necessary. At this point I do say that I question the value of their having those planes and, having added that large expenditure in that field, not seen fit in any respect to contract these other expenditures. I understand the minister stated a few minutes ago that we are still operating the same number of private cars as we have for a great many years in the past. I suggest that is a typical example of piling one expenditure on top of another without proper attention to the elimination of some of these expenditures as they become unnecessary.
Now, some of the uses of these cars are most interesting. A few weeks ago I drew the attention of the house to a trip which the minister had made to Montreal to address a political meeting.

I should like the hon. gentleman, if he is going to talk about that, to confine himself to the facts as they were set forth in the house. The hon. gentleman knows full well, and I told the house at the time, that I went to Montreal not for the primary purpose of attending a political meeting but for the purpose of doing business for my department. It is true, and I admitted at the time, that I had spoken at a political meeting during my visit there.
I think the hon. gentleman, if he ever comes to be minister-
God forbid.

-will find it exceedingly difficult to find what part of him is personal and what part of him is minister. All I can tell the hon. gentleman is that since I have been

Supply-Transport
minister a very small part of me seems to be personal. When I go to Montreal I have very little opportunity of attending to personal matters, and even less time to attend to political matters. I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman but I should like him to stick to the facts and not to say that I went to Montreal to address a political meeting. Let him tell the whole story.

think in fairness to myself that Hansard will show that I was interrupted in the middle of a sentence. It is quite true the minister went to Montreal to address a political meeting and he went by his private car. When he was queried on that, he pointed out he had also done government business at the same time. Those are the facts which the minister has just set before us, and those are the facts which, had he not interrupted me, I would have mentioned.
But you put the cart before the horse.
He gave you a lift to the station, and that was the main mistake.

If we
are going to get through these estimates I suggest the members on the government benches confine themselves to intelligent remarks.
Having made a reference to that, I go ahead and point out one other trip which was made during the month of April which I think is indicative of an improper use or, if not improper, at least more use than is necessary being made of these cars. We find that on April 28 two of these cars left Ottawa and went to Quebec. I can well understand, Mr. Chairman-I should say I can understand, but not very well- that when the minister's argument is applied he may have wanted to work on his way to Quebec. But why run two cars down, one because the Minister of Transport wanted to go and the other because the Minister of Northern Affairs wanted to go.
The other question which arises in my mind is this. This was a Saturday and I am wondering what important government business was taking place on Saturday or Saturday night in Quebec city that required the presence of both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Northern Affairs. I do not know. I do know that Saturday night, April 28, there was a great Liberal rally as the provincial Liberal party of Quebec kicked off their campaign. I do know that both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Northern Affairs were prominently displayed at that rally. If they want to go down to

Quebec and get their brains kicked out in a provincial election, as subsequently happened, that is their business. But I suggest they should not be using government transportation, government private cars, for that particular purpose. I just point out that of course there is no doubt as to when they returned. The car of the Minister of Transport came back on April 28 and that of the Minister of Northern Affairs on April 29, which would indicate to me that they left Ottawa on the Saturday and returned either late Saturday night or Sunday and this rather limits the amount of government business they could have accomplished.
It is within this framework that I rise to ask the Minister of Transport to give every consideration to reducing his expenditures in this field of ultimate luxury. I wonder if any of the ministers of the crown has even bothered to find out what sort of alternative transportation is available on the trains? Let them try once or twice, as some of us do, the very fine accommodation which is available on the ordinary trains including drawing rooms, bedrooms and compartments where they can be by themselves and do their work and by which means the taxpayers of this country will be saved a fairly substantial amount of money.
I hope that the minister will explain to us what necessity there was for these two private cars to go to Quebec on a Saturday and come back on a Sunday and perhaps he would indicate whether or not there was any connection between that trip and their attendance at the opening of the political rally of their party in Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry; but I realize it would be very easy for me to allow this item to carry and leave unanswered on the record the remarks which my hon. friend has just made. Last year his interests turned very largely on the use of government aircraft for the transport of ministers of the crown. After having shown this extraordinary interest last year in the use of government aircraft for the transport of ministers of the crown the hon. member believes it is quite in order to use such aircraft for the transport of ministers of the crown but that it does not appear to be in order to use official cars for that purpose.
I think the hon. member would really like to have the best of both worlds. He wants to criticize members of the government when they travel by air and he likewise likes to criticize them when they travel in these railway cars.

All I can say, Mr. Chairman, so far as I am concerned, is that in using one of these official cars I am following the tradition and the practice that has been followed by a large number of my predecessors. I would like to be able to travel just as my hon. friend does and not be bothered with other people but unfortunately that is not possible. I found that when I was a member of the legislature of Quebec I was lucky if I got past the first page of a newspaper when travelling because everybody who had a bill in the legislature thought I should know what it contained. All I can tell the hon. gentleman is that the situation is no different although I have changed the scene of my activities.
The hon. member appears to find fault with the fact that these cars are available for use by ministers of the crown. He does not seem to be aware of the fact that private cars or business cars, as one might call them, are available not only to the presidents and vicepresidents but are available also to divisional superintendents of both railways. I have not heard him criticize that fact at any time, from which I must infer that he considers it is ail right for a divisional superintendent to have a private car but it is not proper for a minister of the crown to use such a car to carry on government business. Well, Mr. Chairman, I cannot subscribe to that idea because I do not think it conforms to common sense or the realities of the situation.
The hon. gentleman has shown the greatest of interest in my movements. A few moments ago we heard his comments about a trip I made to Montreal. If one will look at Hansard one will find that when I told him what was the purpose of my business in Montreal he went on to ask how it came about that on the same day I did this I actually had a vote in the house. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I have been accustomed in the face of the most bitter political opponents to having what I said as a fact accepted and not questioned to find out whether or not what I had said was true. Not only did the hon. gentleman question in the house the comment I made but he took the trouble to telephone my personal staff to find out about my movements.
Sneak.
I am of the opinion that this is carrying curiosity to a point which exceeds ordinary limits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You are a little snooper.

The hon. gentleman is interested in the fact that there were two cars used on this occasion. My recollection of the situation is that my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, went on an early morning train
Sup p ly

Transport
which was impossible for me to do because, unfortunately, I had to give up my Saturday-morning to deal with C.N.R. business in Montreal, which I may remind the hon. gentleman is not my home, and I can assure him I prefer to spend my Saturdays at home. I was not able to do so. I spent the morning in Montreal and went to Quebec by the afternoon train. I came home on the evening train and returned in time to spend half of the weekend with my family; but, Mr. Chairman, I make no apology for that because I think that is part of my job. I feel that having a car at my disposal enables me to accomplish more work than I would otherwise accomplish.
The hon. member, I think, will readily realize how difficult it would be to travel with documents spread out on adjoining chairs and I am sure he also appreciates how undesirable it would be to spread documents beside other passengers in the train where they could be read.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks further to what the hon. member for Bruce has said about the curtailment of the railroad service up through the peninsula and the counties of Wellington, Huron and Grey.
About three years ago an application was made by the railway to the board of transport commissioners to curtail the service through that part of the country. Representations were made by all the surrounding municipalities and no curtailment was made at that time.
The present situation is this. We hear rumours of curtailment. Today the hon. member for Bruce, the hon. member for Huron and I went over to the board of transport commissioners and talked to them. They said they had no word concerning any curtailment that was going to take place and they had not been advised concerning any lessening of the service on that branch line. We then went over to the postal department and learned that this department had been informed that on September 30 the time card is going to be changed and the service will be curtailed by the railroads on that line.
We are now wondering exactly what is going on. After all, if that service is going to be curtailed the people who will be affected by it should know the facts. Is this a case of slipping something in by the back door? The part of Ontario to which I have referred is going to be developed. If transportation facilities are curtailed the people there will not have the benefit of the rail lines and they will lose the advantage of the new industries that may very well be attracted to

Supply-Transport
locate there. I feel something is going on here that the people of the district should know about.
They have not been told if the rail service is to be curtailed. We understand that the railroads may curtail service to a certain extent without letting the people know about it, but this service concerns a lot of people. They helped to build up the business on this branch line and maintain it through the year. If we are going to have main lines we must have feeder lines. I sometimes think if the railroads would take some of these teams that go around the country to try to find ways of bringing about economies and sent them up through these districts to find ways of promoting railroad traffic everything would be much better.

I spoke on this item four years ago along with the former hon. member for Bruce, Donald Blue; the former hon. member for Perth, James Corry; and the former hon. member for Wellington North, Arnold Darroch. We approached the minister on this same issue and after our representations and private presentations these lines were not closed up. I think it should appear on the record that members from this district four years ago prevented this line from being closed.
Surely the suggestion is not that these decisions are being made on a political basis?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The item before us deals with official railroad cars and I think it is up to me at this moment to point out to the committee that we are dealing with estimates of the Department of Transport not of the Canadian National Railways. I looked through the items to see if I could help hon. members by finding one under which such matters could be discussed and that item would appear to be No. 494 dealing with the board of transport commissioners. I may be wrong in assuming that the curtailment of services is something which might be referred to the transport commissioners. I must insist that the matter of curtailment of services be deferred until item 494.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway-
452. To provide for the difference between the expenditures for operation and maintenance, and revenue accruing from operation during the year ending March 31, 1957, not exceeding, $150,000.

I am glad to see that the deficit in regard to the operation of the Hudson Bay railway is moving in the right direction as this item indicates there is a decrease of $275,000 over the previous year. I do not have to emphasize the importance

of this seaport in the heart of this continent to the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and the Northwest Territories. One of the great handicaps to the development of this particular region is the discriminatory differential in freight rates and my reason for making any observations on this item is to stress once again the importance and significance of the operation of the railroad and the seaport to our prairie economy. I understand that the saving on grain moving through Churchill amounts to 15 to 25 cents per bushel. I should like the minister to comment upon the reason for this decrease in the deficit. I assume it is because of the increased tonnage moving out of the port since the grain elevator facilities were extended.
The minister will recall that last year I made a recommendation concerning tourist excursions and the minister was kind enough to supply me with detailed information of these excursions operated by the C.N.R. I am glad to note that two excursions are now being run in place of one, but I suggest that there is still a wide demand for this particular type of holiday if the services and facilities are made available. There is a large waiting list, particularly of Americans, who are anxious to make this trip to the bay.
I could quote figures on this situation, but I shall not take the time of the committee to do so. It is important to the continued success of the operation of the railroad that we stimulate as far as possible a two-way flow of trade. The outward flow has been increasing at a quite rapid rate since the end of the war. For example, in 1946 there were 3 million bushels of wheat moved through the port while last year there were over 13 million bushels. That is an excellent increase but there is difficulty in connection with the inflow of imports from Europe. While this does not come directly under the jurisdiction of the minister I hope he will use his influence to have our trade commissioners point out the advantages of supplying the midwestern Canadian market through this port.

The reason for the reduced deficit is the satisfactory improvement in the amount of tonnage carried on the railroad. In 1955-56 the revenue tonnage amounted to 578,000 tons as opposed to 458,000 tons in the preceding year. As the hon. gentleman has pointed out, the great difficulty is that the volume of import freight is very small. Of those figures I have just given approximately 2,000 tons in round figures of import freight were handled in each of those two years. As the hon. members will appreciate, that is a very small fraction of the whole.

It is the consumers in western Canada who will have to create a demand for shipments into Churchill rather than shipments out of that port. The hon. gentleman comes from that part of the world and perhaps he can do some missionary work which would help to bridge the distance between 2,000 tons and 578,000 tons.

Last year when the minister's estimates on the Hudson Bay railway were up I asked if a survey had been made of the territory north of Gypsumville. At that time perhaps I was to blame for misleading the minister a little by referring to Hodgson instead of Gypsumville. This time I intend to be more specific and make sure that I do not mislead the minister in any way.
On May 17, 1948 I first raised the question of a cut-off through the interlake country to the Hudson Bay railway and at that time the Honourable Mr. Chevrier said he would bring the matter before the officers of Canadian National Railways. I know discussions have taken place as to the advisability of the railroad being extended 190 miles north to Wekusko, which is at mile 81 on the Hudson Bay railway. In that 190 miles of proposed railroad there is only one bridge that would really cost money, and that would be at Grand Rapids. In 1948 it was estimated at $1 million, but at today's prices it would cost more.
What do you mean by $1 million?

The bridge would cost that. In passing may I say that Grand Rapids is a prospective power site with a drop of some 80 feet there.
In building this 190 miles extension from Gypsumville to Wekusko there would be a saving of 250 miles, as we ship our grain at the present time to Port Churchill.
In 1948 when I talked to the then minister of transport about it I pointed out that it would be an advantage to defence by having a quicker route to Port Churchill. Also there would be a great saving to farmers and shippers sending their produce to Port Churchill. There is a lot of timber in that country and a lot of agricultural land and with a railroad going through it, it could be developed.
With a shorter haul to Port Churchill many benefits could come from that. I have already mentioned national defence-it is a more direct and quicker way to the large military establishment in the north.
If cattle prices should change and we again ship cattle to Britain instead of the United States, then it would mean a lot to the
Supply-Transport
livestock getting to the port as quickly as possible. It has been estimated that the livestock would be 18 to 20 hours less on the road, which would be a big benefit. Shipping by refrigerator cars would be a saving too, because they would not need to be iced as often as going the roundabout way.
Business from Winnipeg would be increased, and it would be possible that the boats would not come in empty but would come loaded with goods and have the grain for the return trip.
While we have ice conditions to contend with and the port is only open 100 days of the year, I feel that in the near future that 100 days is going to be extended to a longer season through the invention of radar and different aids to shipping that they never had in the old days.
This short cut would benefit Manitoba in general-it would open up new country along the railroad and it would also provide work and wages while the line was being built.
One could speak 40 minutes on this proposed route, going into the details and savings that could be achieved, but I want to leave it at that and ask that the minister give some consideration to it, and he can tell the house later whether it would appeal to him or not. When the minister brought in his estimates in March, I had a 40-minute speech ready, and the delays in his estimates have saved him from that. I have condensed it a little further every time his estimates have come up, and now he is only getting the cream of it.
I admire the hon. gentleman's forbearance.

Perhaps if I lived in the east I would look at this in a different light, but being a Manitoban I want to see the benefits of this extension come to Manitoba. But I know from my dealings with the minister in the past that he will look at this from a Canadian point of view.
I am sending over a map of Manitoba to show the minister where the route would go and how it would save haulage miles. I would at this time appeal to the minister to have the officers of his department give some consideration to building this short cut to Churchill.

I would just like to tell the
hon. member that the matter was considered in 1952. At that time the cost was found to be very substantial, with an annual loss in prospect of very close to $1 million. I do not know what the situation would be in 1956 but I shall be very glad to draw the

Supply-Transport
hon. gentleman's remarks to the attention of the Canadian National Railways and see what their reaction is.

The minister suggested that we might do some missionary work on behalf of the port situation at Fort Churchill. There is an excellent book that has been published by the Hudson Bay Route Association, and I am going to take the liberty of sending him a copy. He can read it on one of those railway journeys we were talking about a few moments ago.
It just shows that there is never a dull moment.
Item agreed to.
I wonder whether items 459 to 462 inclusive could be allowed to stand?
That will be quite agreeable to me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that items 459, 460, 461 and 462 stand?

Agreed.
464.	To provide towards the cost of surveys of Newfoundland railway properties entrusted to the Canadian National Railway Company, $17,500.

This is the item to provide for the cost of surveys of Newfoundland Railway properties, $17,500. Can the minister give us a report on the progress that is being made on these surveys and the possibilities of a program being undertaken eventually to change the Newfoundland Railway to a standard gauge railway?

In respect to the first part of the hon. gentleman's question, the item of $17,500 is intended to cover the expenditures which the railway must incur in order to establish the lines of various properties which are under its control in Newfoundland, physical surveys in order to determine boundary lines.
With regard to the question of conversion from narrow gauge to standard gauge, I talked to Mr. Gordon about the matter casually, but the cost always appeared to be staggering.
What is it?

I think it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50 million. My deputy minister points out that he thinks the current estimate is more than that. I think I should tell the hon. gentleman that it is a very substantial sum, and I think it is unlikely from the viewpoint of economics that it would be considered feasible at this time. The railway has spent a great deal of money on new equipment for the narrow gauge, and that, of course, would be completely

wasted. That is a fact that will have to be taken into account. I assume that the question must have been considered after the union of Newfoundland with Canada because I do not believe these very large expenditures would have been made if it had been considered economic to make the change that the hon. member mentioned.

Item agreed to.
465.	Degaussing and strengthening for armament, sea-going merchant ships of Canadian registry of 1,000 gross tons and over, $300,000.
I believe that this item covers coastal vessels. Could the minister tell us whether that program is nearing completion and how long it will take to finish it?

I do not think there is any prospect of this item disappearing. The expenditures last year were estimated to be $290,000. The later figure at the close of the year is $191,503. This expenditure for degaussing and strengthening is applicable to new ships and as new ships are being built the money is being spent. Perhaps we will find there are some ships being built after all.

Item agreed to.
466.	Maritime Freight Rates Act-for the payment to the railway companies operating in the select territory designated by the act, during the fiscal year 1956-57, of the difference occurring on account of the application of the act, between the tariff tolls and normal tolls under approved tariffs (estimated and certified to the Minister of Transport by the Canadian National Railway company and approved by auditors of the said company respecting the eastern lines of the Canadian National Railways and in the case of the other railways by the board of transport commissioners for Canada) on all traffic moved during the calendar year 1956 (chap. 174, R.S.), $11,500,000.

This item with respect to the Maritime Freight Rates Act involves an amount of $11,500,000, and I feel that I should remark briefly on it. A great deal has been said in recent days with respect to freight rate problems in Canada. We had a discussion in the house recently of the various problems that are now coming to the fore with regard to transportation in this large country of ours. Suggestions have been made that a regulatory body would be the answer to our freight rate difficulties. Others have suggested that a new national transportation policy is necessary. I remember reading last year that Mr. Donald Gordon, the president of Canadian National Railways, had suggested in an address in New York city that a complete new look was needed with respect to our freight rate structure in Canada. At present we have the problem of the board of transport commissioners now considering a permanent increase after granting an interim

increase a few months ago. Rather than try to talk in a rambling way about the problems facing the maritimes with respect to their position in the freight rate structure I should like to read part of an editorial from the Fredericton Daily Gleaner of Wednesday, August 8, which just arrived today. I think two paragraphs will be enough to explain the problem that we now have down in the maritimes. The editorial reads as follows:
As far as the Atlantic area is concerned, the freight rate structure is badly out of joint. These four provinces, at the end of the rail lines are wholly dependent on the railways both for buying and marketing products. We require many goods from central Canada, and due to the dense population and heavy purchasing power of Quebec and Ontario, these provinces are our best market outlets.
But the cost of taking our goods to central Canada is almost prohibitive. A series of freight rate increases has hit at the long-haul shipper unfairly. These are horizontal increases, applied by a uniform percentage.
I would ask that the next sentences be noted particularly because they explain our difficulty very clearly.
If a long-haul shipper who pays $20 and a short-haul shipper who pays $10 both have their freight rates increased by, say 50 per cent, the $20-shipper now pays $30 and the $10-shipper $15. The difference between what they pay is now $15 instead of $10.
This merely illustrates the increasing disparity with which the maritimes have found themselves faced as a result of the increases that have taken place since we came under the statutory provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act of 1927. A few days ago the Atlantic premiers met in Fredericton to consider their difficulties. The conference has been referred to here in the house. They examined their problems and tried to get united action with respect to some of the difficulties they saw in our future, and the No. 1 problem was freight rates. They put it in that priority for the future.
The maritime transportation commission has also said it is our No. 1 problem. At this late hour this evening I simply want to say that when the board of transport commissioners is considering these increases they must give more attention to our problems than to
Supply-Transport
those of any other area in Canada. Our problems with respect to freight rates go to the root of our difficulties, economic, geographic and financial, and I seriously suggest that the time has now come when we have to review these provisions that were a help to us and afforded us some consideration many years ago. We have now been put in a very serious competitive position with the central Canadian market on which we in the Atlantic provinces are now so dependent in so many ways.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some three or four weeks ago I spoke at some length about the Canadian trade position, and I do not intend at this time to repeat what I said on that occasion.
Very briefly, our trade is thriving. Exports are at remarkably high levels. Imports continue to pour in to meet the demands generated by our rapid development and prosperity which cannot be satisfied within Canada. As I said before, the resulting deficit on current account is a sign not of weakness but of strength, since it results primarily from developments which strengthen the economic fabric of the country and which will in the future increase exports and reduce imports.
On this occasion I should like to discuss not the figures of trade but the efforts which Canada has made and has participated in

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to maintain our markets abroad and to provide new opportunities for greater trade.
First, a word about the Canadian foreign trade service. During the past year a new office was opened in Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia, bringing to 54 the number of our trade offices located at strategic centres abroad, which compares with a total of 31 only ten years ago. Our files show that in 1955 the 112 trade commissioners who manned these posts played a direct part in bringing to Canada more than $100 million worth of new business. Periodic conferences of trade commissioners are held, such as the recent one held in Ottawa of our officers stationed in Latin America, at which representatives of Canadian industry were present and participated in a valuable exchange of views.
The foreign trade service carries out a continuous review of world markets to determine where our trade interests would benefit through having a resident trade commissioner. This year consideration is being given to the opening of new trade offices in Hamburg, Colombo, Los Angeles and Teheran. To meet the service's growing personnel needs we are seeking to recruit men of the highest caliber, men who are interested in serving Canada in what, to my mind, is one of the most interesting and rewarding careers of government service.
As I indicated a year ago when the decision was made to bring the Canadian international trade fair to an end, greater emphasis is being placed on participation in overseas trade fairs. We are doing everything possible to bring Canadian goods to the attention of the buyer in his own country.
In the course of the current year the Department of Trade and Commerce has prepared major exhibits for ten international trade fairs abroad. The fairs at Utrecht, Osaka, Milan, Brussels and Hanover have already taken place. Later this year we shall be exhibiting at the fairs in Lausanne, Manchester, London, Paris and Bogota. Smaller exhibits were arranged at a nutrition fair in Havana and a food show in Los Angeles, and we shall assist our footwear manufacturers at an industry show in Chicago in October.
In addition to participation at these international fairs and industry shows, we have continued to operate our Canadian showroom in Rockefeller Centre in New York. This "sales laboratory on Fifth avenue" as it has been termed, is enabling some of our manufacturers to test and enter the valuable New York market with their products.
I turn now to Canada's part in trade negotiations, in other words to the efforts being
made to improve the opportunities for trade upon which Canadian prosperity so largely depends. Canada is the fourth largest trading nation and her share of world trade has increased. Our present economic well-being and our continued expansion depends on high levels of trade.
It is for these reasons that Canada has continued to play a leading part in the constructive work of international co-operation under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. As a result of the four rounds of world tariff negotiations held under GATT, tariff levels have been significantly reduced over a very wide area of world trade. We have enjoyed a degree of world tariff security and stability never known before. Canada has taken part in each of the tariff conferences held under GATT, and we have obtained tariff concessions of value to our exporters in every region of Canada and affecting all our major exports in almost every important market.
The United States is by far the largest market for Canadian exports. I am happy to say that our exports to the United States increased by $142 million in the first six months of 1956 in comparison with the first six months of 1955. At present over one-half of our exports to the United States enter that country free of duty. This includes many of our major exports. Of the dutiable goods, over two-thirds now enter at United States rates of duty equivalent to about 10 per cent ad valorem or less. Many of our products enter the United States at tariff levels which had been reduced prior to this year to one-half or less of the levels prevailing before GATT, and to less than one-quarter of the rates in effect in the 1930's.
Here are some examples of Canadian exports on which the United States tariff has been significantly reduced over the years: the United States tariff on apples which was 25 cents a bushel in the 1930's has been reduced to 124 cents a bushel; the United States tariff on birch plywood which was 50 per cent in the 1930's has been progressively reduced to 15 per cent; the duty on a wide range of electrical goods has been reduced from 35 per cent in 1930 to less than 15 per cent; the duty on aluminum was 4 cents a pound in 1930 and will be reduced to 1J cents a pound in the near future; on a wide range of iron and steel manufactures the United States tariff has been cut from 45 per cent before GATT to 19 per cent in the most recent negotiations; on synthetic rubber the duty before GATT was 20 per cent and will shortly be reduced to 84 per cent; the duty on a large variety of chemicals has been reduced in GATT negotiations from 25 per cent to 104 per cent.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
In our relations with the United States we are, of course, most vitally concerned not only with the tariff levels affecting our goods but even more with the direction of United States tariff and trade policies generally. Without wishing in any way to minimize the threats created by United States restrictive action, it is of interest to note that only in two cases has the United States actually withdrawn concessions negotiated with Canada under GATT. Since 1948, of the 57 investigations completed by the United States tariff commission to determine whether imports were causing injury to United States producers, only seven resulted in action by the United States President to increase the tariff, and of these only one case affected Canadian trade. With reference to United States import restrictions upon certain agricultural products, there have been no new developments to report in the past year. We are extremely gratified that the President has recently given approval to the customs simplification act which has been under consideration for a long time. While this act does not go as far as we had originally hoped, it promises to be a real step ahead in the solution of some of our customs valuation difficulties in the United States.
The government has likewise continued at all times to promote the expansion of trade with the United Kingdom in both directions. In so far as the tariff is concerned, Canadian goods enter the United Kingdom either free of duty or at low preferential rates. Similarly, we provide preferential tariff treatment for most United Kingdom exports to Canada. Over the past few years United Kingdom import restrictions have also been considerably relaxed, and most basic foodstuffs and industrial materials, including about 80 per cent of our current exports to the United Kingdom, are now free of all import controls.
One of the most significant features of our trade with the United Kingdom was the sharp rise of Canadian exports to that country. Our exports rose by $116 million above the levels of 1954 to reach a record level of $769 million last year. We are fully aware that the United Kingdom market will be opened up to our goods in direct measure to the success achieved by the United Kingdom in sales to Canada and other countries. In this connection I am happy to note that in the first six months of this year United Kingdom exports to Canada have increased by 30 per cent to record levels and that this appears to be a continuing trend.
Our exports to our commonwealth partners other than the United Kingdom increased in 1955 by $42 million. This increase, which

is being maintained this year, was made possible by extensive relaxations in import restrictions which have taken place in commonwealth countries in recent years. Last month the Australian government announced a tightening up of import restrictions to protect its balance of payments. I am pleased to be able to inform the house that this intensification is apparently not intended to apply to products imported from Canada. We are hopeful, therefore, that we will fully maintain our markets in Australia.
In South Africa further relaxations of import restrictions, particularly on manufactured goods, were introduced to take effect this year. For the last two and a half years these controls have been non-discriminatory. In New Zealand about 150 products or groups of products may now be imported without restriction from Canada. Among these are such products as agricultural machinery, tobacco, textiles, paper products, metal products and a considerable variety of manufactured goods. In the new federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland 500 additional items were removed from import restrictions early this year. These products may now be imported freely from Canada. Hon. members will recall that last month I announced in the house that further products had been removed from import restriction in the British West Indies.
Our sales to European markets have constantly risen in proportion with our growing total export trade, and Europe has retained her traditional position as our third largest trading area, taking about 9 per cent of our exports, the same proportion as pre-war. Last year our exports to Europe rose by $40 million over 1954 to a total of $390 million. In the first five months of this year Canadian exports to Europe increased again by $54 million.
It has been most gratifying to see the significant progress that has been made in the United Kingdom, in other commonwealth countries and in Europe in the dismantling of import restrictions originally imposed for balance of payments reasons. The United Kingdom and other countries that had found it necessary to impose dollar restrictions themselves recognize that their export industries must become fully competitive in world markets. Any other course would breed high costs and inefficiency, and would multiply rather than resolve their basic economic problems.
I now wish to refer briefly to the government's trade agreement program in recent years. Canada now maintains most favoured nation trade relations with almost every country in the world, either through separate trade

treaties or through our participation in GATT. We have paid particular attention to establishing a sound basis for the development of trade with the countries of Latin America. We now have most favoured nations relations with every country in that area.
The trend of our exports to Latin American countries has, however, been disappointing in some respects. The statistical totals are well below the peak level which was achieved in 1952. There were exceptional circumstances, however, such as the high level of wheat sales and the aftermath of the Korean war which accounted for that peak, and it is not too difficult to see why our exports have fallen since then. From a longer point of view, our exports to Latin America are running at a rate which is ten times the level pre-war, say of 1938.
In 1954 Canada concluded a trade agreement with Japan, a country which had become our third largest market. As a result of this agreement Japan removed all discriminatory restrictions on the importation of wheat, barley, flax seed, wood pulp and certain other Canadian products. Our trade with Japan has continued at high levels and is directly contributing to the prosperity of many Canadian industries.
The trade agreements negotiated with Spain and Portugal in 1954 have placed our relations with those countries on a more assured basis and have created, for the first time since the war, continuing opportunities to sell Canadian salt fish in those traditional areas.
On February 29 of this year I announced the conclusion of a trade agreement between Canada and the Soviet union designed to provide a new and important market for Canadian wheat, and which may also create new opportunities for the export of other Canadian products.
To summarize, Mr. Chairman, we are pursuing an active and successful export promotion policy designed to strengthen the Canadian economy and to create favourable conditions for continued growth in the future. We wish to live in a world where Canada has fair and equal access to world markets, where the countries who need our goods can buy from us freely and we in turn can buy from whatever markets are in the best position to supply our import requirements. This, we believe, is the only kind of a trading world that makes sense in the long run for any country dependent on trade, and this is the only kind of trading world in which Canada can fully develop her resources and her industries on a sound competitive basis. Canada's interests can best be served through continued policies of multilateral trade.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, the Department of Trade and Commerce this year asks approval of estimates totalling $24,226,785, which is an increase of $4,859,715 over last year's approved estimates of $19,367,000. As compared with this last figure of approved estimates for the fiscal year 1955-56 the actual expenditures of this department in the fiscal year ended last March 31 were $17,653,459, indicating that the house voted 9 per cent more than the department found it necessary to spend. The increase in this year's estimates over last year's actual expenditure is therefore $6,573,326, or 37 per cent more than the department found it necessary to expend last year.
There are two items in particular in this year's estimates which have been enlarged; they are item No. 423, for the Brussels exhibition, and item No. 429 for the census.
It is usual on this first item to have a general policy debate, and because trade and commerce covers such a wide range of governmental activity and policy usually the debate has ranged widely. This year I think without loss of any profitable discussion the debate can perhaps be somewhat abridged by reason of some recent debates which have been held in this house. I refer in particular to four debates.
The first was the debate on April 18 on the resolution to ratify the trade agreement with Russia. The second was on July 9 and 10 on our Conservative amendment to the supply motion, which amendment set forth our national development policy. That debate embraced our views on trade quite extensively. The third debate was that of August 1, during the review of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs when, as reported at page 6811 of Hansard, we had the opportunity to renew the plea of this party that the government call a commonwealth conference on trade and economic questions. The fourth debate was on August 6 on the resolution to approve the international wheat agreement, during which the whole subject of wheat marketing was extensively debated.
The importance of trade to the world and to Canada has been emphasized by all that has happened since a year ago, when the house debated the estimates of this same department. We are aware that Russia has turned from the cold war to an economic struggle for world mastery. Mr. Khrushchev is reported as having stated to some Americans visiting Russia last autumn:
We value trade least for economic reasons, and most for political purposes.
While Canada has always valued trade for economic purposes, we cannot close our eyes

Supply-Trade and Commerce to the importance that trade holds in a political sense in the kind of world in which we live. We are therefore glad that in 1955 a new record was established in the value of world trade, and that Canada retained fourth place among the trading nations of the world in terms of value, ranking after only the United States, the United Kingdom and the Federal Republic of Germany. On a per capita basis in 1955 Canada ranked second only to New Zealand among the trading countries of the world.
I have a few remarks to make on the subject of total trade. The annual report of the department indicates on page 15 that Canada's total commodity exports in 1955 rose from $3,947 million in 1954 to $4,351 million, an increase of 10-2 per cent. The increase in imports, however, is much more striking, these having risen from $4,093 million in 1954 to $4,712 million in 1955, an increase of 15-1 per cent. In 1955 for the third successive year Canada incurred what is called nowadays a deficit balance on commodity trade. The excess of Canadian purchases over Canadian sales last year was $360 million.
The figures for the first six months of 1956 are perhaps even more striking. Due to the increase in our exports of wheat our total exports rose from $2,063 million in the first six months of 1955 to $2,304 million in the same period of 1956, an increase of 14 per cent. Again our imports have risen in a much more significant degree, from the 1955 total for the first six months of $2,209 million to $2,831 million for the first six months of 1956, an increase of approximately 30 per cent. With this substantial increase in imports has come a remarkable increase in our total trade deficit. During these six months Canada purchased abroad $537,500,000 more than she sold abroad. This is a record total commodity trade deficit.
I have a word to say about the direction of Canada's trade. We have drawn attention repeatedly in the past to the concentration of Canada's trade in one channel. This has been described as placing Canada's trading eggs in one basket, namely the United States. We have drawn attention to the peril of increasing this concentration in one channel, as it makes Canada's external trade position very vulnerable to changes in the trading policies of our friendly neighbour to the south. On page 16 of the annual report of the department for 1955 hon. members can see the figures on trade with certain countries. Our exports to the United States occupy the following percentages of our total exports:

In brief, two-thirds of all our external trade, both export and import, is done in the one channel. I suggest to hon. members that, whilst we all warmly value our friendly relations with the United States, this concentration of Canada's trade in one channel does make Canada's trade position extremely vulnerable.
This same trading relationship with the United States is characterized by a tremendous imbalance. Our trading deficit with that country, by which we express the excess of our imports from that country over our exports to her, amounted in 1954 to $594 million. That figure had increased in 1955 to no less than $840 million, an increase of 41-4 per cent from the year before.
The government applauds this tremendous excess of Canada's imports from the United States over our sales to the United States. The government takes satisfaction in this import balance. Indeed, the minister said this morning that our deficit on current account is a sign not of weakness but of strength. We do not take the same easygoing view of this tremendous excess of Canada's imports over her sales particularly to the United States.
It is to be remembered that this huge trading deficit is paid for by Canada today by importing United States capital. We welcome United States capital in this country, but it should be here for some other purpose than simply to pay for the deficit in our current account. We are mortgaging our patrimony to pay for this huge excess of imports over exports, and many of those imported commodities could with wise policies be produced in Canada by Canadian workmen.
The daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of July 6 points out that "the unusually large capital inflows into Canada have served to finance the import balances". We should like to see those capital inflows serving some more lasting and beneficial purpose than simply paying for a deficit on our current account.
The Financial Times is quoted in a Reuters dispatch of June 22 from London as saying of our present trading deficit:
That must be a record for any country not in the midst of a devaluation crisis. It means that some 25 per cent of Canadian expenditure abroad is not being met out of current income.
Let it not be pretended that this fact is something pointing to strength in Canada's

trading position. Let us examine the trend of 1956. The trend I have spoken of has continued into 1956, not only unabated but actually on the increase. The figures for the six months' period are not available in complete form, but the figures on imports from the United States for the first five months of this year show that our imports from that country were $1,765 million, up 31 per cent from the figure of $1,349 million a year ago. Because our imports from the United States increased very much more than our exports to the United States, the import balance on our commodity trade with the United States rose from $352,800,000 in the first five months of 1955 to $625 million in the first five months of 1956.
That is a record import balance in our trade with the United States. We have been averaging this year a record deficit in our trade with the United States of $125 million a month, and if that continues throughout the whole of the calendar year 1956-and there is no reason to doubt under present conditions that it will-Canada's trading deficit with the United States in the year 1956 will amount to $1,500 million, a figure far exceeding anything that has occurred in past history.
The government does not see any cause for alarm in this tremendous trading deficit. Apparently it sees only reason for satisfaction.
I do not need to repeat what we said in the debate in the house on July 9 and 10 concerning the nature of our trade with countries abroad. We drew attention then to the desirability of processing more of Canada's natural resources here in Canada.
On this matter of direction of trade let me remind the minister and the house that our trade with Latin America, which should be a large potential market for Canada's exports, is declining. It declined to $162 million in 1955 from $188 million in 1954 and $199 million in 1953. We are purchasing very much more from Latin America than we are selling to her. Indeed, in 1955 we purchased twice as much from Latin America as we sold to those countries. Why is our trade with Latin America not rising? The minister made a tour of Latin America some three years ago and came home bringing optimistic reports. Members will recall the report he made in this house, everything pointing to an increase in our trade with that important area of the world. All that has happened since that time has been a steady, unbroken decline in our exports to Latin America.
This morning the minister spoke of the increase last year by one in our trading
Supply-Trade and Commerce posts abroad. The appointment of a Canadian trade commissioner in Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia I am sure will be welcomed by the house. Those of us who had the privilege of visiting Salisbury after the commonwealth parliamentary conference in Africa two years ago could not fail to be impressed by the vigour of the growth of that area and the desirability and opportunity of extending Canadian trade there.
Mr. Ken MacTaggart, in a series of articles written in the Toronto Telegram recently following a very extensive tour of Africa, drew attention particularly to the trade opportunities that await Canada in Nigeria, and I bring that to the attention of the minister. Mr. MacTaggart reported statements made by bankers and businessmen in Nigeria, pointing out that Canada is not grasping the opportunities that await her there for extending her trade in that growing part of the world, on which the benefit of self-government is shortly to be conferred.
The minister had something to say this morning about our trade with Japan. Several years ago the house gave unanimous approval to the new trading agreement with Japan. However, the figures on our trade with that country for 1955 show a decline in our exports to $91 million and a substantial increase in our purchases from Japan to $36-7 million. We still have a substantial surplus in our trade with Japan, an export surplus of $54-3 million last year. That is substantially reduced from other years. Next to the United Kingdom, Japan is the best market for Canadian wheat, but every now and again there come disturbing reports from that quarter of the world. In yesterday morning's press there appeared a report from Montreal, from which I read this opening paragraph:
The entire foreign trade policy of Japan is to use "every possible device and bargaining position to promote exports and, at the same time, restrict imports to essentials", according to a report just released by three members of the Canadian primary textile industry who last fall made the first visit by a group from a Canadian industry to its counterpart in Japan.
W. M. Berry, D. S. MacKay and K. C. Mills have produced a 75,000-word, illustrated, indexed book with 31 appendices that is a thorough study of Japanese business as related to the textile trade.
I am sure all hon. members are aware of the fears of the Canadian textile trade, already suffering severely from imports of textiles. This is a situation, of course, that will need to be watched.
As to our trade with the United Kingdom, I shall not take the time to reargue, but I simply now reassert our demand and our urgent request that the government call a commonwealth conference on trade and economic questions. We dealt with this in the

Supply-Trade and Commerce debate on external affairs last week. The Leader of the Opposition made the request before the Prime Minister left for London to attend the commonwealth prime ministers' conference. It is our earnest view, and we shall continue to urge it.
I have just a few words to say on GATT and the terms of the new agreement announced in the house on June 7. The negotiations for this new agreement were commenced in January, and it represents the fourth general round of multilateral tariff negotiations under GATT. Twenty-two countries negotiated concessions, covering $2J billion worth of trade, or about 3 per cent of the total of world trade of $77 billion, using 1954 figures. Canada negotiated new agreements with the United States and 12 other countries in Europe and Latin America. Canada, however, did not negotiate directly with the United Kingdom or Japan.
The minister has spoken about the prospects of increased trade with the United States. There is no doubt that the recent negotiations will tend to accentuate the concentration of our trade with the United States. Of the $300 million of Canadian exports on which Canada received concessions from other countries, $200 million were exports to the United States. Canada gave concessions on $180 million worth of imports from other countries, of which $80 million were imports from the United States.
It is well to bear in mind, sir, that the United States tariff cuts in favour of our goods will be spread over a three-year period, 5 per cent of the reduction taking effect in each year, the first on June 30, 1956, the second on June 30, 1957 and the third on June 30, 1958 under the provisions of the United States 1955 trade agreements extension act. On the other hand, Canada's tariff reductions will be put into effect in their entirety in one step. The Minister of Finance made a statement to the house, as found at page 4793 of Hansard, when the agreements were announced in the house on June 7, and we assume there should be some statement made in the house concerning the carrying into force of the reductions that Canada has undertaken to make.
But, sir, while we have supported the principle of multilateral trade extension through agreements in this post-war period, we do draw attention to this, that the effect of this fourth extension of the GATT agreements is going to be an acceleration of the tendency to concentrate our external trade in the one channel, namely the channel with the United States. We do not like to see multilateral trade negotiations giving mere lip service to the idea of multilateral trade

and becoming increasingly a contribution to an expansion of bilateral trade simply with one country, where we already have to a dangerous degree concentrated our trade.
The final matter I wish to deal with in these opening remarks relates to crown corporations. There are nine crown corporations that are responsible to the minister in his capacity as Minister of Trade and Commerce, apart from those that were referred to in the debate on the estimates of the Department of Defence Production a month ago. One crown corporation has been added recently to the list of corporations that are responsible to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. The bill that established this corporation was given royal assent on June 7. There is, of course, no power to reopen the debate on that thorny measure, but there is the right on the part of the house to know fully what has happened since June 7 and to compare what has been done with the promises, representations and undertakings given to the house by the government in the course of the passage of that bill through the house.
The house is aware that on June 8 the corporation was established and five directors were appointed, and subsequently a general manager. It will not be forgotten that two facts stood out in the government's submission of that bill to the house. The first was the government's claim of urgency; that extraordinary measures, to put it mildly, had to be taken both in connection with the passage of the bill through the house and in the relationships with the corporation in order to complete the construction of the pipe line from the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary to the vicinity of Winnipeg this year.
The second fact that was outstanding in the government's case in that debate was that the whole reason for favouring Trans-Canada Pipe Lines as the chosen instrument of the government for building the pipe line was that it had the organization, the contracts and, above all, an option on the 34-inch pipe necessary to construct the pipe line. On those representations by the government the majority in this house acted, and a cted ruthlessly.
But we now find since June 7 that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited had an option not on 575 miles of 34-inch pipe required to build this line from the Alberta border to the vicinity of Winnipeg, but on only about 25 per cent of the 34-inch pipe required for that purpose. I therefore say-and I base my remarks upon the record; I shall give hon. members who wish it the page references for what I say-that the house was

misled by the representations and statements made by the government. The house was led by the statements of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to believe that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines had available all the 34-inch pipe that would be required to build this leg across the prairies.
