Our most serious problem arises in respect of our trade situation with the United States. Here is a Canadian Press dispatch that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of August 4. It reads in part as follows:
Imports have risen even faster, hoisting the value of incoming goods to a new record and creating a trade deficit of $537,500,000 for the six months.
Further on it says:
The six-month trade deficit was created in dealings with the United States. The balance in favour of the United States was a record $751,600,000 compared with $420,400,000 in the first half of 1955.
If these agreements that we are entering into are supposed to be helping us, surely the situation confronting us with respect to the United States is one which we should look at very aggressively. Let us not get any idea that everybody appears to play under the same rules in connection with these trade agreements. Here is an article from the Financial Post of December 10, 1955, with respect to the United States situation. It reads in part as follows:
This "how-pure-we-are" yarn about United States tariffs can only be performed by concealing a whole maze of hidden strings and off-stage performers, such as the valuation procedures of U.S. customs, the operations of the tariff commission, the peril points, the escape clauses, the GATT waivers, the agricultural quotas, and the "national security" provisions. The other part of the trick is to make the audience accept a set of completely meaningless statistics. The quickness of the figures deceives the mind. This is where the skill of the performer really counts.
Under the heading, "How to Avoid Competition" it goes on to say:
The dominating characteristic of the United States tariff is that it does exclude most of the goods which might compete with U.S. industry. It bears relatively lightly-apart from quotas and embargoes and appeals to the U.S. tariff commission-on raw materials which the United States wants. It bears so heavily on manufactured goods that very few of them cross at all. Therefore they don't show up in the average rates of duty collected.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The dominating characteristic of the Canadian tariff, by contrast, is that it does not exclude manufactured goods which compete with Canadian industry. It charges them a certain rate of duty; but the duty is still low enough that they do come in in very large quantity.
Here is an indication that whatever the agreements are that we have entered into, we cannot hope by the present system to solve the over-all trade deficit problem. It would appear to me, sir, that when I used the expression "downhill ride" it was a very fair term. It seems to me that we are getting by and balancing our position by an inflow of capital investment for which we are duly grateful, but the day of reckoning must soon arrive and whether or not it affects us certainly at some time it is going to affect succeeding generations of Canadians.
Time.

I think my timekeeper over there has beaten me to the punch, but I shall try to sum up in two or three minutes. We have had the benefit of reading the minister's report, but to me it is a report that is drawn up in the same general manner as the communiques we now read on the results of commonwealth conferences. It really does not tell us too much. In my opinion what we are going to have to know is what methods are used by the trade department to arrive at their figures when they say to us that they have promoted $100 million of trade during the past year. I think we are entitled to know what sales steps are taken by the same people in selling their services. I know we have the picture of the trade counsellor who is in town and the businessman having the opportunity of being there and meeting him, but it seems to me what is going to be required is a most extensive and aggressive expansion of the trade facilities of the department for businessmen who are interested in getting into the United States market. I note that at page 21 of the minister's report he says:
Three senior officers of the department examined the operations of the trade commissioner service in four leading market centres in the United States. As a result of this study, recommendations have been made to strengthen the service in that vital market.
I think what we need from the minister is not a statement that a survey has been made and that steps have been taken, but we should know what steps are being taken, how soon others will be taken and how many people are involved. As a second point, and I shall only mention it in passing because I am informed that this may not be the place to deal with it, I think we would like to know what trade steps are behind the communique issued by the commonwealth conference, is


there anything which indicates that some progress may be made along the lines of obtaining complete convertibility of sterling at some time in the foreseeable future.
There is also a reference to the intelligence service of the commodities section, but we would like answers to these questions. What are they doing? What information is getting to us on the question of the standard of living in various countries in advance of the time when their products are reaching our shores? I think we want to go one step further. We should be able to know what steps they are taking to ensure in advance that unfair trade practices are not being used and are not going to be used. I specifically refer to that because we had an example last year where a product had entered Canada, had been sold and the damage had been done. Then we had to turn back and see whether there was some means of cutting off the supply. At that time the product had already been sold in large quantities in the Canadian market.
Another point is this. What steps are being taken in advance to ensure that the Department of National Revenue is informed as to the countries where subsidies of one kind or another are being used so it is in a position to assess its duties and values on an up to date picture to show, shall I use the term, an unfair competitive situation which may result from conditions in that other country?
There is a complete service.

The minister says there is a complete service and I believe him. What we should like to know is this. Instead of having this bland assertion in a report, we should like to know what is being done along that line. Are we sure we are covering that particular point?
There is a further item that I might mention, namely the use of the Canadian Standards Association. It is used, and has been used in the past, to determine what is considered to be a satisfactory standard from the point of view of safety. At the same time there have been allowed through the customs articles which do not meet the standards set by that association. It seems to me there must be a liaison job required there. I do not think it can be answered by the department simply saying, "That is a provincial responsibility and we are not going to interfere". As well, I think we should like to know how the department has assessed the efficacy of exhibitions as used by the department. We should like to know what value we are getting for our money. What actual amount of trade have their statisticians traced to these exhibitions? We should like to know that so we can see that the best use is being made of them.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Finally, I say that unless we are prepared to go along with a situation which involves a continual drain of natural resources from this country in return for highly competitive manufactured goods, we must start to bargain from strength with the United States. It seems to me that should not be too tough a job. The article in the Financial Post mentions that they have their set-up designed to ensure that they get the flow of natural products which they really need. If we have those things, surely we can suggest to them a system whereby our own manufacturers will be in a position to meet them on fair ground.
When I talk about the expansion of the service in the United States, I simply say this. Any one who has had any business experience and has had to go to Washington in order to ensure that goods get in there will know that help is definitely required. I must say that for my part, when I was there I received the best of help. But at the same time that help should be available in as many cities as possible in the United States.

I shall detain the committee for just a moment. With respect to the question of the right of the province to prevent the export of iron ore, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the government of British Columbia for many years have prevented the export of raw logs that come from crown lands in that province.

I should like to ask the
minister one question, and then I intend to make a suggestion based on a request from tens of thousands of Hungarians across Canada. Would he say what trade agreements have been entered into with Hungary during the past year and whether or not there are at present any being contemplated? What was the subject matter of those agreements, if there were any?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: At the moment, Mr. Chairman, we have no trade agreement with Hungary, but that country has indicated that it wishes a trade agreement. An appointment is being arranged. It will be within the next two or three months, when a delegation will come from Hungary to Canada for the purpose of negotiating for a trade agreement. We have given credit to Hungary. I think we gave credit for 100,000 tons of wheat, and Hungary has drawn on that credit only to the extent of about 20,000 tons.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the minister for that explanation. I now wish to bring to his attention a state of affairs which is of interest particularly to the people of Hungarian origin in Canada, and also to those of other origins who have
relatives behind iron curtain countries. There are about 100,000 Hungarians in this country who are pressed very strongly by their relatives and friends behind the iron curtain for assistance by way of food parcels, clothing and the like. Food parcels can be sent to Hungary through various dealers and agencies generally operating under the aegis or protection of the Hungarian government.
There is a great difference in the handling of these parcels. If they are sent by private persons directly or through dealers who deal particularly in commodities that the peoples of the country might require, you find that the duty that has to be paid on those parcels upon arriving in Hungary is from 60 per cent to 75 per cent, thus making the parcel being sent almost useless to the receiver. With the added transportation costs it is prohibitively expensive to the sender. The obvious purpose of this policy of maintaining so high a tariff and such stringent regulations is to force Canadians to send the assistance through trustees of the Hungarian government, who enjoy a nearly monopolistic privilege in this business. Instead of sending the actual parcel to Hungary, they only ask for payment of a certain pre-fixed tariff price, for which a certain amount of food will be handed out to the receiver of the parcel in Hungary from the state-owned store. There is no duty to be paid on these sendings, but the prices of the goods are exorbitantly high.
One of these agencies operating in Canada has set forth the contents of its sample parcels. One at $12 consists of one pound of coffee, half a pound of tea, two pounds of rice, and one bottle of liquor. Another at $20 consists of two pounds of cocoa, one pound of coffee, one pound of tea, and three boxes of sardines.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In order that I may have an idea of the relative prices, will the hon. member tell me the value of the liquor?
I could not hear what my hon. friend said.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What I asked was this. In order that I may be able to judge the other prices, will my hon. friend tell me the value of the bottle of liquor?

I am going to come to that. That is where the joker is in this matter. I know nothing of that subject and am obliged to speak from second-hand information only. I am in the same position as the minister. As I was saying, the $20 parcel consists of two pounds of cocoa, one pound of coffee, one pound of tea and three boxes of sardines. Then there is a third one

Supply-Trade and Commerce which consists of two pounds of coffee, one pound of cocoa, and two pounds of sugar. That is $15.
What is actually happening is this. The Hungarian government has barter arrangements with certain countries and is receiving the materials which they incorporate over there into these parcels and thereby they are securing for themselves a large amount of Canadian dollars.
As I said a moment ago, there are 100,000 people of Hungarian origin in Canada, and the average amount they send under the present parcel scheme is from $500,000 to $1 million a year, thus making it possible for the Hungarian government, by operating on the emotional reactions of these people, to secure Canadian dollars. The Hungarians in Canada and their organizations have protested both privately and publicly against the discrimination and what they call ruthless extortion introduced by the Hungarian authorities in connection with the parcel traffic, but they have not been able to secure any results. The government at the time had negotiated the Canadian-Polish trade agreement, or at least had entered into trading relationship and removed many of the difficulties that Canadians of Polish origin had suffered theretofor at the hands of the Polish government. The same thing applied in Czechoslovakia.
The people of Hungarian origin ask this. When the next trading arrangements are made with Hungary, permission should be granted as part of the exchange arrangement for Canadians to send parcels containing basic food products such as flour, sugar, fats, bacon, rice, meats and fish, and in that way be of assistance to their people behind the iron curtain who are today in a condition of starvation. At the same time we could secure the consent of the Hungarian government to remove the present unjust regulations. These people in their hearts want to assist. My hon. friend asked me what was the price of the liquor in one parcel. I do not know, but it is something the people do not want-
Is it Canadian liquor?

I do not think they
designated it. I am not sure of that. But the fact remains that these people who are desirous of being of assistance to their friends and relatives are being mulcted to an unfair degree, and this is at the same time, assisting the Hungarian government to secure between $500,000 and $1 million in Canadian dollars.
If when the next trade arrangements are being considered the minister would make representations on this problem in a manner

similar to those that were made and which caused the removal of the injustice in Czechoslovakia and also Poland, the minister might earn the appreciation of 100,000 good Canadians of Hungarian origin, who have stood against communism and who want to stand against it. They do not want to be placed in the position of being subject to extortion by the Hungarian government.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Our trade negotiators will do what they can when any new negotiations come along. The situation in negotiating present day agreements is somewhat different from the old agreements that were negotiated with Poland and Czechoslovakia, which were what we call agreements on commerce and navigation. They differ from the most favoured nation agreements which we are making today. We met the same problem in negotiating with the Russians. All we were able to get them to say was that whatever the duty was it would be non-discriminatory. In other words it would be the same against Canada as against any other country, and that is all we can really insist upon. My hon. friend would not want Canada to agree with Hungary that we would charge only a certain duty on Hungarian shipments.

It is not exactly the point, a difference or discrimination in the tariff. It is a system being used whereby extortion is being practised by the communist Hungarian government against Canadians desirous of helping their friends and relatives behind the iron curtain. All I am asking on behalf of these people is that when any negotiations to correct this situation which, on the face of it, is unfair, unjust and constitutes a method on the part of the Hungarian government of securing Canadian dollars by surreptitious means.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
All I can say is
that we will do our best. I understand the problem, but I would not want to raise the hopes of our citizens of Hungarian origin too high. It will not be through lack of effort if we do not succeed.

Before this item carries I should like to ask the minister if this is the item, or is it some other item of his estimates, under which a person can ask what provision the minister is making, if any, to cushion the effect of the very serious increase in the price of steel which has been announced in the last few days. The minister knows that when the price of steel was advanced $5 per ton back in April, 1946, the impact upon the price structure of Canada made by that increase and the consequent increase in the wages of the steel workers

who asked for their share of that $5, cut the value of the Canadian dollar practically in half.
The minister is very familiar with all that. He knows that ill-advised and foolish people all over the country are calling that horrible thing inflation. It was not inflation. The rise in price was not the result of too much money in circulation in the country for the available goods; it was not the result of any shortage of goods; it was the result of definite price manipulation. If the Steel Company of Canada raised its price $5 per ton, that had nothing to do with money at all; it was a manipulation of price upward, and every commodity in Canada which was made of that steel had to increase in price because of the increased costs, regardless of a scarcity of goods or a surplus of goods. The wage increase for the steel workers resulted in wage increases all across the board in Canada, not one but two or three. The result has been that today our prices are very high compared with what they were in 1946.
If that rise of $5 per ton in the price of steel in 1946 produced this almost calamitous effect on the price structure of Canada, what is likely to be the effect of an increase in the price of steel of $6 or $7? Has the minister given any thought to this matter? Are the people of Canada and the Canadian government to be absolutely helpless in the face of a move of this kind? Would he ssey, if he were doing it over again, that nothing could have been done to cushion the effect of that $5 increase in the price of steel back in 1946? Could not subsidies have been paid by the government to the steel company so that people using steel would be able to get their steel at the same price they were able to get it before the increase of $5 per ton?
I just wanted to ask the minister if he had given this matter any thought. It would come under his department, certainly, and I wondered if he had any suggestions as to what we are going to do. Are we, within the next 10 years, going to have another cut in the value of the Canadian dollar by 50 per cent as a result of the present contemplated increase in the price of steel? I do not wish to go into this matter if this is not the right place, but I should like to know what the minister thinks about the matter or whether I am being alarmed unduly.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We could have a little discussion about the chicken and the egg here. I always thought the wage increase came first and the price changes were consequential upon that wage adjustment. However, my hon. friend knows that this government has no legislative powers to regulate
Supply-Trade and Commerce prices. In order to do that we would need to get emergency powers. Having tried to get emergency powers from this parliament once, I am not trying any more. I am afraid I cannot do anything about it.

The minister means, then, that the Canadian economy and the Canadian people are helpless to prevent this horrible thing which is approaching us and which anybody with any vision at all can see is approaching?
The minister spoke as though it might have been a wage increase which caused the rise in the price of steel back in 1946. I am afraid his very fine memory has failed him in that respect. He knows very well that the steel companies asked for the privilege of increasing the price of steel $5 a ton in February, 1946. The request was granted in April of 1946. Then the steel workers struck for their share of the $5 a ton increase. The minister can very well remember the long meetings we had in the industrial relations committee in which the steel workers presented their case. They continued to strike and hold parades until they finally got the increase after 82 days of idleness. Then other workers demanded comparable increases all across Canada. Thus the costs of production of every commodity ultimately forced up prices. Can the minister give us any more hope as regards the present increase of steel price or is he now advising us that we might just as well look out for economic disasters of almost any kind?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Mr. Chairman, has the minister nothing further to say?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sorry. We are well aware of the cost of steel as well as the key commodities which regulate the cost of living and the government is doing all it can chiefly through fiscal measures at the moment to hold inflation in check, but to apply price controls as a federal responsibility would mean legislation from this parliament and I doubt very much if we could get the legislation approved. I think my hon. friend would vote for it but I doubt if many other hon. members would.

The minister has used that word "inflation" again. He knows that within the last six weeks there has been an increase in the price of a loaf of bread, yet no one even in a nightmare could imagine that this is because there is a shortage of bread or that there is too much money for the amount of bread that is in Canada. It is absolute nonsense to call that an inflationary
7300	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce rise. It is very much the same as the increase in prices which came about as a result of increased steel prices in 1946. If we are going to allow ourselves to be fooled into thinking that such rises in prices are the result of inflation and then the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance assume it is the result of inflation and apply measures calculated to control inflation we are heading for plenty of trouble-real trouble!

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend is taking a slight advantage of me. He is an economist and I am just a run-of-the-mill engineer. I do not understand these matters so I cannot contribute very much to the discussion.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lethbridge has raised a subject in which I am interested but I do not think it is in order at this point.
It is in order because we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Unless we are going to discuss the question of price controls I do not see how it can be in order under this item.
Mr. Pallet!: Mr. Chairman, I was interested in reading the reports before I came down to the house concerning this department, and in listening to the speeches after I came here that are always presented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in an optimistic tone. And I see no reason why they should not have been; after all-

I am sorry, I did not hear what the hon. member said.
Mr. Pallet!: I said that the Minister of Trade and Commerce always gives his report in a very optimistic tone and I see no reason why he would not because after all this country is endowed with the greatest natural resources in the world. We have the native ability of the people of this country to develop those resources and therefore there is no reason why such reports should not be optimistic. In the development of a country such as ours there seems to be an acknowledgment by the minister that we occasionally need government assistance. When things are going well it is because of government assistance and when things are not going well he says it is because of the lack of effort on the part of private individuals.
There is room in the development of a country such as this for certain government participation and I think that participation and leadership in particular has been rather lacking recently despite the kudos some hon. 

members opposite seem to seek for themselves. I refer generally to the standard of living of the average Canadian.
Much has been said concerning this subject. And then we look at the standard of living of our neighbours to the south who have not the per capita national resources we have and we observe the great difference in our standard of living as compared with theirs and this is passed off as being the price of sovereignty. This passing off in these terms is just a little too simple. That is not the real reason for the difference at all. It is because proper encouragement has not been given in the development within this country. The reason that encouragement has not been given-

Where have you been for the last 20 years-resting?
Mr. Pallet!: -is because the government knows that as people attain certain living standards throughout the country it leads them to a type of thinking that is not in keeping with the thinking of hon. members who form the government. There has been a deliberate hold-up by them designed to meet their own political ends.
As one looks at the broad picture over the last few years one becomes aware that this situation has existed for many years. During the time in which this party has been in power this has been a carefully calculated plan and the responsibility, of course, is that of this government. There is no excuse whatsoever for the rapidly widening difference between the standard of living in this country, albeit it is high, and the standard which obtains in the United States.
I think this is a matter with which the Minister of Trade and Commerce should concern himself.
Today, as an example, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the adverse balance of trade is nothing; it is just a slight thing in the consideration of foreign trade. Any two-year-old knows that you buy as cheaply as you can and sell as dearly as you can on foreign markets. That is so fundamental that it is ridiculous for the minister to mention it here. Any two-year-old child also knows that you cannot continue to have an adverse balance of trade with any country for any length of time without encountering serious consequences at home. The minister might at least respect our intelligence to the extent that he would admit this and give us some assurance that he is taking some steps to do something about it. He does not have to do this by government control. Our system of government in Canada has always provided that where leadership is given in certain directions by government,

industry is only too happy to operate without control. That leadership by government is certainly one of the things that has been lacking in this country.
A man may have a reputation but the people of this country are not interested in a reputation; they are interested in what is being done now and what is going to be done in the future. I suggest that the minister should make some effort to provide aggressive leadership in this direction.
Carried.
The only thing that will be carried in the future will be the hon. gentlemen sitting opposite, who will be carried out of this house by the votes of the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Speak for yourself.
Mr. Pallet!: The minister said something about the chicken and the egg in reply to a question. I suggest that our situation concerning the trade balance with the United States is somewhat like that of the farmer in relation to his neighbour.
The farmer owned a cow and was selling milk to his neighbour. One day his neighbour asked if he would sell him more milk. The farmer replied that he did not have another cow. The neighbour said he would provide him with a cow and in return would take a piece of the farmer's land. This process continued until finally the farmer had a herd of cows and his neighbour owned all the land on which the cows stood. The neighbour was soon buying all the milk so he controlled the price. That is the situation we are being led into. If you want a simple analogy, there it is.

It is simple all right.
Mr. Pallet!: It has to be simple for you people across the way to understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
We cannot expect anything else from you.
Mr. Pallet!: You know, it is remarkable that when difficulties arise with the government across the way they always bring up a bogey to get the people's minds off the government's troubles. The bogey they are bringing up now is inflation in order to get the people's minds off what is happening in the house. To do that they spread this bogey of inflation. That is the present bogey.
They pay lip service to this by starting to restrict credit. Industry cannot develop without money; Canadian industry cannot develop without money. Many Canadian industries are young and are just getting on their feet. I suggest most seriously that the Minister of Trade and Commerce as one of the senior
Supply-Trade and Commerce members of the cabinet, as one of the members who formulates government policy, encourage a second look at this. I am pleased to see that the Minister of Finance is now consulting with the Minister of Trade and Commerce on this matter. I did not expect that there would be such an immediate reaction. I suggest that there be a serious second look taken at this restriction of money for Canadians generally and in particular for Canadian industry.
Canadian industry must develop if this country is to be strong industrially and it must develop with Canadian money. That cannot be done if you cut it off. You can say as much as you like that this has nothing to do with you, that the government does not dictate the money policies of this country, but there is no one who will believe you. We know and you know that with a nod from the government the banks follow suit.
It is the other way around.

I suggest that serious consideration be given to lifting the restrictions on credit which have had such a serious effect upon the development of manufacturing and other commercial enterprises in this country.

Mr. Chairman, last Thursday in the city of Brandon after waiting patiently for some five years a very important project finally got under way. The same afternoon rather disconcerting news came out of the east which threatened to dampen the enthusiasm that had been created as a result of the commencement of the installation of the gas pipe lines which would be used to supply natural gas to the city of Brandon. I think there is misunderstanding as to just what is the situation in relation to the continuation of this important $2 million project in my home city and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the only man who can give the final word on the matter. That is my reason for bringing it up briefly this afternoon.
The report came from the Toronto office of Trans-Canada to the effect that gas would not be available this fall and as a result Mr. Frank J. Simington, manager of the Plains-Western Gas and Electric Company Limited, which company has the franchise to supply gas to the city of Brandon, inserted a half page advertisement in the Brandon Daily Sun of August 3 reading as follows:
Brandon Natural Gas Delivery Delayed
Thursday, August 2nd
Trans-Canada Pipelines Ltd. today at 2.00 p.m. informed your gas company that natural gas would not be available for delivery to Brandon or points east until the summer of 1957.
Because of this disappointing news it will now be necessary to delay your applications for service

Supply-Trade and Commerce
lines. Information regarding the servicing of new homes with temporary fuel until natural gas becomes available, will be announced later.
We sincerely regret having to make this announcement which is due to Trans-Canada's inability to deliver natural gas to the area this fall. The construction of the distribution system will continue uninterrupted.
This subject was raised briefly in the house last Friday morning when the Minister ol Trade and Commerce replied, as reported on page 6920 of Hansard, as follows:
No authorized representative has made any statement to anyone that gas will not be delivered in western Canada this year.
Notwithstanding that fact the company laying the lines in the city of Brandon have taken this drastic action. Apparently there is misunderstanding somewhere. When Mr. Simington was confronted with what appeared to be a contradiction he replied as follows:
Contacted by the Sun early this morning after Trans-Canada officials had declined to confirm the Brandon report of six months' delay, Mr. Simington said: "If Mr. Lowe were to say that he would guarantee natural gas would be available at Brandon in 1956, I would be most happy to publicly apologize. Until he says that, I shall wait to be shown."
That is the situation as it stands. There are quite a few people affected by this, because they have been planning on putting in gas this fall. I am wondering if we cannot get some official word which would clear up this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not know anything about the Brandon situation other than what I have been told by the hon. member. He told us there was no hurry about getting the pipe line started, no hurry about building the line or any danger in their being unable to build it this year. The relations between Trans-Canada and the city of Brandon are private matters. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is a private corporation and I assume that the company owning the distributing system in Brandon is a private corporation. I suggest that it might be very helpful to both companies if my hon. friend would just leave it alone.

That is not the kind of reply I had anticipated but it is the reply I might have expected in this case. As I said in my opening remarks, we have been waiting patiently for gas for five years and have never made any attempt to delay the gas line and as far as-
Oh, oh.

-building gas lines is concerned, Soviet Russia builds them too. There is a right way of doing things and a wrong way of doing things. That is the only attitude we have taken in this house. We want natural gas in the city of Brandon.
[Mr. Dinsdale.!

Mr. Chairman, if hon. members have concluded raising the points they wish to raise there are several matters I should like to bring up on this first item in regard to our trade relations with the United States and about which I should like to have some comment by the minister. The first concerns the customs simplification bill recently passed by both houses of congress and which I believe has been signed by President Eisenhower. As I understand it, in terms of 1954 trade the legislation covers about $1-4 billion worth of imports from all countries, representing about 15 per cent of all imports into the United States in the year 1954. Of the remainder about half of all imports into the United States, enter the country duty-free; the balance is taxable at specific rates of duty, and the new formula applies only to the ad valorem rates. Would the minister clarify the situation?
I personally have not seen the text of the bill, but this is a matter of leading importance to Canadian exporters. There have been high hopes held out to them ever since this matter was first discussed at the GATT conference. We all know what a difficulty the so-called jungle of administrative red tape in the United States in relation to customs administration has presented to Canadian exporters. Would the minister make a statement on this and indicate what help now the Canadian exporters can expect to have as a result of the enactment of this measure by congress?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The effect of the bill will be to eliminate the use of "foreign value" and to make "export value" the prime basis for levying ad valorem duties. In other words, duty will be levied on the price at which the goods are freely sold by foreign manufacturers for export to wholesalers in the United States. For practical purposes, this is the optimum valuation hoped for by exporters. In other words, under this arrangement the exporter in Canada fixes the value upon which duty would be based, instead of the customs valuator in the United States who used to fix an arbitrary value which we call the "foreign value".
Is it clear that it applies only on the ad valorem rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

Can the minister assess the value of this measure in general? It has been a matter of discussion now for some years. The minister has had a report on the measure. How far will the measure go to satisfy the objectives of Canadian exporters and, I believe, of the Canadian government in the negotiations on this subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The bill would have satisfied Canadian exporters-it gave them everything we have been asking for in that regard-but unfortunately a rider was applied in the Senate which takes away some of the sunshine.
The Senate version contains a clause which directs the treasury department to publish a list of imported articles, not by country, the values of which would be reduced more than 5 per cent if appraised under the new "export value" procedure. These articles will continue to be valued on the old basis of "foreign value" and will not receive the benefit of the new valuation procedure.
It is difficult to determine which of our exports would not receive the benefit of the new procedure if the Senate amendment remained in the bill. It did remain in the bill. We shall be following the matter closely. That is the situation. We do not know the effect of that Senate rider which provides that the "export value" shall be not more than five per cent less than the "foreign value". It will take time to appraise the working out of that rider in practice.

I shall not pursue that further. It is obviously a matter for a report next year after there has been some experience of working under the new law.
The second point in relation to trade with the United States concerns oil exports to the United States. It will be recalled that in the 1955 session my leader drew attention to reports that efforts were made by the United States government to apply indirect limitations on importations into the United States of oil from Canada. By way of indicating that the matter is apparently by no means dead in the United States, I should like to read two paragraphs from a recent issue of the Journal of Commerce, a United States publication:
Thirty-one American senators have asked defence mobilization director Arthur S. Flemming-
No relation.
-to force oil importers to restrict their imports to the 1954 ratio of imports to domestic production. For the past year, Mr. Flemming has tried to make oil importers comply with the "1954 formula" on a voluntary basis, and Mr. Flemming has recently complained that "no evidence is available to us that oil imports have been, or are being, restricted within the limits determined to be necessary in the interest of national defence".
The importance for Canada of the letter signed by 15 republicans and 16 democrats, representing close to one-third of the membership in the Senate, is that the group also hinted that "exemption of Canadian and Venezuelan oil and all oil into the west coast was circumvention of the intent of the 1955 trade agreements act, which calls for government intervention when imports threaten national security". Pressure may be building up for the application for compulsory restrictions on oil imports into the United States which will directly
Supply-Trade and Commerce
affect the Canadian oil industry. This may not happen, but it is something to watch.
I wonder whether the minister would comment on this subject and on the outlook, because it is a matter obviously of very high importance to Canada in general as well as for the Canadian oil industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Our defence is that to suggest that limitation of exports of Canadian oil into the United States would contribute to the defence of the United States is rather far-fetched. So far that has been accepted by the state department and by the government of the United States, and I believe that the fallacy of any other argument is so obvious that it will continue to be accepted. In the previous limitation, Canada and Venezuela were exempted from the provisions of the restriction. I sincerely believe that Canada will continue to be exempted.

I am glad to hear that statement from the minister.
A third matter in relation to the United States concerns these periodical meetings of Canadian ministers with members of the cabinet in Washington. I understand that these meetings, when they were first undertaken, were to be held at fairly regular intervals but, unless there have been some held in more recent times that I am not aware of, the last one was held a very considerable time ago. Would the minister tell the committee what plans have been made for resumption of these conferences and what items are to appear on the agenda?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The last meeting was held, I believe, last October. The original intention was to hold meetings every six months, but, like other meetings of this kind, it is well not to have them unless they are needed. We call them, or the United States calls them, when there are particular problems to discuss.
An outgrowth of the last meeting held with the ministers was that arrangements were made for meetings between the officials of the United States and the officials of Canada having to do with the marketing of wheat and other grains. Those meetings are held every six weeks and they are most helpful in working out solutions to common problems. I dare say we have never let as long as a year go by without having a top-level meeting, and I dare say we shall arrange one this fall, but with one thing and another we all get very busy, and it takes a good deal of time to arrange a meeting of this kind.

Has the Canadian government been compiling its contribution to the agenda for the next meeting? If so, can the minister tell us what those items will be?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There is no formal agenda prepared long in advance. We have an ad hoc agenda, but there is no great formality associated with these meetings. They usually last one evening and one day and they are carried on with considerable informality.

My next question naturally arises out of the GATT conference and it also has some relation to a report to which I drew the attention of the house some time ago. It is a report that came out of Canberra in a Reuters dispatch last January, indicating that the new Australian minister of trade, Hon. John McEwen, had expressed some strong views on the old preferential tariff treatment within the British commonwealth in the light of the United States policy on disposal of farm surpluses. I should like to ask the minister if he would state the policy of the government in relation to the commonwealth trade preferences.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I might say that Mr. McEwen will be with us here in Ottawa tomorrow and we will know more about his views at that time. I believe he has been expressing his views in London and Washington. In general we support the viewpoint of Australia, although we are not unhappy with our relations with the United Kingdom in that regard. We all agree that the surplus disposal procedures of the United States are very harmful to all of us and we each protest separately, but I rather think that Mr. McEwen's views go somewhat deeper than that. I will know more about them after we have our discussions tomorrow.

With regard to what remains of the commonwealth trade preferences, will the minister state the position of the government? We are aware of what GATT has done in trenching upon these preferences up to a point, but what in general is the policy of the government with regard to the system as it remains?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I should like to make it clear that GATT has not encroached on the empire agreements. GATT agreements contain an exception in favour of the empire agreements, but in carrying out negotiations it is often helpful to have the commonwealth agreements amended. England itself has asked us to amend items so that they could work out a trade arrangement with the United States or with some other country. There have been some amendments but I would not say that it has been a watering down. Canada is quite happy with the commonwealth agreements. We are adjusted to them. We think they are helpful

towards balancing our trade and we have no desire for any alteration. Australia, on the other hand, feels that the commonwealth agreements are working very much in favour of the United Kingdom and against the interests of Australia. That is a separate argument in which Canada is not taking part.

The next matter is one I had expected the member for Waterloo North to raise. I think it is proper at this time that the minister should be asked for and should give some statement to the house in the light of the representations that have been made to him in relation to rubber footwear. This is a subject, I am sure, that has been before the minister frequently. I do not need to remind the house of the problem involved in the decline in Canadian production of canvas footwear and waterproof footwear and the tremendous expansion in imports of these products from countries abroad where the standard of living and consequently the cost of production are very much lower than in Canada. What has the minister to say on this subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think it would not be helpful for me to express an opinion just now. The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour and I are meeting the industry in an attempt to work out something, and I think that to make an announcement of our views at the moment would harm the negotiations. If my hon. friend would let that stand until later I think perhaps we would be more likely to get a reasonable solution. But I will admit at once that in the present situation the industry is very unhappy. Imports, particularly of tennis shoes and shoes of that kind, are seriously interfering with Canadian production. The interference with waterproof shoes is not serious at the moment although it could be in the future. We are examining the position in the hope that we can give the industry some help.
I do not wish to press the point if there is some likelihood of a solution being earnestly sought. The minister asked that it be left until later. Does he mean this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There is no hope of that. The situation will not change when the house adjourns and I hope the house will not wait that long. However, certain approaches are being made which I think might be interfered with by any statement I might make.
Is the solution one likely to involve the necessity for legislative action on the part of parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

The last matter I should like to raise is in regard to the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. There are some questions of a specific nature that I should like to ask the minister. In the regulations promulgated in the Canada Gazette of June 27, containing order in council P.C. 1956-858 of June 7 last, the last of the clauses of bylaw No. 1 of the corporation reads as follows:
The president shall submit to the board for approval prior to submission to the minister proposed budgets of operating and capital expenditures for the next ensuing financial year of the corporation.
I ask the minister if that budget has been submitted to him yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told it has been before the board but it has not reached me yet. It will be submitted to council for approval as soon as it reaches me and the Minister of Finance.
When it reaches the minister and is approved by him as required by the bylaw, will it be made public?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No. The operating budget of every crown corporation is required to be submitted to council by the minister responsible and with the approval of the Minister of Finance. That is routine, but those operating budgets are not made public.
The bylaw requires a budget of proposed capital expenditure as well. Is there any thought of making it public as to the capital expenditure in the budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We do not usually. There is nothing to conceal about the capital expenditure but these cabinet documents are not usually made public.

I cannot ask for it right now because it is not in the minister's hands, but I think it will be necessary for parliament to see it when this house first sits after the budget has been received by the minister and approved by him.
The next question I have is as to financial transactions between the two corporations, namely, Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. What contracts have been signed by the crown company or by the government with either the crown company or Trans-Canada Pipe Lines since the bill was given royal assent on June 7?
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The only contracts are the mortgage indenture and the transfer of bonds with respect to payments made. I am told there has only been one payment made, the $6,775,000 advanced to the borrower on June 18, 1956. That answer has been given twice in the house.
Is there another advance in contemplation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It has not been applied for yet. I think it should be due shortly after the first of the month.
Is it expected there will be any further contracts signed between the two corporations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, the act specifies the relationship between the two. My hon. friend is looking into the future. Eventually there will be the lease of the Northern Ontario section when it is completed.
I was not thinking about that at this stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I anticipate there will be repayment of the advances and discharge of the mortgage some time this autumn, but that of course is provided for in the legislation.
I take it that the government is not a party to any contract that has been signed nor, I take it, is it likely to become a party in any of the contracts between the two corporations.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

Item agreed to.
Exhibitions-
422. Exhibitions generally $535,888.

I should like to ask
whether any consideration has been given during the past year to restoring the trade fair that was abandoned. I refer to the trade fair for the commonwealth and other parts of the world which took place for several years in the city of Toronto and which was so beneficial in bringing together trade representatives from all parts of the world. On the basis of the experience of the last year, is the government giving any consideration to reinstituting once more that fair to the end that there will be made available to all parts of the world representations of Canada's industrial production, thereby encouraging a greater measure of trade with this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the answer is no. We are giving no consideration to reopening the trade fair. The trade fair served an extremely important

Supply-Trade and Commerce purpose after the war in that it was a means of opening up the Canadian market to suppliers whose relations with Canada had been interrupted by the war. During the trade fair a good many British firms were able to re-establish themselves in this market. The same is true with respect to producers in other countries. However, the fair was becoming less and less useful in that regard and the exhibits were changing from business exhibits to prestige exhibits. There was too much of that sort of thing creeping in. We felt that better service could be obtained by taking our goods abroad and using foreign exhibitions to sell Canadian goods. We still believe that procedure is much more useful in the present phase. For instance, in Lausanne each year there is one building set aside for one particular country. This year that country is Canada. We have an excellent exhibit at Lausanne this year. I may say that Canadian manufacturers are giving us plenty of support with respect to that exhibit. We have had very good results in the trade fairs on the continent, particularly with Canadian furs. We have sold not only Canadian furs but Canadian fur garments. We have been most successful in doing that. Really I think it surprised our fashion establishments to find out what can be done simply by providing means of bringing our fashions into European markets. We think that is the proper way to spend the exhibition vote. The purpose is to carry on with that particular policy.

Item agreed to.
423. Canadian participation in the Brussels universal and international exhibition 1958, $750,000.

In view of the importance of the Brussels exhibition, and the substantial increase in the item appropriated for Canada's participation in it, I should like to ask the minister if he would make a statement in relation to the exhibition. May I also suggest that it might be appropriate to call item 705 of the supplementary estimates along with this one. It relates to the same subject. I have a question to ask on it. Item 705 is as follows:
705. Canadian participation in the Brussels Universal and International Exhibition 1958-further amount required to authorize payment, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, of an honorarium to Mr. J. J. Olson, $1.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. I should be glad to have them considered together. The fair in Belgium is a world fair. It is not a trade fair in any sense. It is a world exhibition. We regard it as an extremely important matter for Canada to be well represented at the fair. We are constructing a Canadian building there at a cost of $1
Why not give us the highlights of the essay instead of the whole essay?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The government placed the responsibility of planning, organizing and administering Canada's participation upon the Canadian government exhibition commission. To assist and guide the director of the commission, the government appointed an interdepartmental advisory committee of senior civil servants.
Under the authority of this interdepartmental advisory committee an architectural advisory committee was established to guide the preparation of plans for the Canadian pavilion. The committee consists of two representatives appointed by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada; the chief architect and liaison architect, Department of Public Works; the consulting architect of the commission; the chief designer of the commission; the superintendent of exhibits and, as chairman, the director of the commission.
Early in 1955 tentative arrangements were made with the exhibition authorities of Belgium for the Canadian site. This site, with minor adjustments, was confirmed in October. The Canadian site is located on one of the highest elevations in the exhibition area. Preliminary plans, were developed and finally approved by the cabinet on March 1, 1956. Because of the world-wide shortage in structural steel, the plans and specifications for the steel structure were completed and tenders called for from Belgium. Belgian steel was selected because at the conclusion of the exhibition the pavilion has to be dismantled and the steel salvaged in Belgium.
I think that is fairly well the thought. The work at present is that of getting on with the construction of the building and working

with the provinces to work out provincial exhibitions. On that point may I say that recently a meeting of the representatives of the provinces, appointed by the provincial premiers, was held in Ottawa. At this meeting the plans of the pavilion and the plans for presenting the Canadian Story were reviewed. While the government of Canada assumes the responsibility for the cost and is not asking for contributions from the provinces in the form of rent for space, it was considered advisable to secure the views and suggestions of the provinces with respect to the proposed plans. I am pleased to state that at this meeting the officials responsible for Canada's participation received wholehearted support from the representatives at the meeting, as well as an expressed willingness to assist in every possible way.
My hon. friend has referred to the item in the supplementary estimates for Mr. Olson. Mr. Olson is an officer of the Department of Public Works. It was not possible for the Department of Public Works to assign him full time to the job, but an arrangement was made with him to prepare specifications for the building in his own time. It was important to have Mr. Olson do it because the Department of Public Works will supervise the construction of the building. We wanted specifications which met with the standards of the Department of Public Works. Under a vote in the supplementaries he is supposed to be granted an honorarium of $500 for his work outside of the line of duty in preparing the specifications for this building.

Item agreed to.
Dominion bureau of statistics-
427. Administration, $177,729.

In this connection, I should like to ask the minister whether or not there is an annual report of the dominion bureau of statistics published in the French language? I communicated with the distribution branch and there may have been a mistake in the information I received, but I was advised that such was not the case. Would the minister say what the situation is?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told there is no report in the French language. I presume it is because the report is practically all statistical in form and numbers read the same in both languages; that is the only reason I can think of. I am told there never has been a report of the bureau of statistics in the French language.

I should like to ask the
minister one other question and it is this. I notice that throughout the report there are
Supply-Trade and Commerce references describing the bureau of statistics as the "dominion bureau of statistics". I have before me the annual report, and it is so described. I have a copy of a letter to His Excellency, as signed by the minister himself, which refers to the dominion statistician, and the report is of the dominion statistician. All of this is quite proper and is in accordance with the statute.
Can the minister give the house any information as to why it is that the building occupied by this body, the dominion bureau of statistics, has had the word "dominion" removed from it? Was that a decision of the government or was that the action only of the Department of Public Works? It is a very strange thing that the plaque in the front of this building, a building performing a function important to this country, contains a description that is improper, incorrect, and completely unjustified under the statute setting up this bureau.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether it was an economy move on the part of the Department of Public Works. As a matter of fact, I think my hon. friend is wrong and that the statute provides for a dominion statistician but I doubt if it provides for the dominion bureau of statistics. I am getting that checked.

Oh yes, it does. I have not the statute here, but I can send out for it. The statute describes this bureau as the dominion bureau of statistics. I am glad to have the explanation of the minister, that on the plaque identifying this building the word is omitted for economy purposes. How much would it have cost to have indented, if that is the proper expression, the word, "dominion" on the brass plate in addition to the words "bureau of statistics"? I have heard all kinds of explanations for the removal of the word "dominion", but I think in this case the Minister of Trade and Commerce has achieved the ultimate in the matter. Cost is the reason why the word "dominion" does not appear on the plaques in front of the bureau of statistics building.
I commend the minister for the novelty of his explanation. Certainly it has nothing much more than novelty to commend it to me. I think it only proper to add that it is a strange thing that up to the present moment that explanation, the most grotesque of all, should be advanced for a significant course of action being followed by this government in so many ways of outlawing by action rather than by parliament the use of the expression "dominion". I will say no more at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am sure my hon. friend, in discussing the parliament buildings, always refers to them as the
7308	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce dominion parliament buildings. I am sure he would, he is so anxious to get in the word, but I have never seen any sign which says these are the dominion parliament buildings.
No, and there is no statute which says that is the name, but there is a statute which says it is t'he dominion bureau of statistics.

I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Prince Albert. It is simply a reflection on the government of Canada that it has gone forward and dropped "dominion", dropped the "Rule Britannia" song for the navy, et cetera, and all without consulting this parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I noticed my hon. friend dropped the word "dominion". He said "government of Canada", and surely he ought to be consistent and say the government of the Dominion of Canada. I might say we dropped nothing so far as the sign on the bureau of statistics is concerned because the word was never there.
I will say the dominion government of Canada, in order to be consistent.

I should like to think that the minister's concern about economy in the operation of this branch under his department might be extended to allow some of the companies carrying on business in this country the same opportunity to economize. I think it is about time someone drew to the attention of the government the fact this department is plaguing business enterprises from one end of the country to the other with the number of forms it requires to be filled out now to cover your corporation tax, whether it be only federal or federal and provincial; whether it covers as well your security transfer tax or whether it is merely an information return. We have now a series of questionnaires which *come out almost daily asking questions of these companies. If the minister is so concerned about economy I suggest he might take a look at one of these questionnaires I have before me. It would take a Philadelphia lawyer to fill it out. It is three pages long, and this time they are attempting to get a few statistics about the operation of trucks.
The little pamphlet in question is to be carried around by the truck driver. At ten o'clock and three o'clock in the afternoon you can see him stopping his truck, running around to the rear and looking at the cargo and estimating the weight of his truck load at that particular time. At the same time he has to make a notation each time he fills the gas tank during this period showing how 

many gallons of gas he uses. He has to indicate daily how many miles are travelled by the truck and the total tonnage of the material that is transported. He has to give a few additional statistics. I say to the minister, how ridiculous can we get? How much more trouble are you going to cause businessmen in carrying out their business? I can see the truck driver who is carrying this pamphlet stopping his truck and making a mental calculation every time an item in this little book has to be filled in. I strongly suggest that if we are going to economize anywhere we might take steps now to economize a little on the effort that is required by our companies in keeping up with this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend is right. I do not like to expand the work of the bureau but the fact remains that we have no statistics on trucking. The board of transport commissioners requested us to provide statistics and the 10 provinces have all asked us to do so. We reluctantly added to our staff with that in view.
All the pressure that comes to me about the bureau is for more statistics. I presume they must be valuable to business and government or we would not be pressed to have them. If a government agency and all the provinces say that they need the statistics it usually becomes the job of the bureau with my approval to undertake to gather the statistics. That is the position of the statistics on trucking.
If my hon. friend thinks we can get along without them I will put his views forward to the various interested agencies.

Mr. Chairman, in closing, I would like to say this. I am sure the minister is well aware of the number of forms that need completion. It seems to me a very useful job might be undertaken by this particular department if it considered how much time and effort are consumed in the completion of these reports. The minister might give some leadership in connection with the matter I have raised. It seems to me that most of the information required by the department is very different from the survey I spoke about which involves the source of capital, and questions relating to the number of shares held by foreign shareholders and the number of shares outstanding.
If the government was looking at the situation from the standpoint of economy and considered the number of tax returns which must come in each fiscal year, if the bureau wanted to co-operate and economize they

could arrange for a perforated slip to be put at the bottom of that form. If it was for information such as a return to a provincial corporation's branch the slip could be torn off and turned in. Information concerning special items such as the ownership of shares, capital and where the money comes from could be put on at the same time. Once a year upon completion of the tax return the information could be given to the dominion bureau of statistics and they could compile it for their financial returns.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I might say that when I came to the Department of Trade and Commerce I was under the impression that the bureau had too many types of reports and a committee was set up to reduce the number of investigations and reports that the bureau was making. One provision that I insisted on at the time was that, if a report could not be ready within six months of securing the data that the report was not very valuable in any case.
I do not remember the figures but there was a very substantial reduction effected by the committee in the number of reports and an improvement was made in getting the reports out more promptly after their due date. I am sorry to say that recently the department has been slipping somewhat owing to the fact that we have not been able to get the staff we require for the work. We hope to improve that situation and you will notice that we have a little larger budget this year. The objective is always to get out the minimum requirement needed to carry on the business of Canada and to get it out promptly.

Mr. Chairman, I was rather surprised to hear the questions asked by the hon. member for York West regarding the trucking industry and I was equally surprised to hear the minister reply that 10 provinces had requested the information. It seems to me the provinces know more about the trucking industry than does anybody else because they licence the trucks. It seems rather strange to me that the 10 provinces should suddenly request that information. What is the federal government going to do with the information when they get it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Give it to the provinces.
And to the public.

Is there a penalty attached if the truck-owner or driver does not comply with this request for information?
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would think not, probably. I do not think the individual truck drivers would fill out these forms. I think they will be filled out by the trucking companies. If a large trucking company refuses to comply with a request from the dominion bureau of statistics the owner may hear from them. I imagine he would because there is the Statistics Act in existence in this country which provides certain penalties.

That is exactly what I am coming to. The minister says there is the act and if the form is sent out and the man does not comply by filling it out he will hear about it pretty soon. I can confirm this and I know what I am talking about because I have been a victim of this sort of thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: One should always comply with the law.

Yes. A form came to me as a processor and packer. Having had a crop failure that year I did not fill it out. Pretty soon I received a letter, and then another, and finally a registered letter. I informed the writer to come to my office in the parliament buildings to discuss the matter and I have not heard about it since.

Mr. Chairman, I simply wish to clarify one point. In relation to these reports requested from the truckers I think the minister ought to make it clear that this is a particular survey and it is not intended that this should be a continuing form of return required to be made by those operating trucks.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, that is the case.

I want to ask a few brief questions regarding the availability of some figures I have not been able to obtain. The first set of figures concerns our wheat shipments to Poland. In this case it may just be necessary for the minister to say why the figures are not available. I do not care whether or not I receive the figures now but I would like to know why they are not available. I am interested in the figure for the total amount of wheat in bushels rather than the total amount of wheat expressed in dollars. I would also like to know the places where the wheat was bought from the wheat board; that is, whether the quantities were shipped through Prince Rupert or Vancouver, and so forth. I would also like to know the cost of the wheat to the Manitoba Northern Sales, the amount of export credit insurance payable by the shipper, the amount of interest paid or payable to the federal government for these moneys that have been advanced, and
7310	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce then I also want to know the dates of the shipments, and the names of the ships.
If the minister does not have this answer readily available perhaps he will tell me why the information is not available, and if I might expect it at some future date.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
This is a case
which is sub judice. My hon. friend is trying to help out some of his lawyer friends. Such facts as are available are published by the dominion bureau of statistics. My hon. friend is well aware of that. This is a private row and he had better let the boys do the best they can and I will do the same.

That is all right. I just wanted to know why the information is not available.
I want to ask again this year if it is still not possible to obtain monthly figures of the exports of Canadian goods through Canadian ports and United States ports? Those have never been made available on a monthly basis in the same way that the imports are made available and I would like to know why it is not possible without too much extra effort to obtain monthly figures for exports similar to those which we obtain for imports.
I might say we are vitally concerned with these figures and in this way we would have a comparison by the month. Without these figures we will be unable to ascertain what progress is being made to eliminate the sad injustice which is in existence in Canadian ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I presume the reason is that the United States figures come from authorities in that country.
I understand it is a matter of delay in receiving the United States figures and I do not know of any other reason. Of course, at the year-end my hon. friend has no trouble in obtaining them because all those reports are published by the bureau of statistics. It seems to be a matter of delay in getting the information to the United States authorities which prevents the monthly statements coming out.

That may be true. The department compiles records of imports coming into Canada through Canadian and United States ports and I presume that in one case the figures would be United States and in the other they would be our own, or would they both be United States figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have complete figures with regard to imports, this would be Canadian information.
When those are available, why cannot they be obtained for exports?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Our customs
authorities are not interested in exports. The customs department gets no percentage out of exports. The customs are interested in imports but not in exports.

I realize that, but I suggest that it would not be much trouble. Surely there is some kind of check on goods going out of this country. If you can compile them on a yearly basis it should not be too much trouble to compile them on a monthly basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have no one here really to advise me on that problem but I shall look into it. If it is possible to improve the situation I shall be glad to do it.
