Mr. Chairman, the description that the Prime Minister has given of the Ottawa to be is one that I know will meet with the support of Canadians everywhere, a capital plan making this, the capital of Canada, a city in keeping with the aspirations of the Canadian people. All of us, regardless of what part of Canada we come from, are joined in agreement that what is being done is in accordance with Canada's potential greatness and will bring joy to generations yet to come.

Can the Prime Minister tell us whether the planning committee intends to maintain the cobblestone drive from the west gate up the hill for the next hundred years or whether something can be done to cover them up?

Mr. Chairman, before this item is dealt with may I bring to the minister's attention the fact that on Saturday last, as reported at page 7040 of Hansard and as also found at page 2 of the English translations

I did not overlook it at all. I ignored it.

With respect to item 440, would the minister explain to the committee just what part his department plays in this search and rescue service?

Mr. Chairman, on re-reading in yesterday's Hansard what I said last night I think perhaps I may have given a wrong impression in some of the comments that I made after the hon. gentleman's first question. The impression that I wished to give was that the responsibility for the co-ordination of search and rescue activities was the primary responsibility of the Department of National Defence. The responsibility for providing the vessels that would take part in search and rescue operations would, I think, fall on the Department of Transport primarily-
For which?

For the provision of vessels in connection with the search and rescue operations, because I think the department unquestionably has more of those vessels than any of the other departments of government. But I should like to correct any misapprehension that my remarks may have caused last night that the whole responsibility rested on the Department of National Defence. Their responsibility is that of coordination of the activities but it is not a sole and exclusive responsibility.
Suppose there is a wreck on the west coast. Who has the authority to order out the ships belonging to the Department of Transport?

I am informed, as I think my remarks indicated, that the responsibility rests on the air force, the Department of National Defence, for communicating with the various agencies concerned and apprising them of the circumstances and determining whether or not they are in a position to be able to afford assistance.

Does the air force have the authority to order a vessel belonging to the Department of Transport to go to the scene of the wreck or must that go from the air force to the Department of Transport and then from the Department of Transport to the master of the vessel in question?

My information is that the request would be conveyed directly to the master of the vessel and not to the department itself. The hon. gentleman has used the word "order". I think perhaps if he changed it to say "request" that would be more appropriate language to use. I do not think it is the intention or the practice that the search and rescue organization should order other departments, even including the navy, but I am sure the hon. gentleman will realize that we are really merely bandying words if we talk about an order or a request whenever the vessels are available.

I take it that when the minister suggests that government vessels commence a search or rescue operation on the initiative of the search and rescue co-ordination centre he is referring to the general departmental vessels of his department and also other departments such as the Department of Fisheries. However, I believe that that situation-and I should like to know whether my understanding is correct-would not apply to the boats at the lifeboat stations on the west coast of Vancouver island. Is it not true that those lifeboat stations have the authority to undertake a search or rescue operation on their own initiative without reference necessarily to the search and rescue co-ordination centre?

My information is that there are only a few of the stations to which the hon. gentleman refers, two, I believe, and that they may act on their own authority or they may act on the request of the search and rescue organization.
As the minister well knows, there are many people who think that two are not enough. However, I will not pursue that question further.

Would the minister like to take this opportunity to reply to my few remarks on icebreaking? The three new icebreakers are listed under this item. It would be a good opportunity to have my reply. As an hon. gentleman has just said, would the minister like to break the ice at this point?

If the hon. gentleman is saying it for himself, I shall not give an affirmative answer to that question. Mr. Chairman, what I should like to say on the subject of icebreaking is simply this. As hon. members know, we had the misfortune to lose the Lady Grey not in the winter just past but in the winter before last. That loss has naturally thrust a considerable burden on the remaining icebreakers. We have endeavoured to meet the situation first of all by providing for the construction of an additional icebreaker to replace the Lady Grey. It is at present under construction at Levis, Quebec. We hope it will be available for service in the coming winter.
We have recently called for tenders for the building of a further icebreaker of what I might describe as intermediate size. I hope it will be possible before too long to award the contract for the construction of that vessel. As my deputy minister points out, that vessel would be assigned principally to service in Newfoundland and in the gulf of St. Lawrence.
We also have in mind the construction of a larger icebreaker of the same general class as the D'Iberville. I hope it will be possible to call for tenders for the construction of that vessel some time later this year.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has any specific questions with regard to icebreaking. I may tell him that we are in receipt of a large number of requests to which it is quite impossible for us to accede, having regard to the dimensions of the icebreaker fleet at the present time. When these new icebreakers are in service we hope to be able to do more than we are doing at the present time.
[Mr. Marler.)
Another most important factor in connection with icebreakers, of course, is the use to which they are put during the summer months for carrying out the northern supply mission to the many points in the north which can be served only by ships accompanied by an icebreaker or by icebreakers themselves.
The minister has more or less explained away the reasons why we must have three new icebreakers in the estimates this year or plans for three new icebreakers.
No; plans for two.
Yes, but there are three icebreakers.

Yes; the item includes expenditures on three. As I say, one we hope will be in service shortly; the second has been the subject of a tender call already; and the third we hope will be the subject of calls later this year.

I realize that it is probably difficult to make a definite statement about this icebreaking matter generally; but frankly, I may say it is increasing now to a stage where they have the St. Lawrence open for a period that extends at least a full month into the close of the season and they have an early opening of about that same period. As I have said before on many occasions- and I am not going into the history of it-we are worried about the plans for the future in the St. Lawrence. The other night I mentioned the new icebreakers that are available. The old excuse of flooding in the St. Lawrence does not mean anything to me now, because the flooding has always been there. If one icebreaker could look after that condition formerly, surely it has not increased to the extent that more icebreakers would be necessary. A great many of these vessels are icebreakers and other types of ships; in other words, they combine two duties. I say that it is a back-door method to continue icebreaking early in the St. Lawrence. We had trouble last February, I believe, with respect to the early opening of the St. Lawrence. Vessels were damaged and pilots made statements that the season was being pushed to an extent that was alarming. Frankly, we are worried about it in Saint John and I think they must be in Halifax, as it affects the future of our ports.
Two or three times I have asked questions regarding the additional costs or for an estimate of the cost of these icebreaking operations. It should be possible to estimate the length of time that these vessels are on duty. It should be possible to give the payroll and other additional expenses. I think

that we are entitled to a statement regarding the future plans. Here we are subsidizing the icebreaking and increasing the length of the season in the St. Lawrence, while at the same time we are spending money on the harbours at Saint John and Halifax. These two expenditures are definitely in conflict. We only have the winter business and the season has been decreased now to an extent where our longshoremen, as I said the other night, cannot even get 24 weeks of work in order to qualify for unemployment insurance. I should like the minister to say if the department has examined this icebreaking matter. Helicopters are used, I understand, to survey the weak spots in the ice and see where it is possible to break a channel. The modern vessels have reinforced plates and each year the season for our ports grows shorter. We are worried about our future, and I feel it is going to be an increasing worry and burden. The department must tell us just what is going on, and what their plans are about icebreaking.

I would hope I could disabuse the mind of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, Mr. Chairman, as to the icebreaking activity in that portion of the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. It is not a matter of subterfuge. We have endeavoured to ameliorate the conditions of flooding below Montreal. The activity of the icebreakers has materially cut down that flooding in the last few years, and our purpose in carrying out icebreaking is not to make possible the use of the port of Montreal at an earlier date than common sense dictates. The prime purpose of carrying out the operation is to relieve conditions that would otherwise result in flooding.
The hon. gentleman seems to be concerned about the possibility of icebreakers being used in the St. Lawrence to the disadvantage of the port of Saint John. I think that is the substance of the comments he has just made. The difficulty, Mr. Chairman, is that we are not faced with a request for additional icebreaking only in the upper St. Lawrence. We are faced with a request for icebreaking from places on the Gulf of St. Lawrence and down in the province of New Brunswick. They have asked us to do something to make their ports available during the winter months. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman wants me to say we propose, because of the representations that he has made, to turn a deaf ear to the representations of other ports in New Brunswick, and refuse to provide icebreakers for them so that the port of Saint John will enjoy an exclusive advantage over the others. I do not think that is in his mind.
Supply-Transport
I fully understand that he wishes to promote the interests of Saint John and that I think is quite natural. Unfortunately, or perhaps fortunately, it is not possible for us to administer an icebreaking program designed to favour one port in particular. We have to meet this flooding condition that arises below Montreal. I believe we will have to expand our activities in the Gulf of St. Lawrence where there are important developments which will need facilities open to a much greater extent than at present. I think the same applies to ports in New Brunswick which, in my perhaps uninformed opinion, have made out a pretty good case for interest on our part in facilitating a greater use during the winter months of what seemed to me quite natural and suitable facilities.
The hon. gentleman, either on Saturday or today, has spoken about the comments of a pilot who attributed a collision which took place in the lower St. Lawrence to the fact that navigation was opening too early. The collision occurred in the lower St. Lawrence at a point, as I remember, somewhat above Quebec. I should like to tell the hon. gentleman that a most thorough inquiry was made into the circumstances of that particular incident and the pilot was not regarded as being excused by the conditions to which he referred. In fact, as I understand the circumstances, the pilot referred to was suspended as a consequence of that particular accident.

I will leave this item now, but I do want to say for the record that the money of the taxpayers of Canada is being used to provide icebreakers which in turn are opening the port of Montreal and other ports on the St. Lawrence early to the detriment of the business of eastern Canadian ports. I realize that there are some other explanations for the use of icebreakers. As I say, it may be a back door method, but in the very near future I can see that we will not have any business in eastern Canadian ports and that with modern methods the expenses of the department will be greatly increased because the St. Lawrence will be open all winter long.

I do not want to provoke a discussion, but I would hesitate to peer into the future as far as the hon. gentleman and predict the time when the St. Lawrence is going to be open all year round for navigation between Quebec and Montreal. He has more confidence in the economic possibilities of that than I have. While I fully appreciate that he may wish to take a particular attitude with regard to the port of Saint John it is

Supply-Transport
quite impossible for me, as Minister of Transport, to accept the position that I am going to discourage operations in the St. Lawrence regarding flood conditions that we are attempting to correct, and say that this is done so that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert will have a port that will be more useful under the circumstances.
I am surprised that he should talk about that just at the time when the port has had a record-breaking year in the transportation of grain. I find it strange in the face of conditions which are record breaking that the hon. gentleman should have so little optimism as to the future of his own port.

We did have a good winter in both Halifax and Saint John, but it was mainly due to the grain shipments going through. The general cargo picture is not very much better. The point I am trying to make, and the minister hedges around it, is that the money of the Canadian taxpayers is being used to provide icebreakers, which in turn are allowing the St. Lawrence to open earlier and private vessels are thus enabled to move up to the St. Lawrence ports above Quebec and Montreal, and in that way we are losing out in the competitive battle. It is not free competition any more.

When the minister was speaking on March 16 in opening the discussion of the estimates of his department he made a statement on page 2212 of Hansard to this effect. A little before that, on the same page, he mentioned that amongst the vessels to be completed this year was a marine agency vessel for Victoria. I should like to ask the minister whether this marine agency vessel for Victoria will be equipped with an emergency helicopter deck?
While I am on my feet-

Perhaps I can answer that one before the hon. member gets another one off his chest. Mr. Chairman, with regard to the Victoria agency vessel, the plans of the vessel were too far advanced to make changes in order to permit helicopter operations from that particular vessel. In the case of the agency vessel which was to be built for the Prince Rupert agency, it is the intention to provide for helicopter accommodation.

My only further question in the same connection is this. In view of the fact that it is not going to be possible to have helicopter accommodation for that vessel, are

any special plans being developed for carrying rescue equipment on that vessel?
The minister may recall that when speaking earlier in the session I pointed out that so far as my observation went departmental vessels on the coast did not carry such rescue equipment. I am wondering whether this vessel is being designed and equipped so that it may be more adequately prepared to deal with emergencies at sea than are some of the older vessels?

Mr. Chairman, the anwser to the hon. gentleman's question is that neither of the vessels to which I refer, the Victoria agency vessel nor the Prince Rupert agency vessel, will have special rescue or salvage equipment. I am not sure whether I said it last night but I would like to confirm this evening that we are giving consideration to the possibility of designing a vessel which would be suitable for agency purposes and which would also be more suitable than the present agency vessels for operations of that kind.

A further amendment in 1952 revised the rates as follows. Where one assistant only is employed payment may not exceed $1,800 per annum. Where two assistants are authorized payment may not exceed $1,800 per annum for the first assistant and $1,620 per annum for the second assistant, except at Prince Rupert and Victoria where the rate has been set at $2,100 per annum for both assistants.
When you take the details of the requirement-perhaps I might spare the committee the details-you arrive at an over-all requirement of $459,960 less an anticipated short fall in expenditure-our experience in previous years is that not all lights require a full year's employment for assistants-in the amount of $104,339, so that the net requirement is $355,621.

With regard to the other question, Mr. Chairman, I think in a general way that we endeavour when there are vacancies in lights or positions in the more settled and attractive points to provide opportunities for advancement to those who are at the remote stations so that there is some prospect for people in remote stations to move back to conditions that are probably more agreeable and certainly more attractive than being in some remote place where conditions are perhaps somewhat lonely and desolate. I think that covers the situation in a general way and if the hon. gentleman has any further questions I will certainly try to answer them.

What I was wondering is this. These assistant lighthouse keepers apparently are not considered as civil servants because earlier in the item there are shown quite large numbers of lightkeepers of different classes. There are no lightkeepers' assistants in that list and they are shown in the supplementary list. I take it from this that they are not engaged as regular employees of the department; at least, they cannot become permanent civil servants. Is that correct? If so, why is there not some permanence to this position of assistant lighthouse keeper?
The minister has pointed out that a lighthouse keeper who is serving at a remote point would be given the opportunity to take a position at a less remote and more agreeable centre and I think that is a very wise policy. Does the same policy apply to the assistant lighthouse keepers? That is, do they get any advantage at all or are they merely hired as temporary employees?
I have heard that they are hired by the lighthouse keeper; in other words, that the man keeping a light hires his own assistant. I did run across one case in which that appeared to have been done. There may be good reasons for a policy of that kind, but perhaps the minister would explain what is the actual policy followed by the department with regard to these assistant lighthouse keepers.

Mr. Chairman, I might say that it is somewhat like choosing a wife. One chooses a wife with compatibility as one of the qualifications. The same thing applies to the selection of lighthouse keepers' assistants.
Well, compatibility is a factor.

My hon. friend would realize, of course, how undesirable it would be if the assistant of the lighthouse keeper was incompatible with the keeper himself and, as my deputy minister has just pointed out, these men have to board together. I am sure the hon. member will realize that whatever
Supply-Transport
merits there might be in making this a civil service appointment the difficulty posed by incompatibility is not one that can be covered by the usual tests.
As the hon. gentleman has indicated the appointment is in effect made by the light-keeper. He chooses the man who is to be his assistant, and while I admit there is not the permanency of a civil service appointment we are trying to see what we can do to keep these men in permanent employment although it is not always possible.

Suppose, for example, that the lightkeeper and his assistant fall out? That happened in the case to which I referred. I suppose the poor assistant lightkeeper just gets kicked off the island. In the case I am referring to the assistant was taken to the boat and told to go. Is there not some way in which the assistant whose only fault is that the lighthouse keeper does not like him can be given a chance to get work at another lighthouse, or is he just out of luck?

We are trying in a few places to provide separate accommodation so the compatability of the two may not be put to too severe a test. I take it that there are instances where the only solution is to put the assistant in a boat and say goodbye to him.

Has any attempt been made by the department to work out a scheme whereby the department would assume some responsibility for these men? It seems to me that where a man is hired and is working at a lighthouse he must be a pretty reliable sort of man. Should there not be some provision made in the case of a lighthouse keeper and his assistant falling out whereby the assistant would have an opportunity to take a job with the department in some other locality?

I understand that when incidents like that occur the marine agency do endeavour to find other employment for the assistant. I should like to say to the hon. gentleman that I agree with much of what he has said as to the desirability of assuring as much permanence as is possible to these assistants. I understand that the departmental officials have a plan under consideration by which something can be done to improve the position of these assistants.

There is one problem in Kincardine which has not been solved yet to my satisfaction. An occasion arose whereby it was necessary to appoint a lighthouse keeper and I understand that arrangements were made to transfer a man from another lighthouse to Kincardine. Answers which were made to questions I put on the

Supply-Transport
order paper lead me to believe that these transfers are not always above board. As of yet no appointment has been made to Kincardine and I wonder if the minister can give me any information as to just what is the situation at the present time.
There are several veterans in Kincardine, some of whom are receiving pensions, and any of these men could handle this situation. I think that would be better than to bring in somebody from outside who would have only a part-time job and have to look for another one in the off-season. Does the minister expect to make this appointment shortly?

I understand that the hon. member would like to see some local person appointed to this position whereas these appointments are made by the civil service commission after a promotional competition. I will admit that a promotional competition may not always produce the best results and certainly may not always satisfy the hon. gentleman, but it seems to me that it is the fairest method we can adopt where you have a lighthouse in a settled community which would offer attractions to others to come in from a remote point and undertake a period of service. I think we must recognize that that system has merit, even though it may not always be acceptable to the local member.

The answers to my questions brought out the fact that new appointments have been made by the civil service commission to locations where any person who wanted to be a lighthouse keeper would be willing to stay there for the rest of his life. I am just wondering if that is always followed out all through the service. I am inclined to think probably it is not. If I am wrong I should like to be shown where I am wrong.

I should like to refer to a situation which has been in existence at some time at a place called Bright's Grove not far from Sarnia. For the information of hon. members who may not know this area, Bright's Grove is quite a popular summer resort for people from the United States and southern Ontario, and there are a great many pleasure boats and small craft in the area. Lake Huron can get exceedingly rough at times and when small boats are caught in a storm in this area the only place they can run to is Perch creek at Bright's Grove. However, there are no marker buoys or harbour works of any kind at this point. I should like to quote briefly from the Sarnia Observer of Tuesday, July 3, as follows:
Perch creek at Bright's Grove which has been under discussion for many years as a haven for pleasure craft saved many lives during Sunday's storm.
Pleasure craft caught on the lake sought shelter of the creek and managed to make the entrance but with extreme difficulty.
Many narrow escapes were reported by boat operators. Joseph Partridge of 10 Cedar crescent, Sarnia who in company with his wife and two sons was making the return trip from Blue Point was caught in the storm. He knew the area well but with no buoy or marker he overshot the Perch creek opening and had to take shelter behind a groyne.
Apparently this area has become increasingly important as a refuge in case of storms on lake Huron and apparently there is not even a marker at the entrance. The minister might pass on this information to the department to be looked into.
I shall be glad to do that.

On the west coast, as the hon. gentleman knows, there are a number of organizations and a

number of facilities of a kind to provide salvage, whereas on the east coast we are not nearly so fortunately placed, and in fact there is nothing apart from this Foundation Maritime organization.

I notice in the details of the estimates on page 551 that last year provision was made for a chief registrar of shipping. Apparently that position has been abolished, for there is no such item this year. Can the minister explain why that change has been made?

447. Steamship inspection service, including the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions lor the safety of life at sea and load lines, and contributions as detailed in the estimates, $739,710.

This is the steamship inspection service, and I would ask the minister to explain just what control his department exercises over other government ships in order to see that they comply with the various laws and regulations. This question arises -because last winter-it may have been in the fall but I think it was last winter-one of the vessels of the Department of Public Works, the Hilunga, was sent on a voyage for which she was not built and in the course of the voyage she foundered. Fortunately there were no lives lost, but I think the Department of Public Works incurred damages amounting to almost the value of the vessel itself. I put a question on the order paper asking to what extent the ships owned by the different departments were registered, and the return that was brought down showed that some departments register their vessels and others do not. For example, the Department of National Defence and the defence research board do not. The answer of the Department of Transport was:
1.	No. Registration is at the discretion of the department concerned.
2.	A record is kept of registered ships only.
3.	All Department of Transport ships are registered, except a few small scows, landing craft specially designed for northern waters and motor launches.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police answered that they register none of their vessels. The Department of Public Works register all but some dredges and scows. Apparently there is no set rule that a government vessel must be registered. I would ask the minister why this practice is followed. It does seem to me that there should be more control of government vessels and that they should comply with all the laws that have to be obeyed by others. Apparently that is not the case and there is a discretion allowed to the departments to carry on as they see fit.

I was hoping to lay my hands on a note I had on the subject, but my understanding is that the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act do not make it mandatory that all government vessels be registered. That is a statutory provision. It is not a question of policy but it is a matter of the Canada Shipping Act. I should like to say to the hon. gentleman, however, that with the exception of the ships belonging to the R.C.M.P., as to which discussions are currently being carried on, the other vessels

belonging to the various government departments have been registered or are in the process of carrying out the formalities for registration.
The significance of that is that when vessels are registered they are then subject to the same kind of inspection to which ordinary commercial vessels are subject. I do not think it is necessary to enlighten the hon. gentleman on that score because I think he is quite familiar with the extent of the steamship inspection. I hope I have cleared up any doubt in his mind as to the situation. Where there is registration there is inspection, where there is no registration there is no inspection, but so far as government vessels are concerned, with the exception of the vessels operated by the R.C.M.P., as to which discussions are going on currently, the others are registered or in process of being registered.
That has now been adopted as a general policy, that all government vessels must be registered?
I would not like to accept the interpretation of the hon. gentleman. I would merely say it is a fact that it is being done but I do not think I should declare that it is a matter of policy.
Why do the R.C.M.P. vessels not register and be subject to similar inspection?

I think I made it clear that discussions were going on with them as to the registration of their vessels. By that I do not mean to imply that they will agree to register but I do say that the matter is under discussion with them. I am not in a position to speak for them because I think the Minister of Justice should deal with that point on his estimates.

Transport minister Marler announced today that work will start this spring on a four year dredging program to widen and deepen the St. Lawrence ship channel from Montreal to below Quebec city. 450.	Contract dredging, including acquisition of land for ship channel improvement, $3,544,200.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the committee that last year a small departmental committee considered the whole question of dredging on the St. Lawrence and that the principal purpose of this item is to provide for improvements to the ship channel which are required in order to reduce the hazards to ocean going shipping which plies the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal. The work which it is proposed to carry out consists of the further widening of curves and critical sections of the dredged channel between Quebec and Montreal as recommended in a detailed and very complete report which this committee of officials prepared and completed earlier this year.
In addition to the rather broad description I have just given, the work contemplates the completion of dredging in certain areas under the 1952 contract which could not be accomplished in 1955. That is a relatively small item. In addition there is the cost of expropriating Boat island which is six miles below Sorel just above lake St. Peter in order to straighten the channel to a minimum 800 feet and improve the run of ice which jams here. Then there is quite a long list of proposed dredging projects which are to be carried out under contract in 1956 as recommended by the committee. Unless the hon. gentleman would like to have the details, perhaps I might not burden the committee with them.
I should like to say that the experience of the department has been that it is good business to call for a four-year contract to carry out a long term program rather than to do it piecemeal from year to year. The contract was awarded after tenders had been called for publicly and the successful tenderer was the lowest tenderer. The practice is, I think, good, sound common sense. I think that is the way in which we can best spend our money in carrying out the dredging.
I should like to point out to the committee that the increased use of the St. Lawrence which is expected to result from the opening of the seaway is one of the main reasons which prompt us to continue this work of improving the channel which, as the hon. gentleman knows, is probably something like 150 miles in length. It has been progressively widened over the years with, I think,

very satisfactory results so far as St. Lawrence navigation is concerned.

For the four-year program. The expected expenditures this year amount to a little over $3J million.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to compliment the minister on the way in which he has answered our questions. That is one of the reasons why we like to assist him as much as possible. I should like to get some information from him. It is in connection with the rumoured curtailment of service up in Bruce. I might read this copy of a letter which has been sent to our postal clerks on the railways between Kincardine, Palmerston and Southampton. It reads as follows:
Plans of the Canadian National Railways call for removal from service of a number of passenger trains effective 30th September, 1956. This will necessitate considerable changes in the railway mail service in this district.
Plans have not yet been finalized but it now appears practically certain the railway mail clerk positions at Southampton, Kincardine and Goderich headquarters will be abolished.
You are, of course, vitally interested and I am therefore, passing this information along to you at this time.
It is anticipated that no postal car will operate in the Palmerston and Southampton branch, (also Kincardine and Goderich lines), and the only postal car operations between London and Palmerston will be in Trs. 168 and 169-29.
That letter is signed by J. A. Flaherty, district director, London. I may say that the hon. member for Huron, who is not able to be here tonight, is also very much interested in this prospective change. I am happy to see that the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has recently come into the house. I think probably he will be interested as well, because it affects part of his district. I should like to say that on August 3 the minister answered a question of mine. My question, as reported at 6923 of Hansard, was as follows:
I have one more question, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask the minister if he thinks it is wise to curtail train service into Bruce county at

Supp ly-Transport
this stage when it is expected by all economists in Canada that the population of this country is going to increase very greatly.
The minister answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I could not answer the question in general terms in which it was put. I think every case must be considered on its own merits.
At the present time I should be very glad if the minister could give us an idea as to what merits we have up there in Bruce in not wanting this train service cut off. As I think it has been suggested previously in this house, we are increasing in population and in industrial production up there. I should therefore like to know the minister's views on what we may expect up in that part of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I am not in any better position to reply to his question than I was the other day when the hon. gentleman first brought the matter up in the house. I may say that I communicated his observations to the Canadian National Railways but I have not yet received a reply to the inquiry which I addressed to them. In the second place, I am not in a position to express any opinion with regard to the service to which he has referred. I will say this, however: I think that all railway companies would hesitate to give up services that are profitable. I have merely inferred from the questions that have been put that if a reduction in service is being contemplated or is being put into effect, it is because the service as at present rendered is not proving to be profitable.
I would share the hon. gentleman's regret if it is found to be necessary to curtail service over the lines to which he has referred. I should like, first of all, to point out that this is a decision of the management of the railway, not of the Department of Transport; and I think it is guided by the factors of public interest, its responsibilities to the community it serves and also the general consideration of what its effect is on the accounts of the railway company.
Did the minister say that it is a decision of the transport commission?

No. I said that the decision to reduce such service, if such a decision has been taken, was that of the management of Canadian National Railways. I do not want to appear to be too apologetic for the fact that I do not know every detail of the Canadian National Railways administration, but I should like the hon. member to understand that the reason for my unfamiliarity with the matter is that it is a C.N.R. decision and not one by the Department of Transport.

I realize that the minister is doing a good job and a big job, and we would not expect him to know all these things. But after the questions that were asked the other day, I would think he might have familiarized himself with what has happened. If I may be allowed to tell the minister what has happened, I shall do so. The C.N.R. has notified the postal department that these trains are going to be cut off. I think it would be wise for the minister to familiarize himself with the situation and look into it, because he is at the helm.

Mr. Chairman, this item is one that deals with the private railway cars owned by the government. I think it would be interesting to have a little bit of information from the minister at this point. How many cars are there actually in operation at the present time, including the governor general's, those used by the board of transport commissioners and those used by the cabinet ministers? Concurrently with that answer, could the minister give us any comparative mileage travelled by those cars, for instance, this year, the year under examination, in comparison with that in previous years so that we may see what use is being made of them?

Mr. Chairman, I must say at once that we do not keep a record of the mileage of the cars. So far as I am concerned myself, in the last 12 months I think altogether I have travelled between 50,000 and 60,000 miles. I do not want to suggest that I have travelled all of that mileage by rail. If I had done so, I would be on the railroad 365 days of the year. However, I have travelled very extensively by rail. All I can say is that I think these cars serve a very useful purpose. I think perhaps hon. members may imagine that when one gets into a railroad car, the first thing one does is to sit down, relax and enjoy the greatest of luxury therein wherever one happens to be going. Unfortunately, it has not been my experience to be able to use for those purposes the official car which is at my disposal. So far as I am concerned, I have found that it was merely a sort of extension of my office. It had the great advantage of privacy. I could read confidential documents and lay out plans. I could accomplish a lot of uninterrupted reading that I can assure hon. gentlemen opposite is very difficult to accomplish in one's office.
At all events, if I could reply more directly to the hon. gentleman's question, this vote includes five cars, two of which are at the disposal of His Excellency; one for the Prime Minister; one for the Minister of Transport

and one for general use. There has been no change in the situation while I have been minister. I think that the number has remained the same for some considerable time. I should like to add one further word of explanation in connection with the cars and that is that the railway companies move these cars without any charge whatever to the government so that it is not a matter of paying a substantial sum each time a cabinet minister uses an official car to go from one point to another.

Just to deal very briefly with the minister's observation, I must say that I sympathize with him in so far as the value of being at ease and being able to work while travelling on a railway is concerned. Some of us poor, ordinary commoners who do not have the benefit of private railway cars, find we can operate quite successfully in a bedroom or compartment.
Oh, oh, bragging.
That is not an admission I would care to make.

I am
afraid, Mr. Chairman, that is the level to which the government will sink in order to find something to misinterpret in one's remarks. I find I was not operating at a very high level.
It shows the directions of the hon. gentleman's thoughts, anyway.

I do
not know of what value it is to have a private dining room or how much assistance that is in the minister's reading. I do not know how much the chef assists him in his work or the car steward. I would point out to him that there are many businessmen across this country who do manage to do business quite successfully in the usual type of accommodation which is provided by the railways.
The heads of railways who are in the transport business have private cars.
think the president of the Canadian National and the president of the Canadian Pacific do have their own private railway car.
And each vice-president.

Certainly, I would be quite happy to see the Prime Minister have a car on occasion but I am not aware that each director of the C.P.R. has a car.

Each vice-president and every divisional superintendent across the country has cars.

I am
not arguing with that. If we extend that argument indefinitely, we are going to find the government arguing that a deputy minister should have a private railway car. The point I am making-

speechtext: The point you are making is pure jealousy.
He wants a bigger field of operation.

The
point I am making is this. In the past several years the trend in business has been away from the rails to the air. Now, some of the uses of these cars are most interesting. A few weeks ago I drew the attention of the house to a trip which the minister had made to Montreal to address a political meeting.

I should like the hon. gentleman, if he is going to talk about that, to confine himself to the facts as they were set forth in the house. The hon. gentleman knows full well, and I told the house at the time, that I went to Montreal not for the primary purpose of attending a political meeting but for the purpose of doing business for my department. It is true, and I admitted at the time, that I had spoken at a political meeting during my visit there.
I think the hon. gentleman, if he ever comes to be minister-
God forbid.

-will find it exceedingly difficult to find what part of him is personal and what part of him is minister. All I can tell the hon. gentleman is that since I have been

Supply-Transport
minister a very small part of me seems to be personal. When I go to Montreal I have very little opportunity of attending to personal matters, and even less time to attend to political matters. I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman but I should like him to stick to the facts and not to say that I went to Montreal to address a political meeting. Let him tell the whole story.

think in fairness to myself that Hansard will show that I was interrupted in the middle of a sentence. It is quite true the minister went to Montreal to address a political meeting and he went by his private car. When he was queried on that, he pointed out he had also done government business at the same time. Those are the facts which the minister has just set before us, and those are the facts which, had he not interrupted me, I would have mentioned.
But you put the cart before the horse.
He gave you a lift to the station, and that was the main mistake.

If we
are going to get through these estimates I suggest the members on the government benches confine themselves to intelligent remarks.
Having made a reference to that, I go ahead and point out one other trip which was made during the month of April which I think is indicative of an improper use or, if not improper, at least more use than is necessary being made of these cars. We find that on April 28 two of these cars left Ottawa and went to Quebec. I can well understand, Mr. Chairman-I should say I can understand, but not very well- that when the minister's argument is applied he may have wanted to work on his way to Quebec. The other question which arises in my mind is this. This was a Saturday and I am wondering what important government business was taking place on Saturday or Saturday night in Quebec city that required the presence of both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Northern Affairs. I do not know. I do know that Saturday night, April 28, there was a great Liberal rally as the provincial Liberal party of Quebec kicked off their campaign. I do know that both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Northern Affairs were prominently displayed at that rally. If they want to go down to

Quebec and get their brains kicked out in a provincial election, as subsequently happened, that is their business. But I suggest they should not be using government transportation, government private cars, for that particular purpose. I just point out that of course there is no doubt as to when they returned. The car of the Minister of Transport came back on April 28 and that of the Minister of Northern Affairs on April 29, which would indicate to me that they left Ottawa on the Saturday and returned either late Saturday night or Sunday and this rather limits the amount of government business they could have accomplished.
It is within this framework that I rise to ask the Minister of Transport to give every consideration to reducing his expenditures in this field of ultimate luxury. I wonder if any of the ministers of the crown has even bothered to find out what sort of alternative transportation is available on the trains? Let them try once or twice, as some of us do, the very fine accommodation which is available on the ordinary trains including drawing rooms, bedrooms and compartments where they can be by themselves and do their work and by which means the taxpayers of this country will be saved a fairly substantial amount of money.
I hope that the minister will explain to us what necessity there was for these two private cars to go to Quebec on a Saturday and come back on a Sunday and perhaps he would indicate whether or not there was any connection between that trip and their attendance at the opening of the political rally of their party in Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry; but I realize it would be very easy for me to allow this item to carry and leave unanswered on the record the remarks which my hon. friend has just made. Last year his interests turned very largely on the use of government aircraft for the transport of ministers of the crown. After having shown this extraordinary interest last year in the use of government aircraft for the transport of ministers of the crown the hon. member believes it is quite in order to use such aircraft for the transport of ministers of the crown but that it does not appear to be in order to use official cars for that purpose.
I think the hon. member would really like to have the best of both worlds. He wants to criticize members of the government when they travel by air and he likewise likes to criticize them when they travel in these railway cars.

All I can say, Mr. Chairman, so far as I am concerned, is that in using one of these official cars I am following the tradition and the practice that has been followed by a large number of my predecessors. I would like to be able to travel just as my hon. friend does and not be bothered with other people but unfortunately that is not possible. I found that when I was a member of the legislature of Quebec I was lucky if I got past the first page of a newspaper when travelling because everybody who had a bill in the legislature thought I should know what it contained. All I can tell the hon. gentleman is that the situation is no different although I have changed the scene of my activities.
The hon. member appears to find fault with the fact that these cars are available for use by ministers of the crown. He does not seem to be aware of the fact that private cars or business cars, as one might call them, are available not only to the presidents and vicepresidents but are available also to divisional superintendents of both railways. I have not heard him criticize that fact at any time, from which I must infer that he considers it is ail right for a divisional superintendent to have a private car but it is not proper for a minister of the crown to use such a car to carry on government business. Well, Mr. Chairman, I cannot subscribe to that idea because I do not think it conforms to common sense or the realities of the situation.
The hon. gentleman has shown the greatest of interest in my movements. A few moments ago we heard his comments about a trip I made to Montreal. If one will look at Hansard one will find that when I told him what was the purpose of my business in Montreal he went on to ask how it came about that on the same day I did this I actually had a vote in the house. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I have been accustomed in the face of the most bitter political opponents to having what I said as a fact accepted and not questioned to find out whether or not what I had said was true. Not only did the hon. gentleman question in the house the comment I made but he took the trouble to telephone my personal staff to find out about my movements.
Sneak.
I am of the opinion that this is carrying curiosity to a point which exceeds ordinary limits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: You are a little snooper.

The hon. gentleman is interested in the fact that there were two cars used on this occasion. My recollection of the situation is that my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, went on an early morning train

Transport
which was impossible for me to do because, unfortunately, I had to give up my Saturday-morning to deal with C.N.R. business in Montreal, which I may remind the hon. gentleman is not my home, and I can assure him I prefer to spend my Saturdays at home. I was not able to do so. I spent the morning in Montreal and went to Quebec by the afternoon train. I came home on the evening train and returned in time to spend half of the weekend with my family; but, Mr. Chairman, I make no apology for that because I think that is part of my job. I feel that having a car at my disposal enables me to accomplish more work than I would otherwise accomplish.
The hon. member, I think, will readily realize how difficult it would be to travel with documents spread out on adjoining chairs and I am sure he also appreciates how undesirable it would be to spread documents beside other passengers in the train where they could be read.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks further to what the hon. member for Bruce has said about the curtailment of the railroad service up through the peninsula and the counties of Wellington, Huron and Grey.
About three years ago an application was made by the railway to the board of transport commissioners to curtail the service through that part of the country. Representations were made by all the surrounding municipalities and no curtailment was made at that time.
The present situation is this. We hear rumours of curtailment. Today the hon. member for Bruce, the hon. member for Huron and I went over to the board of transport commissioners and talked to them. They said they had no word concerning any curtailment that was going to take place and they had not been advised concerning any lessening of the service on that branch line. We then went over to the postal department and learned that this department had been informed that on September 30 the time card is going to be changed and the service will be curtailed by the railroads on that line.
We are now wondering exactly what is going on. After all, if that service is going to be curtailed the people who will be affected by it should know the facts. Is this a case of slipping something in by the back door? The part of Ontario to which I have referred is going to be developed. If transportation facilities are curtailed the people there will not have the benefit of the rail lines and they will lose the advantage of the new industries that may very well be attracted to

Supply-Transport
locate there. I feel something is going on here that the people of the district should know about.
They have not been told if the rail service is to be curtailed. We understand that the railroads may curtail service to a certain extent without letting the people know about it, but this service concerns a lot of people. They helped to build up the business on this branch line and maintain it through the year. If we are going to have main lines we must have feeder lines. I sometimes think if the railroads would take some of these teams that go around the country to try to find ways of bringing about economies and sent them up through these districts to find ways of promoting railroad traffic everything would be much better.

I spoke on this item four years ago along with the former hon. member for Bruce, Donald Blue; the former hon. member for Perth, James Corry; and the former hon. member for Wellington North, Arnold Darroch. We approached the minister on this same issue and after our representations and private presentations these lines were not closed up. I think it should appear on the record that members from this district four years ago prevented this line from being closed.
Surely the suggestion is not that these decisions are being made on a political basis?

speechtext: The item before us deals with official railroad cars and I think it is up to me at this moment to point out to the committee that we are dealing with estimates of the Department of Transport not of the Canadian National Railways. Hudson Bay railway-
452. To provide for the difference between the expenditures for operation and maintenance, and revenue accruing from operation during the year ending March 31, 1957, not exceeding, $150,000.

I am glad to see that the deficit in regard to the operation of the Hudson Bay railway is moving in the right direction as this item indicates there is a decrease of $275,000 over the previous year. I do not have to emphasize the importance

of this seaport in the heart of this continent to the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and the Northwest Territories. One of the great handicaps to the development of this particular region is the discriminatory differential in freight rates and my reason for making any observations on this item is to stress once again the importance and significance of the operation of the railroad and the seaport to our prairie economy. I understand that the saving on grain moving through Churchill amounts to 15 to 25 cents per bushel. I should like the minister to comment upon the reason for this decrease in the deficit. I assume it is because of the increased tonnage moving out of the port since the grain elevator facilities were extended.
The minister will recall that last year I made a recommendation concerning tourist excursions and the minister was kind enough to supply me with detailed information of these excursions operated by the C.N.R. I am glad to note that two excursions are now being run in place of one, but I suggest that there is still a wide demand for this particular type of holiday if the services and facilities are made available. There is a large waiting list, particularly of Americans, who are anxious to make this trip to the bay.
I could quote figures on this situation, but I shall not take the time of the committee to do so. It is important to the continued success of the operation of the railroad that we stimulate as far as possible a two-way flow of trade. The outward flow has been increasing at a quite rapid rate since the end of the war. For example, in 1946 there were 3 million bushels of wheat moved through the port while last year there were over 13 million bushels. That is an excellent increase but there is difficulty in connection with the inflow of imports from Europe. While this does not come directly under the jurisdiction of the minister I hope he will use his influence to have our trade commissioners point out the advantages of supplying the midwestern Canadian market through this port.

The reason for the reduced deficit is the satisfactory improvement in the amount of tonnage carried on the railroad. In 1955-56 the revenue tonnage amounted to 578,000 tons as opposed to
458,000	tons in the preceding year. As the hon. gentleman has pointed out, the great difficulty is that the volume of import freight is very small. Of those figures I have just given approximately 2,000 tons in round figures of import freight were handled in each of those two years. As the hon. members will appreciate, that is a very small fraction of the whole.

It is the consumers in western Canada who will have to create a demand for shipments into Churchill rather than shipments out of that port. The hon. gentleman comes from that part of the world and perhaps he can do some missionary work which would help to bridge the distance between 2,000 tons and 578,000 tons.

Last year when the minister's estimates on the Hudson Bay railway were up I asked if a survey had been made of the territory north of Gypsumville. At that time perhaps I was to blame for misleading the minister a little by referring to Hodgson instead of Gypsumville. This time I intend to be more specific and make sure that I do not mislead the minister in any way.
On May 17, 1948 I first raised the question of a cut-off through the interlake country to the Hudson Bay railway and at that time the Honourable Mr. Chevrier said he would bring the matter before the officers of Canadian National Railways. I know discussions have taken place as to the advisability of the railroad being extended 190 miles north to Wekusko, which is at mile 81 on the Hudson Bay railway. In that 190 miles of proposed railroad there is only one bridge that would really cost money, and that would be at Grand Rapids. In 1948 it was estimated at $1 million, but at today's prices it would cost more.
What do you mean by $1 million?

The bridge would cost that. In passing may I say that Grand Rapids is a prospective power site with a drop of some 80 feet there.
In building this 190 miles extension from Gypsumville to Wekusko there would be a saving of 250 miles, as we ship our grain at the present time to Port Churchill.
In 1948 when I talked to the then minister of transport about it I pointed out that it would be an advantage to defence by having a quicker route to Port Churchill. Also there would be a great saving to farmers and shippers sending their produce to Port Churchill. There is a lot of timber in that country and a lot of agricultural land and with a railroad going through it, it could be developed.
With a shorter haul to Port Churchill many benefits could come from that. I have already mentioned national defence-it is a more direct and quicker way to the large military establishment in the north.
If cattle prices should change and we again ship cattle to Britain instead of the United States, then it would mean a lot to the
Supply-Transport
livestock getting to the port as quickly as possible. It has been estimated that the livestock would be 18 to 20 hours less on the road, which would be a big benefit. Shipping by refrigerator cars would be a saving too, because they would not need to be iced as often as going the roundabout way.
Business from Winnipeg would be increased, and it would be possible that the boats would not come in empty but would come loaded with goods and have the grain for the return trip.
While we have ice conditions to contend with and the port is only open 100 days of the year, I feel that in the near future that 100 days is going to be extended to a longer season through the invention of radar and different aids to shipping that they never had in the old days.
This short cut would benefit Manitoba in general-it would open up new country along the railroad and it would also provide work and wages while the line was being built.
One could speak 40 minutes on this proposed route, going into the details and savings that could be achieved, but I want to leave it at that and ask that the minister give some consideration to it, and he can tell the house later whether it would appeal to him or not. When the minister brought in his estimates in March, I had a 40-minute speech ready, and the delays in his estimates have saved him from that. I have condensed it a little further every time his estimates have come up, and now he is only getting the cream of it.
I admire the hon. gentleman's forbearance.

Perhaps if I lived in the east I would look at this in a different light, but being a Manitoban I want to see the benefits of this extension come to Manitoba. But I know from my dealings with the minister in the past that he will look at this from a Canadian point of view.
I am sending over a map of Manitoba to show the minister where the route would go and how it would save haulage miles. I would at this time appeal to the minister to have the officers of his department give some consideration to building this short cut to Churchill.

I would just like to tell the
hon. member that the matter was considered in 1952. At that time the cost was found to be very substantial, with an annual loss in prospect of very close to $1 million. I do not know what the situation would be in 1956 but I shall be very glad to draw the

Supply-Transport
hon. gentleman's remarks to the attention of the Canadian National Railways and see what their reaction is.

The minister suggested that we might do some missionary work on behalf of the port situation at Fort Churchill. There is an excellent book that has been published by the Hudson Bay Route Association, and I am going to take the liberty of sending him a copy. He can read it on one of those railway journeys we were talking about a few moments ago.
It just shows that there is never a dull moment.
Item agreed to.

That will be quite agreeable to me.

This is the item to provide for the cost of surveys of Newfoundland Railway properties, $17,500. With regard to the question of conversion from narrow gauge to standard gauge, I talked to Mr. Gordon about the matter casually, but the cost always appeared to be staggering.
What is it?

I think it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50 million. My deputy minister points out that he thinks the current estimate is more than that. I think I should tell the hon. gentleman that it is a very substantial sum, and I think it is unlikely from the viewpoint of economics that it would be considered feasible at this time. wasted. That is a fact that will have to be taken into account. 466.	Maritime Freight Rates Act-for the payment to the railway companies operating in the select territory designated by the act, during the fiscal year 1956-57, of the difference occurring on account of the application of the act, between the tariff tolls and normal tolls under approved tariffs (estimated and certified to the Minister of Transport by the Canadian National Railway company and approved by auditors of the said company respecting the eastern lines of the Canadian National Railways and in the case of the other railways by the board of transport commissioners for Canada) on all traffic moved during the calendar year 1956 (chap. 174, R.S.), $11,500,000.

This item with respect to the Maritime Freight Rates Act involves an amount of $11,500,000, and I feel that I should remark briefly on it. A great deal has been said in recent days with respect to freight rate problems in Canada. We had a discussion in the house recently of the various problems that are now coming to the fore with regard to transportation in this large country of ours. Suggestions have been made that a regulatory body would be the answer to our freight rate difficulties. Others have suggested that a new national transportation policy is necessary. I remember reading last year that Mr. Donald Gordon, the president of Canadian National Railways, had suggested in an address in New York city that a complete new look was needed with respect to our freight rate structure in Canada. At present we have the problem of the board of transport commissioners now considering a permanent increase after granting an interim

increase a few months ago. Rather than try to talk in a rambling way about the problems facing the maritimes with respect to their position in the freight rate structure I should like to read part of an editorial from the Fredericton Daily Gleaner of Wednesday, August 8, which just arrived today. I think two paragraphs will be enough to explain the problem that we now have down in the maritimes. The editorial reads as follows:
As far as the Atlantic area is concerned, the freight rate structure is badly out of joint. These four provinces, at the end of the rail lines are wholly dependent on the railways both for buying and marketing products. We require many goods from central Canada, and due to the dense population and heavy purchasing power of Quebec and Ontario, these provinces are our best market outlets.
But the cost of taking our goods to central Canada is almost prohibitive. A series of freight rate increases has hit at the long-haul shipper unfairly. These are horizontal increases, applied by a uniform percentage.
I would ask that the next sentences be noted particularly because they explain our difficulty very clearly.
If a long-haul shipper who pays $20 and a short-haul shipper who pays $10 both have their freight rates increased by, say 50 per cent, the $20-shipper now pays $30 and the $10-shipper $15. The difference between what they pay is now $15 instead of $10.
This merely illustrates the increasing disparity with which the maritimes have found themselves faced as a result of the increases that have taken place since we came under the statutory provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act of 1927. A few days ago the Atlantic premiers met in Fredericton to consider their difficulties. The conference has been referred to here in the house. They examined their problems and tried to get united action with respect to some of the difficulties they saw in our future, and the No. 1 problem was freight rates. They put it in that priority for the future.
The maritime transportation commission has also said it is our No. 1 problem. At this late hour this evening I simply want to say that when the board of transport commissioners is considering these increases they must give more attention to our problems than to
Supply-Transport
those of any other area in Canada. Our problems with respect to freight rates go to the root of our difficulties, economic, geographic and financial, and I seriously suggest that the time has now come when we have to review these provisions that were a help to us and afforded us some consideration many years ago. We have now been put in a very serious competitive position with the central Canadian market on which we in the Atlantic provinces are now so dependent in so many ways.
Item agreed to.
